full_judgment:
Mr. Khademul Islam Chowdury, J :- This Full Bench is constituted to decide the point whether the Government is empowered to extend the period of detention beyond 30 days when the initial order of detention is passed for 30 days by District Magistrate or an Additional 
District Magistrate. 

2. It has been held by different Benches of this court that when the period of detention is specified in any order passed by the District Magistrate or Additional District Magistrate Under 
Section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 the same can not be extended by the Government under Section 3(3) of the said Act inasmuch as Section 3(3) of the said Act empowers Government only to approve an order of detention passed by the District Magistrate or Additional Magistrate for a period beyond 30 days but in deciding writ petition no. 463 of 
2002 their Lordships differed with the aforesaid decision and are of the view that the use of word approved in Section 3(3) of the Act has given the power to the Government to pass an order to the effect that the initial order of detention passed by the District Magistrate or the Additional District Magistrate shall remain in force for a period beyond 30 days and as such it will not be an illegality if the expression 'extension' is used for the word 'approval', because giving approval of the order beyond the period of  30 days will amount to extension of the order and that there will not be any difference in the legal consequence if the Government passes a fresh order of extends the detention period on the basis of the materials before the Government inasmuch as the effect remains the same i.e. the result of either of these two orders will be the same. In view of the aforesaid deference of opinion the matter has been referred to the full bench as per provision 
of Chapter VII of the High Court Rules. 

3. Fact in short relevant for our purpose is that the detenu  challenged the detention order dated 4.12.2001 in writ petition no. 6911 of 2001 in which the rule issued was discharged holding that the order of detention as passed under, Section 3(2) of the Act was valid. 

4. The detention was passed on 4.12.2002 for a period of 30 days. Thereafter the Government vide memo no. 3332 /SHA: MA.: (NIRA-3) dated 27.12.2001 extended the period of detention for 3 months effective from 2.1.2002 under Section 3(3) of the Act. The writ 
petitioner in writ petition no. 463 of 2002 challenged the said extension of the detention period communicated vide memo No. 3332/SA:MA: (NIRA-3) dated 27.12.2001 as being issued without lawful authority inasmuch as the Government is not empowered to give such extension to any detention period passed under section 3(2) of the Act. The said writ petition has been 
heard and disposed of by the Division bench presided over by Mr. Justice Harnidul Haque and the said Bench having differed with the decisions reported in 47 DLR-12, 15 BALD-655 and 18 BLD-165 referred the matter to a full bend'. 

5. Dr. M. Zahir the learned advocate appearing for the petitioner submitted that Section 3(3) of the Special Powers Act does not empower the Government to extend an 'order of etention passed by the District Magistrate or by Additional District Magistrate under Section 3(2) of the said Act and the High Court Division consistently held the same view in the case of Eskander Loskor -Vs.- Bangladesh and others reported in 15 BLD-655 and in the case of Abdus Samad -Vs.- Bangladesh 18 BLD-165. The learned Advocate submitted that the word 'approved' used in Section 3(3) of the Act is applicable only in cases where the detention order passed by District 
Magistrate or Additional District Magistrate, hereinafter referred as to the District Magistrate, is for a period more then 30 days only and no such approval is necessary in cases where the period of detention is for 30 days or less. The learned Advocate submits that if the Government has reasons to keep a detenu under Detention for further period the Government may passed fresh order of detention under Section 3(1) of the Act. In passing order of detention the authority 
must satisfy itself as to the grounds for making such order of detention and that a detention under Special Powers Act, 1974 is not a punishment but is a preventive process to restrain a person from doing a prejudicial Act as defined in .Section 2 of the said Act. The 'satisfaction' required 
must be based on good grounds inasmuch as by such detention the right to liberty of person is curtailed which infringes fundamental right of a citizen. The learned Advocate submitted that the Special Powers Act has provided provisions for extension of the detention period. In elaborating his submissions the learned Advocate took us though Sections 9,10,11,12 and 13 of the Act. Section 9 provides for constitution of a Advisory Board which consists of two members having qualification to act as Judge of the High Court Division and that shows the importance and weight of such Board. This has been done having regard to the fundamental right of the citizen as to right to freedom and libery which can not be curtailed arbitrarily or whimsically. Sections 10 of the Act provides that every detention order passed under the Act should be placed before the Advisory Board for its scrutiny. Section 11 provides the procedure for considering the materials for passing detention order and for giving report or opinion as to the sufficiency of the cause for such detention. Section 12 provides for action under the report of the Advisory Board i.e. if the Advisory Board finds sufficient cause passing for such detention order the Government may con-firm the detention order and continue the detention for such period as it thinks fit and in case the Advisory Board finds no sufficient cause for such detention the Government shall revoke the detention order and cause the person to be released forthwith. The learned Advocate stressing upon Section 12 of the Act submits that sub-Section (1) of the said section 12 empowers the Government to extend the period of detention provided the Advisory Board holds the detention order valid. The learned Advocate submits that in the said sub section the word 'extension' has not been used but the words 'may confirm the detention order and continue the detention' have been used and the word 'con-firm' and the word 'approve' bears the same meaning as per dictionary meaning and that the words 'continue the detention' means 'extension of existing order of detention,.' Thus no period of detention can be ordered to continue for the ther period by the Government unless the Advisory Board on consideration of the materials placed before it and or upon calling for such further information as it deem necessary and affording the detenu an opportunity being heard in person submit its report as required under Section 11 of the Act to be placed before the Government holding the detention order to be valid and as such the Government is also not empowered to approve any detention order beyond 30 days period without placing such detention order before the Advisory Board as required under Section 10 of the Act inasmuch the word 'approval' used in Section 3(3) of the Act does not mean a mechanical process of giving approval by the Government.

6. The learned advocate submitted that the words used in any Section of statute should be given it's ordinary meaning and in interpreting entire statute should be considered in deciding any issue relating thereto. It has been asserted that where the liberty of the citizen is in question the Court will certainly construe the Government orders and actions very strictly and in support of his contention the learned advocate referred to the decision in the case of Bangladesh-Vs.- Dr. Dhiman reported in 47 DLR (AD)-52 and also in the case of Nasima Begum -Vs. - Government of the Peoples Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary Ministry of Home Affairs and others reported in 49 DLR CAD)-102. The learned Advocate submitted that the statutes which encroach on the rights of the subject whether as regard person or property, are subject to strict construction, in sup-port of which the learned advocate placed the case of Yusuf Ali Chowdhury -Vs.-Province of East Pakistan reported in 11 DLR (SC)316 and page 289 of Maxwell on Interpretation of Statutes, 9th Addition, The learned advocate also submitted that the statutes that takes away the rights of subject are to be construed strictly and in case of ambiguity the interpreation of the statutes should be in favour of the subject and is support of his contention he place the decision in the case of Yusuf All Chowdhury -Vs.- East Pakistan reported in 9 DLR(DAC)-674 wherein it has been observed that when word are plain and clear the duty of the Court is to gather the intention of the legislature from the word used in the statutes taking it's plain and ordinary meaning. Placing the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan on a reference by the President reported in 9 DLR(SC)-178 the learned advocate sub-mitted that the rule of construction of a statute is to gather, what the legislature meant, is from the words they have actually expressed and not the consequent would be and whe the words of the statute are in themselves precise and unambiguous no more is necessary them to expound those words in their natural and ordinary sense, and that intention of the legislature ought to be derived from a consideration of the whole enactment in order arrive at a consistent plan. Placing the case of Rashid Ahmed-Vs.- the state the case reported in 21 DLR (SC) 297 the learned advocate relied on the observation of the lordships that-

'As a general rule, it is not permissible for a Court of law to alter the language of a statute for the purpose of supplying a meaning. As observed in Hals bury's Laws of England, volume 
36, page 390, if blunders are found in legislation, they must be corrected by the legislature and it is not function of the Court to repair them. Thus, if the words used by a legislature, in their primary sense, do not mean what the legislature intended then in is for the legislature to amend the statute and not for the Court to attempt the necessary amendment by speculating as to the true intent of the law maker. It is only where the words of a statute are obscure or doubtful or the literal construction would involve the creation of unintended anomalies that a departure from this rule is permissible. Keeping the principle in view, as also the principle that in constitution-al provision conferring a right the Courts ought not to adopt a construction which would unduly restrict that right, for, a constitutional provision is not to be construed 'in any narrow and pedantic sense.' and submitted that the Division Bench presided over by Mr. Justice Hamidul Haque in disposing of the rule has gone beyond the limitation in adopting the meaning of the word approval as contained in Section 3(3) of the Act as 'extension' and thus arrived at an erroneous decision. 

7. The learned advocate further sub-mitted that the bench presided over by Mr. Justice Md. Hamidul Haque in deciding the rule and particularly the authority of the Government to give extension to the period of the detention did not consider the provisions of Sections 9-12 of the Act in that they failed to take notice of the fact that the power of approval of the Government as mentioned in Section 3(3) of the Act is dependent on the ponion of the Advisory Board, which is mandatory in view of Section 10 of the Act, and the opinion of the Advisory Board as contemplated in Section 11 of the Act and the Government is empowered to give extension only when the Advisory Board approves any detention. order as contemplated Section 12(1) of the Act. The learned advocate referring to the judgment under scrutiny submitted that their Lordships erred in not considering the fact that unless specific power or authority is expressly given the same should not be enforced in cases where citizens rights are affected and the same view is consistently upheld by the Superior Courts of the sub-continent. The judgment under scrutiny shows that their Lordships decided the mater on consideration that the authority of approval and the authority to pass fresh order of detention by the Government in fact gives the same result in that by approval the detention period beyond 30 days is legalized which is in fact extension of the detention period beyond 30 days and by passing a fresh order under Section 3(1) of the Act the Government in fact extends the detention period of the detenu passed under Section 3(2) of the Act. 

8. The learned advocate further sub-mitted that their Lordships have also held that the fundamental rights of the detenu if at all has been violated was by the initial order 'passed under Section 3(2) of the Act and not by the subsequent order extending the period of detention which is incorrect inasmuch as their Lordships failed to consider that in case of violation of fundamental rights or curtailing the liberty of citizen, the violation is continuing and no person can be put in detention without due process of law. 

9. Mr. Abdur Razzak Khan the learned Additional Attorney General submitted that Special Powers Act is a special law and the detention given under the provisions of the Act is a preventive measure to restrain a person from doing any prejudicial act as defined in the said Act. The detenu is not an accused and, therefore, in order to pass an order of detention the back ground of the detenu as well as the prevailing condition and circumstance:- are to be taken into consideration and on being satisfied that the person concerned is required to be detained otherwise he is likely to commit a prejudicial Act as defined in Section 2 of the Act i.e. there 
must be some material or information before the authority for forming an opinion as to whether a detention order is necessary to be passed_ In the instant case the detention order passed by the District Magistrate has been found be valid by this Court in deciding writ petition No. 6911 of 
2001 filed by the detenu. There being sufficient ground for detaining the detenu the extension of the period of detention as made by the Government cannot be said to be illegal. The learned Additional Attorney General submits that as the Government has the power to pass a fresh' 
order of detention under Section 3(1) of the Act, there is no reason why the Government cannot extend the period of detention under Section 3(3) of the Act which empowers the Government to 
"approve" the order of detention passed under Section 3(2) of the Act. The learned Advocate referring to the cases reported in 31 DLR(AD)-1 (Mirza Abdul Late case in 40 DLR. (AD)-178, case Sajeza Parvin Bhanu Case 47 DLR (AD)-52 (Dr. Dhiman) Case 47 DLR (AD)-109 (Nasima Begun') case 45 DLR (AD)-89 (Habiba Mahbub) Case 47 DLR (HCD)165 Abdus Samad case, submitted that in all these cases the fact of "extension" of the period of initial detention order was in existence but in none of the cases such extension has been held to be illegal. The learned Attorney General, however, submitted that in case of orders and actions of the Government curtailing the liberty of citizen the courts will certainly consider the same strictly but with leniency in favour of the citizen. The learned advocate then referring to 2(two) cases of the Indian Jurisdiction namely Puranlal Lakhan Pal case reported in AIR 1958(SC)-163 and Deb Shadan case reported AIR 1972 (SC)-924 submitted that those cases also relate to the preventive law as that of our Special Powers Act and in those decisions it has been held that the order of detention need not be placed before the Advisory Board if the detention period is not more then 3 
months which was said to be mandatory period. The learned Additional Attorney General referring to Section 21 of the General clauses Act submitted that the Government has been empowered to amend add alter and modify any order and that the word 'approved' as appearing in Section 3(3) of the Act is synonymous to the word "extension" and that the requirement of "approval" is that the order of detention must be in force. It has been lastly submitted Government being satisfied on the basis of the material/information with it to justify the detention of the detenu and to keep the detenu for further period in detention, the impugned order 
as passed is a valid order and no exception can be taken there against. The learned Additional Attorney General submitted that in order to keep the detenu under detention for further period to restrain him from doing prejudicial act the Government has in the meantime passed fresh order of detention for a period of 60 days under Section 3(1) of the Act and that the case of the detenu has already be sent to the Advisory Board for its opinion. 

10. The Special Powers Act, 1974 briefly the Act amongst others provides for preventive detention of certain person with a view to preventing them from doing prejudicial act as defined in Section 2(f)(i)- (viii) whereby right to liberty of a Citizen has been restricted under a law. 

11. A brief analysis of the related provisions for preventive detention of the Special Powers Act, 1974 is set forth below: Under Section 2, Clause (c) of the Act "detention order" means an order of detention made under Section 3. Provision of Section 3(1), (2) & (3) of the Act relating to the powers to make orders detaining certain persons:-
"(1) The Government may, if satisfied with respect to any person that with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act it is necessary so to do, make an order - 
(a) directing that such person be detained; 
(b) directing him to remove himself from Bangladesh in such manner, before such time and by such route as may be specified in the order: Provided that no order of removal shall be made in respect of any citizen of Bangladesh. 
(2) Any District Magistrate or Additional District Magistrate may, if satisfied with respect to any person that with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act within 
the meaning of Section 2(f)(iii), (iv), (v), (vii) or (viii) it is necessary so to do, make an order directing that such person be detained. 
(3) When any order is made under sub-Section (2), the District Magistrate or the Additional District Magistrate making the order shall forthwith report the fact to the Government 
together with the grounds on which the order has been made and such other particulars as, in his opinion, have a bearing on the matter, and no such order shall remain in force for more than thirty days after the making thereof unless in the meantime it has been approved by the Government." 
(4)    ------ 
(5)    ------ 
Section 9 provides for constitution of the Advisory Board. There are 3 sub-sections in Section 9. Sub-section 1 says that the Government shall "whenever necessary" constitute an Advisory Board. Sub-section 2 provides that the Advisory Board shall consist of 3 persons of whom to shall be persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as judges of the High Court Division and the other shall be person who is a Senior Officer in the service of the Republic. Sub-section 3 provides that the Government shall appoint one of the members of the Advisory Board who is, or has been or is qualified to be appointed as a judge of the High Court Division to be its Chairman. Section 10 states that "every case" where detention order has been made under this Act the Government "shall" place before the Advisory Board constituted under Section 9 the grounds on which the order has been made, and the representation if any made by person affected by the order with-in maximum time limit of 120 days. Section 11 contains the procedure of Advisory Board. The Advisory Board is required to submit its report to the Government within 170 days from the date of detention. It is made clear that the report shall specify, in a separate part thereof, the opinion of the Advisory Board as to whether or not there is sufficient cause for the detention of the person concern. The action upon the report of the Advisory Board is provided in Section 12. Section 12(1) of the Act provides that in any case where the Advisory Board has reported that there is, in its opinion, sufficient cause for the detention of a person, the Government may "confirm" and "continue the detention" of the person "for such period" as "it thinks fit" and that the Advisory Board shall, after affording the person concerned an opportunity of being heard in person, review such detention order, unless revoked earlier, once in every six months from the date of such detention order and the Government shall inform the person concerned of the result of such review. Sub-section (2) of Section. 12 lays down that in any case where an Advisory Board has reported that there is, in its opinion, no sufficient cause for the detention of the person concerned, the Government shall revoke the detention order and cause the person to be released forthwith, 

12. It may be noted that this scheme of the Advisory Board is a constitutional device as enshrined in part III of the Constitution relating to fundamental rights. Article 33(4)-(6) of the Constitution reads: 
"(4) No law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a period exceeding six months unless an Advisory Board consisting of three persons, of whom two shall be persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as, Judges of the Supreme Court and the other shall be a person who is a senior officer in the service of the Republic, has, after affording him an opportunity of being heard in person, reported before the expiration of the said period of six months that there is, in its opinion, sufficient cause for such detention. (5) When any person is detained in pursuance of an order made under any law providing for preventive detention, the authority making the order shall, as soon as may be communicate to such person the grounds on which the order has been made, and shall afford him the earliest opportunity of making a representation against the order: 
Provided that the authority making any such order may refuse to disclose facts which such authority considers to against the public interest to dis-close. 
(6) Parliament may by law pre-scribe the procedure to be followed by an Advisory Board in an inquiry under clause (4)." 

13. The inalienable right of every citizen to enjoy the protection of law and to be treated only in accordance with law and that only in accordance with law as pro-claimed in Article 31 of the Constitution, and that no person shall  deprived of life or personal liberty save in accordance with law as provided under Article 32 of the Constitution are considered to be the most cherished fundamental human rights. Sub Article 33(4) provides safeguard as to arrest and detention. It is the settled principle established by our Appellate Division in long line of judicial decisions that the High Court Division in order to discharge its Constitutional function of judicial review is to make an objective assessment of the materials on which the satisfaction of the detaining authority has been based. 

14. Authorities lay down that the cardinal Rule of interpretation is that a provision of statute which encroached on the liberty of citizen should be construed strictly and that such interpretation of statute or law which preserves fundamental right is to be given rather then which destroys it. The following decisions, referred to by the learned advocate for the petitioner, supports the above Abdul Latif  Mirza Vs. Government of Bangladesh, 31 DLR (AD)-1, Government of East Pakistan Vs. Rowshan Bijaya Showkat All Khan (1966) 18 DLR (SC) 214, Government of West Pakistan Vs. Begum Aga Abdul Karim Shorish Kashmiri (1969) 21 DLR (SC) 1. 

15. Under the Special Powers Act 1974, the mandatory requirement of Section 10 is that the Government shall within 120 days from the date of detention under the Act 1974 place before the Advisory Board constituted under Section 9, the grounds on which the order has been made and the representation, if any, made by the person affected by the order. On perusal of Section lilt appears that no duty is cast upon the Advisory Board to determine for what period any person should be detained but the Advisory Board shall submit its report to the Government within one hundred and seventy days from the date of detention and the board shall specify, in a separate part thereof, its opinion as to whether or not there is sufficient cause for the detention of the person concerned. Form the provision of Section 12 of the Act, it is clear that in any case where the Advisory has reported that there is, in its opinion, sufficient cause for the detention of a person the Government may 'confirm' the detention order and "continue the detention" of the person concerned "for such period" as it thinks fit. It is thus obvious that if the Advisory Board on consideration of the materials placed before it reports that there is no sufficient cause for detention question of according 'approval' and "ordering continuation of the detention under the initial order of detention, by the Government does not arise at all rather law provides for immediate revocation of the detention and release of the detenue. 

16. On perusal of the provisions of Section 3 and Sections 9-12 of the Act it appears that the scheme of the Act is that in every case where initial order for detention of a person for longer period has been made under Section 3(2) of the Act by the District Magistrate or the Additional District Magistrate, the Government shall within 30 days, place the grounds, on which the order has been based and the representation, if any, made by a person affected by the order before the Advisory Board constituted under Section 9 of the Act and the Advisory Board on consideration of the materials placed before it, and calling for further information, as it may deem necessary, from the Government or from the person concerned and after affording the person concerned an opportunity of hearing shall submit its report to the Government, specifying, in a separate part thereof, whether or not there is sufficient cause for the detention of the person concerned. If the Advisory Board reports that the detention is justified, only then the Government will determine the period of detention i.e. whether to give approval to period of detention contained in the detention order passed under Section 3(2) of the Act or to continue the detention for further period. On the other hand if the Advisory Board reports that the detention is not justified then the detained person must be released. The setting up of the Advisory Board is the mechanism to check and control the illegal, unauthorized and arbitrary detention. 

17. In our view "to continue the detention" of person concerned "for such period as it thinks fit" as couched in Section 12(1) presupposes and imply that after receipt of the report of the Advisory Board the Government is to consider and decide as to whether the first or the initial order of detention should be continued i.e. extended for further period, and if yes, then for what period and in case of further extension if so required, must be dependent on fresh report of the Advisory Board. 

18. The dictionary meaning of the word "approve" as found in the Revised and Enlarged 5th Edition of Samsad English Bengali Dictionary is to "confirm". It is clear from Section 12(1) that the Government may "confirm" the detention order and continue the detention of the person concerned where the Advisory Board has reported that there is sufficient cause for the detention. To our perception, having regard to the entire scheme of preventive detention, from reading Sections 3(1)(2) and (3)m 10 and 12 together the word "approved" used in Section 3 under-scores the power of the Government to "confirm" the detention beyond the 30 days i.e. the initial order of detention of the person concerned passed under Section 3(2) of the Act after receipt of the report of the Advisory Board that there is sufficient cause for detention which is consistent and harmonious to the scheme in as much as there is no guide line given in the act as to the procedure for giving such "approval" as contemplated in Section 3(3) of the Act.

19. It appears to us that there is no express provision in the Act for extension of period (s) of any detention under Section 3(1) or 3(3) of the Act. but the words "Government any confirm the detention order and continue the detention of the person concerned for such period as it thinks fit" as appearing in Section 2(1) of the Act leads no to the authority given to the government to extend the period of detention but subject to the report of the Advisory Board as contemplated under Sections-10, 11 and 12 of the Act. Thus we are of the view that the government is the authority to extend the period of detention undergoing by any per-son under Section 3(1) or 3(3) of the Act and such authority of the government is not independent or discretionary but dependent on the report of the Advisory Board otherwise the object and purpose of setting up of Advisory Board will be frustrated and defeated. In this connection the 
intention of the law framers to check the abuse of the law in detaining a person i.e. curtailing the right to liberty and freedom of person guaranteed by the Constitution is clear through the Constitution of an Advisory Board, which consists of two persons out of three are qualified to be judge of the Supreme Court, and that too show the importance and weight of such Advisory Board. 

20. Our above view finds support from the view of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Puran Lal Lakhan Pal Vs. the Union of India reported in AIR 1958 (SC)-163. 

21. To note the background of the case briefly. The detenu Puranlal Lakhan Pal was arrested on July 24th 1956 and taken in custody on the same date under Section 3 of the Preventive Detention Act, 4 of 1950 (with provisions similar to those in the Special Powers Act, 1974) grounds of detention were communicated to the detenu under Section 7. The case of the 
detenu was then sent to the Advisory Board and the said Board having reported that there was in its opinion sufficient cause for detention, the central Government confirmed the detention on 
August 20, 1956 and stated further that the detenu shall continue in detention for 12 months from the date of detention. This order was passed under sub-section 1 of Section 11 of the said Act (corresponding to Section 12 of the Special Powers Act, 1974). Before that date, how-ever the appellant (detenu) moved the Punjab High Court as also the Supreme Court of India, challenging Section 11 as unconstitutional, praying for issuing writ in the nature of writ of Habeas Corpus. 
The Supreme Court dismissed the petition. Before the Punjab High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution the petitioner was permitted to urge an additional ground to the effect that sub Section (1) of Section 11 of the said Act (reference to Advisory Board) is unconsitutional as it 
offended Article 22(4)(a) of the Constitution of India authorizing maximum preventive detention for 3 months (corresponding to Article 33(4) of ours authorizing maximum detention for 6 months). The High Court dismissed the petition where upon the appellant obtained Special leave to appeal. The Supreme observed that the detention of the detenu is of preventive nature and the 
Executive has necessarily to consider whether a person should be detained and the period for which he should be detained. It could not have been the intention to give the power of determining the necessity of detention of a particular person to the Executive and leave to another authority, the Board in this case to say whether the detention should be for three months or more. In the very nature of things the decision as to the period of detention must be of the detaining authority because it is the authority upon which responsibility for detention has been 
placed. The reference to the Advisory Board is only a safeguard to the detenu against Executive vagaries and high handed action and is a machinery devised by the Constitution and the Act to review the decision of the Executive on the basis of representation made by the detenu, if any, 
the grounds of detention and where the order is by an officer the report of such officer as to the sufficiency of cause existing for such detention. It is not a limitation on the Executive's discretion as to the discharge of its duties connected with preventive detention but it is a safeguard against misuse of power. 

22. The Supreme Court of India held that the Government must determine what the period of detention should be, only after the Advisory Board, to which the case is referred, reports that the detention is justified. It is held that it would be some what farcical to provide, that after a man has been detained for 89 days an Advisory Board is to say whether the initial detention was justified on the other hand the determination of the question whether prolonged detention for more then 3 months is justified must necessarily involve the determination of question whether the detention was justified at all and such an interpretation only can give real meaning and effectiveness to the pro-vision, the provision being in the nature of a protection or safeguard. We are in respectful agreement with above view. 

23. We are unable to agree with the view that Government has been conferred power to extend the detention and the line of reasoning that there will be no difference in the legal consequence if the Government passed a fresh order or extends the period of detention on the same material. It appears that the extended period of detention expired on 0104.2002. A fresh order of detention under Section-3(1) of the Act has been issued under memo No. 967 SAA:MA (NIRA-3) dated 28.3.2002 extending the period of detention of the detenu for another 60 days with effect from 1.4.2002 (copy of the memo is annexed to the writ petition as annexure-'D' to the supplementary affidavit sworn by the petitioner on 2.4.2002). It is settled by our Appellate Division that an order of detention must co-exist with the fact of detention. In view of our discussion above we hold that the Government is not empowered to extend the period of detention under sub-Section (3) of Section 3 of the Act and therefore the order extending the initial detention period of the detenue for the period 3 (three) months vide Memo No. 3332/SHA:MA: (NIRA-3) dated 27.12.2001 Annexure-'C' to the Writ. Petition passed by the Government under Section-3(3) of the Act is illegal and without lawfull authority. 

24. On perusal of the order dated 28.3.2002 (Annexure-D) we find that said order has been passed in continuance of the "illegal extension of the detention" dated 27.12.2001 (Annexure-'C'). Suffice it to say that illegal detention is not cured by passing of a subsequent valid order of detention as has been decided by our Appellate Division in the case of Abdul Latif Mirza Vs. Bangladesh reported in 31 DLR (AD)- 1. In the case of the Government of East Pakistan Vs. Rowshan Bijaya Showkat Ali Khan (1966), reported in 18 DLR (SC) 214, Pakistan Supreme Court has held that "an illegal order of detention cannot be continued by a subsequent order of detention ever though the latter is otherwise valid". An illegal detention equally cannot be continued by an independent valid order of detention. 

25. As per the scheme of the Act every order of detention passed under Section 3 of the Act has to be placed before the Advisory Board and only when the Advisory Board makes its report justifying the detention the Government can continue (extend) and fix the period of detention under Sub-Section 1 of Section 12. 

26. In the case of Eskandar Lasker Vs. District Magistrate reported in 47 DLR-12 it is held that the District Magistrate can make an order detaining the detenu with a view prevent him from doing any prejudicial act under Sub-Section (2) of Section 3 for a period beyond 30 days. Such order requires approval by the Government within the 30 days and in the absence of any such approval the order will have force only up to 30 days but once approval is accorded the order will continue. This view was followed in the cases reported 15 DLR-655 and 18 BLD-165: In the Rule referred to us, the Division Bench on consideration of Sub-section 3 of Section 3 of 
the Act, differed with the view held in the above cited cases which held that the Government has no power to extend the period of the detention under Section 3(3) of the Act. 

27. In the instant Rule it is on record that the initial order for detention of the detenu communicated by Memo dated 04.12.2001 has  found to valid in Writ Petition No. 6911 of 2001 filed by the Writ Petitioner. In the instant Rule the order of extension of the initial period of detention of the detenu for further period of 3 (three) months passed by the government under 
Section 3(3) of the Act (Communicated by the Memo No. 3332/SHA:IVIA:(NIRA-3) dated 27.12.2001 Annexure-'C' to the Writ Petition) has been challenged. No materials could be placed before us that to show that the order passed under Section 3(3) of the Act is based on a report of an Advisory Board Constituted under Section-3 and submitted complying with the provisions 
of Section 10, 11 and 12 of the Act. Further we are of the view that orders relating to detention beyond 30 days passed under Section 3(2) approval is dependent on the report of the Advisory 
Board in terms of Sections 11 and 12 of the Act and the government is empowered to extend the period of detention only under Section 12(1) of the Act and that too on the basis of the report of the Advisory Board. 

28. The continuation of the detention of the detenu after expiry of the initial order of detention for 30 (thirty) days is, therefore violative of Article 31 and 32 of the Constitution and as such we find the instant writ petition on this score is quite maintainable. The learned Additional Attorney General did not raise the ground of maintainability which we think quite 
justifiably. 

29. In view of the above we are of the opinion that the impugned order of extension of the period of detention passed by the government is illegal and the detenu has been held in custody illegally in unlawful manner. Since the impugned order of extension of the detention period is found to be illegal, the fresh order of detention of the detenu passed by the 
Government under Section 3(1) of the Act giving continuity to the earlier illegal order is bad in law and can't be maintained. 

30. Accordingly the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The Government has not been empowered under Section 3(3) of the Special Powers Act to extend the period of detention passed by the District Magistrate  or Additional District Magistrate under 
Section 3(2) of the Act which however it can do under Section 12 of the said Act subject to report of the Advisory Board. Thus we find that the detenu Alhaj Mokbul Hossain has been held in detention without any lawful authority and in an unlawful' manner. Hence the detenu Al-haj Mokbul Hossain, son of late Mohammad Ali, of 12/1; Tajmahal Road, Block-C, Mohamrnadpur, District-Dhaka, now detained in Dhaka Central Jail, be set at liberty immediately if not wanted in any other case. 

31. The prayer for stay operation of the judgment as made by Mr. Zaman Akhtar, the learned Assistant Attorney General is refused,

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Mohammad Abdur Rashid, J: This Rule was issued at the instance of defendant No. 1 against judgment and decree dated 09.09.2002 passed by the Additional District Judge. Third Court at Rangpur in other Appeal No. 71 of 2000 reversing those dated 30.04.2000 passed by Subordinate Judge, Court No. 1 at Rangpur and in decreeing the suit. 

2. Plaintiffs instituted the suit for declaration that the order of lease dated 16.08.1995 granted by defendant no. 2 in favour of defendant no. 1 in respect of Schedule 'Ka' land was illegal and ineffective as was obtained by defendant No. 1 by practicing fraud; and that the plaintiffs were entitled to get lease of said land. 

3 Plaint case in short is that the plaintiffs were owners in possession by way of purchase from co-sharers. A part of the suit land was acquired by the government and handed over to the Roads and Highways Department for construction of road. After the construction of the road the suit land remained unused. The plaintiffs were co-owners in possession with said Department. Plaintiffs required the suit land as an access to their land as they have got no other pathway. 

4. Further case of the plaintiffs is that the suit land was leased out to defendant no. 1 without holding any local enquiry or following the Rules issued by the Government. Lease devalued the land of plaintiffs and created obstruction to the construction of factory in the land of plaintiffs. If defendant established a petrol pump in the suit land that might catch fire, which would be hazardous to the entire locality. 

5. Defendant no. 1 and defendants No. 2 to 4 contested the suit by filing two sets of written statement. Case of defendant No. 1 in brief, is that the suit was bad for want of cause of action and the relief prayed for was barred under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as they got no right to sue. 

6. His further case is that the suit land remained unused in possession of the Department of Roads and Highways. On his prayer for lease of the suit land for setting up a petrol pump, the concerned authority held proper inquiry and following the rules and all formalities granted him lease. He also obtained necessary license for the pump. The plaintiffs have got access to the land without going through the suit land. Besides, there was an old road adjacent to the land of plaintiffs. 

7. By filing a separate written statement the defendant No. 2 to 4 supported the case of defendant No.1 In their written statement, it is stated that after conclusion of the acquisition, he land was handed over to the Roads and Highways Department for construction of a road. After holding necessary inquiry and observing all formalities lease was granted to defendant No. 1 for establishing of a petrol pump. The plaintiffs had pathway for ingress and egress to their land. 

8. On the pleadings of the parties, different issues settled include whether the suit was maintainable in the form and manner; whether the plaintiffs have got any cause of action; whether the order of lease granted in favour of defendant No. 1 was illegal and or void; or whether the plaintiffs got any rights to get the lease. 

9. Plaintiffs examined 4 witnesses including plaintiff No. 2 and the documents adduced by them were marked as Exhibit 1 to 5 while defendant No. 1 examined 3 witnesses including him and defendant No. 2 to 4 one. The documents of the defendants were marked as Exhibit 'Ka'. to 'Umma'. 'Cha' series, 'Ccha' to Nio' and 'Ks 1"Kha-1"Ga-1. 

10. On consideration of the evidence, oral or documentary the trial Court dismissed the suit.

11. On appeal therefrom at the instance of plaintiffs, the appeal was however allowed and the suit was decreed by impugned judgment and decree. 

12. Mr. Quiyum Khan, the learned advocate for the petitioner submits that impugned judgment is not a proper judgment of reversal in that it neither reversed the material findings nor it adverted to the reasons of the trial Court given for its findings. 

13. He submits that the appellate court erred in law as well as on facts to find that the plaintiffs were in joint possession in the suit land. 
He submits that the suit as framed is not maintainable for a decree of declaration simplicitor without a consequential relief.
Next, he submits that having never prayed for lease, the plaintiffs could not validly challenge the lease granted to defendant No. 1 on the grounds of non-following the Rules. Lastly, he submits that the plaintiffs have got no locus standi to sue for a decree as prayed for in the suit land. 

14. Opposing the Rule, Mr. Rabi Sankar Chakrabarty, the learned advocate for the opposite parties submits that the defendant no. 1 having failed to prove that the lease was granted in accordance with the law, the Court of Appeal below rightly set aside the decree of the trial court, allowed the appeal and decreed the suit. 

15. He further submits that on consideration of the evidence on record, the Appellate Court found that the plaintiffs as co-owners were holding land contiguous to the land leased out and as such, they were entitled to get the lease and that the defendant no. 2 to 4 illegally granted lease to defendant No. 1 in violation of the rules framed by the Government and upon such findings, the appellate Court did not commit any error in decreeing the suit. 

16. We have perused the records and heard the learned advocates. 

17. The facts are not disputed that the suit land along with other land was originally acquired by the government and handed over to the Roads Highways Department for construction of a road. After the construction of said road, the spit land remained unused. 
Akram Hossain & Ors. 11 BLT (HCD)2003  On or about 11.12.1994, the defendant applied for lease of the suit land for setting up a petrol pump and by order dated 16.081995 defendant no 2 granted lease to defendant No.1 

18. On or about 17.09.1997 the suit was instituted for a decree of declarations that the lease granted to defendant no. 1 was illegal and that the plaintiffs were instituted the suit mainly on the grounds that they were co-owners with the Roads and Highways Department; that they were holding land contiguous to the suit land and that they required the suit land for ingress and egress to their land. Opposite party No. 1 and 2 purchased the land of said plaintiffs by a registered deed dated 12.10.1997 and they got themselves substituted in place of original plaintiffs Md. Joynal Adedin and others by deleting their names by order dated 02.03.1998. 

19. Opposite party No. 1 and 2 adopted the plaint toto. Further case of the plaintiffs is that they as co-owners were holding land contiguous to the suit land. They require the suit land since they have got no other pathway except the suit land for access to their land. Without holding any local enquiry and without following the rules framed by the Government, the lease was granted to defendant No. 1. 
20. To prove the case, the plaintiffs examined 4 witnesses and adduced documents Exhibit 1 to 5. 

21. Trail Court came to finding that plaintiff failed to prove that they had got no road for going to their land except the suit land. Plaintiffs have got a pathway by the south of their land. Secondly, the trial court found that the case of plaintiffs that without holding any local inquiry lease was granted was disproved by Exhibit-1' adduced by the plaintiffs. Thirdly, trail Court found that plaintiffs failed to prove that lease was obtained by fraud and collusion and that the plaintiffs also failed to prove their rights to the decree prayed for and they have right to sue, Such finding appear to be based on consideration of the evidence both oral and documentary on record. 

22. The Court of Appeal below on the other hand appears to have set aside some of findings of trial Court and held that the plaintiffs were co-owners with the Roads and Highways Department and entitled to get lease as such owners holding land contiguous to the suit land in view of the rules dated 21.04.1991 that the authority granted lease violating the rules; and that the plaintiffs got right to sue against the illegal lease. Upon such findings, it set aside the judgment of the trial Court and decreed the suit. 

23. It is now well settled, after completion of acquisition, the acquired land vests in the Government free from all encumbrances. On vesting, all incidents of joint ownership, if any, are severed. When such land is handed over to the requiring body such body possesses the land absolutely against the whole world. No one could in Law be said to be a co-owner in possession with such requiring body. In view of such legal position, the court of Appeal below misconceived the whole case and fell in serious error in holding that the plaintiffs were co-owners in possession with the Roads and Highways Department and as such owners holding land contiguous to the suit land were entitled to get lease. 

24. Secondly, admittedly the present plaintiffs or original plaintiffs never ever prayed for lease of the suit land. Had they applied for lease on such ground of holding land contiguous to the land leased out, which is based on the right of priority, they might have enforced such right against other claimants, in accordance with the rules. But in the suit brought they are not entitled to raise violation of the rules on such rights. The Court of Appeal below again misconceived the 
scope of inquiry on such point as well. It dwelled upon unnecessary exercise to see whether the lease was granted in accordance with the Rules and Regulations based on such rights. 

25. After the lease was granted which the trial court correctly found validly, the plaintiffs have got no right under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act to challenge such lease just on the ground that they hold land contiguous to the land leased out and such a suit definitely hits the provision of aforesaid section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The Court of Appeal also missed such an important point. 

26. We find, without consideration of the evidence on record oral or documentary Court of Appeal below set aside some of he finding of the trail court on existence of a pathway etc. which must be ignored. Moreover, existence of pathway etc could not be a valid consideration in such suit. 

27. The defendants by adducing voluminous documents proved as found by the trial court that defendant no. 2 granted lease to defendant no. 1 by following the rules and holding proper inquiry. In the absence of any findings on collusion, abuse of public power, fraud and or mala fide the court of Appeal below most illegally decreed the suit. 

28. In the above view of the matter, the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court cannot be sustained in law.

 29. In the result, the Rule is made absolute with cost Impugned Judgment and decree are set aside and those of the trail Court are restored. The suit is hereby dismissed. 

30. The order directing the parties to maintain status quo as was passed at the time issue of the Rule on 23.11.2002 is hereby recalled and vacated.

 Send down the records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. A. B. M. Khairul Haque, J: This is an application under Section 43 of the Companies Act, 1994, praying for rectification of share register of Al-Rajhi Hospital (Pvt) Limited, the Company. 

2. It is stated in the petition that in the meeting of the Board of Directors of the respondent company held on 17th May, 2002, the respondents no. 17 along with his allies allotted 13,500 shares in favour of the respondent No. 2 to 16 who are outsider without offering any shares either to the petitioner or to any of the existing share holders that although the petitioner has the right to offer of allotment of shares and was waiting for the offer but he was not allowed to participate and has been deprived by the respondent no. 17 from his legal right of allotment and also purchase of the shares of respondent nos. 15 and 16. 

3. In this matter, three affidavits-in-opposition were filed, one on behalf of the respondent-company and the respondents no 17, the Chairman of the Company, another one on behalf of the respondent-company represented by Dr. Ruhul Amin, the Managing Director of the Company and the third one was filed on behalf of Dr. A. S. M. Didarul Alam, the respondents no. 4. 

4. In the affidavit-in-opposition sworn by the respondent no. 17, the Chairman of the respondent-company, it is contended inter alia, that since the respondent company was in a constant threat of eviction from its earlier premises, it was resolved in its Board Meeting held on 11th May, 2001 (Annexue-5) to purchase a premises at a nearby newly constructed building, namely, Concord Centre Point, that in order to raise the funds of Tk. 3.00 crore to purchase the said Concord premises, the Boards of Directors resolved in its meetings held on 5th October, 2001 which continued to 6th October, 2001 by allotment of new shares to the existing share-holders but their non participation within 30th October, 2001 would be taken as their no objection to allot in favour of the outsiders Accordingly, a memo dated 9th October, 2001 under the signature of respondent no. 17 and Dr. Ruhul Amin was circulated amongst all the share-holders in pursuance to the resolutions of the Board meeting held on 5th and 6th October, 2001 to deposit their call money within 17th October, 2001 so that the first installment could be paid in time to Concord. In response to he said memo, seven existing share-holders gave their partial payments. Thereafter the respondents nos. 2 to 16 were invited to participate and they on various dates paid in total Tk. 1,35,00,000/- in favour of the respondent company and the receipts were duly issued on behalf of the company by the respondents no. 17, Dr. Ruhul Amin and Dr. Gafoor. In due course, payment of Tk. 1,87,22,269/- was made in installments till 07.07.2002 in favour of Concord towards purchase of 8467 squire feet of premises by two deeds of agreements dated 15th June and 7th July, 2002. In reply to the allegations of the petitioner made in para 8 and 9 of the petition it is stated that the meeting of the Board of Directors held on 17th May, 2002 was in pursuance to the notice issued on 14th May, 2002, under the signatures of both the respondent no 17 and Dr. Ruhul Amin, in order to approve transfer of shares and allotment of new shares and the copes of the said notice, under the signature of Dr. Ruhul Amin, were also circulated to the respondent nos. 2 to 16 to be present in the said meeting as observers. In the said affidavit-in-opposition, the allegations made in the petition was denied and it is contended that the petitioner purposely without making Dr. Ruhul Amin, his brother-in-law, a party in the petition, was shown him in the cause- title of the petition, as representing the respondent company as its Managing Director, in order to facilitate supporting the petition although he was never so authorized by the Board of Directors to represent the respondent company. It is further contended that the pre-emptive right of the existing share-holders was respected and the allotment of shares were made to new share-holders bona fide in the interest of the company in order to purchase a new valuable one.

5. A counter affidavit has been filed on behalf of the petitioner on 2nd April 2003. In the counter affidavit it is alleged on behalf of the petitioner that no Board Meeting was held on 25th January 2003, since without issuing a notice to the Managing Director, no such meeting can be held. Besides, the allegation of collusion of the petitioner with Dr. Ruhul Amin has been specifically denied. 

6. A separate affidavit-in-opposition was sworn by Dr. Ruhul Amin on 3rd April, 2003 as the Managing Director of the respondent-company. 

7. 22. I have heard the learned advocates and examined Section 155 of the Companies Act, Section 155 reads as follows. 
"155 Further issue of capital — (1) where the directors decided to increase the subscribed capital of the company by issue of further shares within limit of the authorized capital — 
(a) Such further shares shall be offered to the members in proportion as nearly as circumstances admit, to the capital paid up on the existing share held by such member irrespective of class, at the date of the offer. 
(b) Such offer shall be made by notice specifying the member of shares offered and specifying the time limit, not being less than fifteen days from the date of the offer, within which the offer if not accepted, will be deemed to have been declined. 

(c) After the expiry of the time specified in the notice aforesaid or on receipt of earlier intimation from the members to whom such notice is given that he declines to accept the shares offered, the directors may dispose of the same in such manner as they may think most beneficial to the company.
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), the further shares aforesaid may be offered to any person whether or not those person include the persons referred to in clause (a) of that sub-section in any manner whatsoever, (the underlinings are mine) 

23. A plain reading of the above provision shows that the rights of a member of a company as given in sub section I has been withdrawn in sub section 2. Sub section 2 made the obligations of the company to offer its further shares to its members unless declined, virtually meaningless when the said provision authorizes offer of further shares to any person and not restricted to the members of the company as stipulated under clause (a) to sub section 1 This contradictory nature of the two sub-sections in Section 155 is too obvious to be missed or ignored. 

24. The contention of Dr. Zahir that sub section 2 becomes effective only when the persons mentioned in Sub-Section 1 fails to accept the offer of the shares is too far fetched and not correct. The Court will not read anything in an Act of Parliament which is not there as in the following words of words of Lord Atkin in the case of Naayana Swami Vs. Emperor AIR 1939 PC 47. 
"---- in truth when the meaning of words is palin it is not duty of the Courts ty busy themselves with supposed intentions." 
It is true and I agree with the opinion of both the learned Advocates that this provision ought not to have been made applicable in case of further issue, of shares of a private limited company, as recommended in the Report of the Company Law Reforms Committee but a Court of Law cannot legislate, it can only hold and explain what the law is. In this connection it will be worthwhile to quote Lord Loreburn. L. C. in the case of Vickers. sons of Maxim Limited Vs. Evans 1910 AC 444: 
My Lords, this appeal may serve to remind us of a truth sometimes forgotten, that this House sitting judicially does not sit for the purpose of hearing appeal against Acts of Parliament, or of providing by judicial construction what ought to be an Act, but simply of construing what the Act says. We are considering hare not what the Act ought to have said, but what it does say;  Although under sub-section 2 of Section 155, further shares of a company may be offered to any person but such discretion cannot be arbitrary or absolute, rather, the company in such matters, is guided by its Articles of Association, An Article in this connection had been defined in clause (a) under Section 2(1) as follows: 
"(a) "articles" means the articles of association of a company including, so far as they apply to the company the regulations contained in Schedule 1 to this Act: Provided that the articles of association of a company framed under any law relating to companies at any time in force before the commencement of this Act shall, so far as they are not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, be deemed to be articles of association of that company framed in accordance with the provisions of the Act."
The Legal effect of memorandum and articles under Section 22 is as follows: 
"22. Effect of memorandum and articles. - (1) The memorandum and articles shall when registered bind the company and the members thereof to the same extent as if they respectively had been signed by each member and contained a covenant on the part of each member his heirs and legal representatives to observe all the provisions of the memorandum and of the articles subject to the provisions of this Act.
 (2)   ------ 
 In the instant case, Article-7 of he Articles of Association of the respondent-company reads as follows: 
"7. The shares shall be under control of the Directors. The shares to be issued will first be offered to the existing members of the Company is proportion to their initial holding of shares, if any one declines in writing to take any share to the Directors, the refuse shares will then be offered to the rest of the members in same proportion, in case none of the existing members are willing to subscribe the shares then the same will be offered to person other than initial subscribers on terms most beneficial of the Company." 
On a plain reading of Article-7 would show that it does not come into conflict with Section 155 of the Companies Act or any other provision, rather, it provides the guideline as to whom and in what manner the further issue of shares, if offered under sub section 2, would be made. 
In this connection, it may be noted that making of the provisions in the Act subject to the provisions in the articles, as provided in sub section 2 of Section 85 as argued by Mr. Rafiqui-ul-Huq was necessary because the provisions made under sub section 1 shall have effect notwithstanding any provisions made in the articles of Association of a company. 

25, As such, the contention of Mr. Rafiql-ul-Huq, Senior Advocate that the provisions made in the articles of the company shall have no effect unless specifically provided in the Act itself is not correct, rather, the articles will be applicable unless it is inconsistent with any of the provisions of the Act or is made inapplicable by a specific provision as in the case of sub section 1 of Section 85. 

26. Under such circumstances, Article-7 of the Articles of Association of the respondent-company remains valid and its provisions are applicable inspite of repeal of the earlier Act of 1913 and applicability of sub section 2 of Section 155 of the Companies Act, 1994.

At least no evidence was led in that respect either by the petitioner or on behalf of Dr. Ruhul Amin.
