Vs.
Abdur Rob Talukdar ----- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
Ranadhir Sen J: This Rule, at the instance of the plaintiff, is directed against an order of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge restoring under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a proceeding under Order IX rule 13 of the Code which was dismissed for default.

2. The plaintiff filed Money Suit No. 2 of 1966 for recovery of a certain sum of money. The defendant appeared and filed a written statement to contest the suit. The suit was how-ever, decreed ex-parte on 22-5-72. The defendant filed an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex-parte decree. Miscellaneous Case No. 63 of 1972 was started on the said application. This case was fixed for hearing on 31-1-73. That was a Hartal day. The defendant was also suffering from acute dysentery and an application for adjournment was filed on his behalf by the learned Advocate for the defendant. The application was not moved and was rejected. Consequently, Misc. Case No. 63 of 1972 was dismissed for default. The defendant came to know about the order of dismissal on 1-2-73. He filed an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 151 of the Code for restoration of Misc. Case No. 63 of 1972.

3. The plaintiff filed a written objection contending, inter alia, that the application was not maintainable. According to him the defendant intentionally defaulted in appearing before the Court on 31-1-73. The fact of "Hartal" was also denied. There was means of communication and the defendant could have attended the court if he had intended to do so.

4. On these facts Misc. Case No. 8 of 1973 came up for hearing before the learned Subordinate Judge who, on consideration of the relevant facts and evidence, allowed the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. According to the Court below, the application was maintainable under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. On assessment of the evidence, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge accepted the defendant petitioner's case and relied upon the evidence of PWs 2 and 3, who, according to him, were disinterested witnesses. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge came to a finding that the defendant was prevented by a sufficient cause from appearing before the Court on 31-1-73.

5. This Rule was obtained by the plain tiff on the contentions that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge erred in the exercise of jurisdiction and acted illegally and with material irregularity in the exercise of jurisdiction in applying section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the face of clear and specific provision in the Code itself. It has been further contended by Mr. Habibur Rahman Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff petitioner that an order of dismissal for default of an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure is appealable under Order XLIII, rule 1(d) of the Code.

6. Mr Mujibur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant, contends that section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies and the learned Sub-ordinate Judge acted within his jurisdiction in applying the said provisions, in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. According to Mr. Mahibur Rahman, Order XLIII, rule 1(d) contemplates an appeal against the judgment and order of a contested matter of rejection on merits of an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. An order of dismissal for default does not come within the scope of Order XLIII, rule 1(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Mujibur Rahman contends that there is a difference between the words rejected and 'dismissed.' In support of his contention. Mr. Mujibur Rahman has relied on the case of Md. Hashim Khan vs Major Fazal Elahi Kim reported in PLD 1959 Quetta 1. In this decision the learned Single Judge has made out a distinction between the words 'rejected' and 'dismissed'. The word 'rejected' implies an order on merits while the word 'dismissed' implies an order parsed not on merits, but on account of non-appearance of a party. This decision also lays down that section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure should be called in aid when justness of the cause is recognised. The aforesaid views were noticed with agreement in the case of Ahmed Ali vs Registrar, Co-operative Societies, PLD 1971 Karachi 182. In this case, it has been held that in consonance with the principles laid down in section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a second application under Order IX, rule 13 may be filed and in case of dismissal for default of an application under Order IX, rule 13, section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies. The learned Judges noticed some of the decisions resting on the question. The case of Md Hashim Khan Vs Major Pawl Elahi Khan (supra) was noticed. The decision of Solaiman, J, in the case of Ganesh Prased vs Bhagelu Ram, AIR 1925 Allahabad 773 and the case of Nandalal vs Jetharam, AIR 1929 Lahore 878 along with some other decisions were considered. The learned Judges also noticed the case of Thakur Prasad vs Shaikh Fakirulla (1849) 22 IA 44 and the case of Sarat Krishana Bose vs. Biseswar Mitra Anil, AIR Cal. 534 and also the Allahabad decision in the case of Pitambar Lal vs Dodi Singh, ILR 46 Allahabad 319. The case of Saraju Prasad vs Sitaram ILR 10 Allahabad 7 was also noticed. The learned Judges preferred the view that in the absence of express statutory bar, section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was applicable. The learned Judges, on consideration of the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, held:—

“......a second application under Order IX for restoration of a previously dismissed application under the same provision would lie, either under Order IX itself or under section 151 CPC and absence in the Limitation Act of express provision for period of limitation for such applications should not stand as a bar to deprive a party of this remedy which is not expressly prohibited by the Code of Civil Procedure or by any other statute."

As against the aforesaid contentions and the authorities Mr Habibur Rahman Khan has relied upon the case of Abdur Rahman Miaji vs Abdul Wadud Mia, 2 PLD (Dacca) 287. Mr Khan contends that the principle laid down by Ibrahim, J. in the said case has been consistency followed by the Dacca High Court and this Court Elaborating the principle laid down in the said case, Mr Khan has referred to the case of Bajit Lal Pathak vs Maharajadhiraj Sir Rameshwar Sing Bahadhur, 7 ILR Pat. 333. The distinction sought to be made out in the Quetta case has been answered in the case of Abdur Rahman Miji. The expression "rejecting an application" has the same meaning as dismissing an application for default. Order XLIII, rule 1(d), CPC speaks of rejecting an application. It does not disclose whether on merits or for default. 'Rejection' has a comprehensive connotation to include dismissal for default Ibrahim, J accordingly held that the distinction is without a difference. On this question, the case of Kumud Kumar Bose vs Hari Mohan Samaddar, 21 CLI 628 come up for consideration where Mukherjee, J, expressed himself in the following terms:

"The order assailed by way of appeal was& an order under rule, 13 of Order IX, it was immaterial that the application to set-aside the ex-parte decree had been dis-missed, not on merits, but for default.

This decision was followed by the Patna High Court in the case of Mufti Reasuddin vs Lila Maheshanand, ILT 8 Pat. 533.

7. Mr Habibur Rahman Khan, has referred to the case of Mahabar Shaha vs Shamat Ali and others 18 DLR (Dacca) 473 MR Khan, J, held that:

"The inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure being the residuary power of a Court cannot be invoked unless the Court has exhausted its powers under the specific provisions of that Code, nor can it be invoked where the exercise of that power would be contrary to some express provision of the Code or defeat any provision thereof the inherent power is intended to exceptional cases and is not intended to enable the Court to ignore the provisions of law which govern procedure."

In the case of Pujari Chatur Bhuj Das vs Saiyeda Jobeda Begum, 22 DLR (Dacca) 383, Maksum-ul-Hakim, J on a consideration of a large number of cases including the case of Abdur Rahman Miji (Supra) held that: —

"A proceeding under section 151, Civil Procedure Code cannot be taken when there are other remedies available for securing the redress. The inherent power conferred on the court under section 151, Civil Procedure Code should only be resorted to in a case where there is no other provision or procedure for providing redress or rectifying a clear injustice. It is never an alternative mode for securing relief."

In the case of Suriya Begum vs Alimulla Mallik, (1972) 24 DLR (Dacca) 133, Nurul Islam, J, expressed himself in the following terms-:

"In exercising inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure the principle that where there is alternative remedy the said inherent power should not be exercised by the court and the benefit of said inherent powers under the residuary provision of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure should not be made available to any party who, in fact, has an alternative remedy in a case. The provision of section 151 should be taken recourse to only when where is likelihood of the abuse of process and also for ends of justice."

In the case of Ch. Mohd. Afazal vs MI Sarder Begum, AIR 1949 Lahore 69 Cornelius, J (as his Lordship then was) observed in the following terms:-

"It is an error to suppose that Section 151 confers any new power on the courts. The inherent powers to act on debit justice, and to prevent abuse of process existed before the Code became law. Since the Code contains detailed and express procedural provision to cover nearly every contingency which might arise in the exercise of civil Jurisdictions the maxim 'expresser uniusest axclusio alterius" might have been invoked to support the argument that the Courts could exercise no power which was not expressly given by the Code. This inference is avoided by the enactment of S. 151, Civil PC but only to the extent specified."

In the case of SM Yousuf and another vs Khondker Hafizur Rahman 26 DLR 124; a Division Bench of this Court observed:—

"These powers, contemplated in section 151 of CP Code are intended to supplement, the other provisions of the Code, as a Legislature cannot foresee and provide for every eventually which may occur, but they are not for the purpose of evading or ignoring the express provisions of the law or for inventing a new "procedure according to the individual inclination of a particular Judge. Under the cover of these powers, a court cannot override the express provisions of the law applicable to a particular case. These powers cannot be invoked in a case which is fully covered by a specific provision in the Code, or, where there is a positive prohibition regarding a particular act or order or where there is an alternative remedy." In the case of Rajendra Shirali vs Mahadev Shirali 27 DLR 232 it has been held that the Court is not powerless in appropriate case to rectify its own mistake or the mistake of an officer of the court under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Similar view appears to have been expressed in the case of Muhammad Jamil & Co. Hyderabad vs AM Wazir Ali, 1968 (SC) MR 1283(2). Sattar, J held that the court may apply the provision of section 151 for rectifying its mistake.

In the case of Mannujan Bagum vs A Samad Molla, 29 DLR (SC) 282 their Lordships observed:—

"It is no doubt correct that when a court wants to stay the proceeding in execution of a decree the validity of which is under investigation in an independent suit instituted in a court of coordinate jurisdiction, it can do so only by restraining the decree-holder, if he is a party before it, by means of temporary injunction in exercise of its inherent powers under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as the provisions of Order 39 of the Code do not generally apply in terms of such a case. Since such an action can be taken in exercise of its inherent power, the court have to be satisfied about the justice of the case, namely, that the general conditions for granting temporary injunction as have been laid down by the judicial authorities are in existence."

In the case of Punjab All Pramanik vs Md  Mokarrant Hossain 29 DLR (SC) 185 their Lordships considered a large number of decisions and expressed themselves in the following terms:—

"It appears to us that the preponderant judicial view which emerges out of the authorities referred to above and with which we find ourselves in agreement, is that the Court should not presume the exercise of inherent power to do that for which specific provision has been made by a statute and should not invest itself with such jurisdiction for the purpose of getting round the express provisions of the law. Unintentional or inadvertent mistake of a court causing some injustice to a party, however stands on a different footing and in the case of such a mistake, the exercise of inherent power of a court is not subject to these limitations on its exercise which have been set down by the judicial authorities noticed above."

8. Mr Mujibur Rahman has referred to the case of Sarabeswar Mondal vs Fakirchand Sarkar 14 DLR 256 in support of his analogical contention that section 151 applies in a case where an application under Order IX, rule, 13 CPC was allowed ex-parte. This case stands on a different footing.

9. An alternative contention, as raised by Mr. Mujibur Rahman, is that assuming an appeal was maintainable tinder Order XLIII, rule 1(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, but there was no material in support of the case of defaulter, namely, the defendant petitioner in the case under Order IX rule 13 disclosing the grounds for default or making out a case of sufficient cause. True, evidently there is no material, but the Code of Civil Procedure contains adequate provisions to meet such a contingency. The powers of the appellate Court have been well defined and the appellate Court, in appropriate cases, may record evidence to decide a matter finally. Therefore, the contention of Mr Mujibur Rahman does not seen to stand on a sound footing.

<u>10. On a scrutiny of the decisions cited by the learned Advocates it appears that the case of, Abdul Rahman Miji vs Abdul Wadud Min (Supra) was not noticed in the two cases of West Pakistan referred to and relied upon by Mr. Mujibur Rahman. The decision in the case of Abdur Rahman Miji stands on the strength of a number of cases well reasoned. The distinction sought to be made between the word 'rejected' and the word 'dismissed' appears to be a distinction without a difference. The words 'rejected' struck off 'closed' recorded' and 'dismissed' have similar import, but differently used with reference to the facts and circumstances of each case and there is no distinction between them in substance. We are in respectful agreement with the opinion of Ibrahim, J in the case of Abdur Rahman Miji (supra). In our view, a defaulter whose application under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been dismissed for default has a lawful remedy in an appeal under Order XLIII, rule 1(d). The expression 'rejected' is wide enough to include a dismissal for default under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Accordingly, we hold that such an order is appeal able. Since the statute provides remedy to the aggrieved person whose application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been dismissed for default, section 151 of the Code has no application. But there may be exceptional circumstances. Where the default was due to the mistake of the officer of the Court or the Court itself, the aggrieved person may avail of the provisions of section 151 in appropriate cases. This view finds support in the case of Muhammad Jamil & CI, Hyderabad vs AM Wazir Ali 1968 SC MR 283. (Supra). We are not inclined to extend the scope of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the way done in the case of Ahmed All vs Registrar, Co-operative Societies, PLD 1971 Karachi 182. We have noticed the hypothesis in the approach, but with great respect, do not subscribe to the views taken therein.</u>

<u>For the reasons stated above, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and order of the learned sub-ordinate Judge restoring the Misc. Case No. 63 of 1972 by allowing the Misc. Case No. 8 of 1973 are set-aside. Having regard to the circumstances of the case, we make no order as to costs.</u>

End.

Vs.

full_judgment:
Syed Md. Ziaul Karim, J: By this appeal, the plaintiff appellant has challenged the legality and propriety of the judgment and decree dated 21-10-2014 passed by learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka, rejecting the plaint of Money Suit no. 35 of 2012 under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure (briefly as the Code).

2. Material facts leading to this appeal are that on 28-08-2012 the appellant as plaintiff instituted Money Suit no. 35 of 2012 in the Fifth Court of Joint District Judge, ,Dhaka impleading the respondents as defendants for realization of money for Tk. 1,72,22,376/- from the defendants. The relieves claimed in the suit reads as hereunder:

(a) To pass a money decree against defendant and in favour of the plaintiff for Tk.1,72,22,376/- (one crore seventy two lacs twenty two thousand three hundred seventy six) only;

(b) Interest at the rate up to the date of realization to be paid within the time to be specified by the learned Court;

(c) To pass a decree for the entire cost of the suit, and/or (d) For such further and other relief as this learned Court may deems fit and proper in the circumstances of the case and to which the plaintiffs is entitled in law, equity and justice.

3. In suit, on 06-11-2012 defendants filed an application under Order VII Rule 11. of the Code stating that the suit is barred under law.

4. The plaintiff also filed written objection against such application.

5. After hearing the learned Judge by the impugned judgment and decree dated 21-10-2014 rejected the plaint of the suit under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code, on the ground that the suit is barred under Section 7 of the Arbitration Act.

6. Feeling aggrieved the plaintiff as appellant preferred the instant appeal.

7. The learned Advocate appearing for the appellant seeks to impeach the impugned judgment and decree on there fold arguments:

Firstly: The defendants were entrusted to carry certain quantum of cable wire from Chittagong to Dhaka but in course of transportation it was found that there was a shortage of wire thereby the plaintiff instituted the instant suit.

Secondly:  The plaint clearly disclosed the cause of action and from plain reading of the plaint it appears that there is no such statement that the suit is barred under law so the plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code.

Third and lastly:  The learned Judge of the Court below without considering the settle principle of law rejected the plaint and dismissed of the suit which is absolutely without jurisdiction, so the same cannot be sustained in the eye of law.

8. In support of his contentions he refers the following cases:

1. In the case of Afzal Hossain Diptee Vs. Radha Kanta Korati and others 15 BLC 196 held: "Code of Civil Procedure

Order VII rule 11

On going to materials on record it transpires that the grounds urged for rejection of the plaint are absolutely the subject matter of evidence, which cannot he decided before taking evidence. On plain reading of the statements of the plaint it is evident that the same clearly discloses the cause of action, the relief claimed is not under valued, the plaint was not written upon paper insufficiently stamped and not barred by any other law. The question whether the plaint is liable to be rejected being barred by law must be apparent from the statement made in the plaint itself and not from the written statement or any other material other than that has been put in the plaint."

2. In the case of Abdul Malek Sawdager Vs. Md. Mahbubey Alam and others 57 DLR(AD)-18 held:

" Code of Civil Procedure Order VII rule 11

The question whether the plaint is liable to be rejected being barred by law must he apparent from the statement made in the plaint itself and not from the written statement or any other material other than that has been put in the plaint."

3. In the case of Bangladesh Water Development Board Vs. Contractor, Manu Barrage 9 BLT 21 held:

" Arbitration Act, 1940 Section -32

Whether the suit instituted in presence of the arbitration agreement is maintainable.

Held: We find no such provisions in the Act barring a suit on the ground of existence of an arbitration agreement."

4. In the case of Shari A. Chowdhury Vs. Pubali Bank Ltd. and others 54 DLR 310 held:

" Section 11 & Order VII rule 11 of the Code.

Ordinarily, a plaint should not be rejected under Order VII rule 11 of the Code on the ground of res judicata unless it is so palpably clear and obvious from a meaningful reading of the plaint that no further evidence is required."

5. In the case of Abul Khair (Md.) Vs. Pubali Bank Ltd. and another 53 DLR 62 held:

"Code of Civil Procedure Order VII rule I1

The Court while deciding application about rejection of plaint is not permitted in law to travel beyond the averments made in the plaint."

9. The learned Advocate appearing for the defendant respondents opposes the appeal and submits that virtually the shortage was done by the exporting country, so the defendants are not at all liable for such shortage. He adds that there was an agreement between the plaintiff and defendants to the effect that if any dispute arise in course of their business transaction the matter should be settled by Arbitration. The plaintiff without seeking his redress to Arbitration instituted the suit, so the same is barred under law. He lastly submits that the learned Judge after considering the materials on record rightly rejected the plaint.

10. In support of his contentions he refers the following decisions:

1. In the case of Badsha Miah and others Vs. Abdul Kader and others 5 MLR(AD)66 held:

"Arbitration Act, 1940-

Sections 32 and 33- No Suit challenging the arbitration agreement or an award without having recourse to section 33 is maintainable-

Section 32 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 puts a clear bar on bringing suit challenging arbitration agreement or an award without having recourse to the remedy by way of an application under section 33 of the Act. Therefore the instant suit since instituted in contravention of the provision of section 33 is not maintainable.

Section 32 of the Act provides that no suit shall lie on any ground for a declaration upon the validity of an arbitration award nor such award can he set aside "otherwise than as provided in the Act". The remedy by a suit is taken away by section 32 of the Act. The Expression "otherwise than as provided in this Act" used in section 32 brings provision of section 33 within its ambit. Under section 33 of the Act any party to an arbitration agreement can challenge the existence or validity of such agreement or an award or to have the effect of either determined upon an application to the Court. A suit to challenge the existence of an arbitration agreement or an award is not maintainable by reason of section 33 which provides that such a challenge must be made by means of an application and not by means of a suit. Thus from a reading of section 32 and 33 of the Act it seems to me that without having recourse to section 33 no declaration that an arbitration agreement or an award or the effect of either for an existence or validity can be obtained in a suit like the present one and such remedy can be had by filing an application under section 33 of the Act. The learned Single Judge rightly held that no suit for declaration that the arbitral award was void can be filed without recourse to section 33 of the Act and section 32 bars a suit of the present nature."

2. In the case of Abdul Quayum Vs. International Finance Investment and Commerce Bank Ltd. and others 63 DLR-359 held:

"Code of Civil Procedure Order VII, rule 11.

Where the proceeding of the suit against the defendant is barred under the law the filing of the application for rejecting of the plaint before filing of the written statement or not is immaterial. "

11. In order to appreciate their submissions we have gone through the records and given our anxious consideration to their submissions.

12. The point for consideration whether the impugned judgment and decree calls for interference by this Court.

<u>13. For the convenience of understanding the provisions of Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as hereunder:</u>

<u>"11- The plaint shall be rejected on the following issues:</u>

<u>(a) Where it does not disclose a cause of action.</u>

<u>(b) Where the relief claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so;</u>

<u>(c) Where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails do so.</u>

<u>(d) Where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law."</u>

14. Provided that the time fixed by the Court for the correction of the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not exceed twenty one days.

<u>15. On going to the materials on record it transpires that the plaintiff instituted Money Suit no. 35 of 2012 for realisation of money for Tk.1,72,22,376/- from the defendants. The only point urged by the learned Counsel for the defendant respondents are that the suit is barred under law i.e. under Arbitration Act, so the plaint should be rejected. The question whether the plaint is liable to be rejected being barred by law must be apparent from the statement made in the plaint itself and not from the written statement or any other material other than that has been put in the plaint.</u>

16. From the plain reading of the statements of plaint of the instant suit it is evident that the same clearly discloses the cause of action; the relief claimed is not undervalued; the plaint was not written upon paper insufficiently stamped; from the statement of the plaint it does not appear that the suit is barred by any law.

17. Now coming to clause (d) of rule 11, it appears that clause (d) of the rule authorise the rejection of a plaint when the suit appears from the statements in the plaint to be barred by any law. This clause applies when it appear from the statements in the plaint that the suit is barred but it has no application where there is no clear or specific admission in the plaint suggesting that the suit is barred. This clause is attracted only when on the admitted facts as appearing from the plaint itself the suit is prima facie barred. As for instance when from the statements made in the plaint it appears that the cause of action arose beyond the period of limitation fixed under the statute and no indication is given that limitation has been saved, the plaint may be rejected. In a proper case, when it appears to be barred by limitation, the plaint may be allowed to be amended without rejection. It is not mandatory for the Court to reject the pliant. It may ask the plaintiff to amend it so as to make suit maintainable. Where the plaintiff does not comply with such an order the Court may reject the plaint. Reference may be made to the cases reported in 18 CWN 1340. AIR 1928 Oudh 495 and AIR 1953 Ca1.222.

18. In the case of Ratan Chand Dharam Chand Vs. The Secretary of State for India in Council and another, reported in 18 CWN 1340, a Division Bench of Calcutta High Court while considering the scope of Order VII, rule 11(d) observed as follows:-

"That rule obviously has no application, for there was no statement in the plaint which suggested that the suit was barred. On the contrary it was specifically stated that notice under sec. 80 had been served on the "Collector" without .specifying the district. The defect was not discovered till after the defendants had entered appearance and it was then too late to reject the plaint ". Similarly in the case of Maqsood Ali Vs. Deputy Commissioner, Bara Banki and another, reported in A.I.R. 1928, Oudh, 495, a Division Bench of Oudh held that if-the suit was not on the face of it barred by any law, Order VII, rule 11(d) had no application. The relevant portion of the judgment ran as follows:

"We do not consider that the suit appeared from the statement in the plaint to be barred by law and we do not think that rule had any application. He has pointed out to us that in a suit which was .filed in a similar manner a Bench of the Allahabad High Court stated in Nachhu Vs.. Secy. of State that the plaint ought to have been rejected under the proviso of s. 54(c) of the old Code of Civil Procedure, that clause was exactly the same as Order VII rule 11(d). The learned Judge composing the Bench gave no reasons for this conclusion and did not give any effect to it for we find that the suit with which they were concerned had been dismissed but the Subordinate Judge and as their order was an order dismissing the appeal, the plaint was apparently not rejected. Their Lordships said : " It ought to have been rejected" but gave no effect to that view. We have only to note in respect of this point that exactly the same question could have been raised in Bhagchand Dagadusa Vs. Secy. of State. There the suit had been dismissed by the District Judge. The appeal had been dismissed by the High Court and the appeal was again dismissed by their Lordships of the Judicial Committee. It was not there suggested that the proper procedure was to reject the plaint. In a case such as this we are of opinion that the suit is not on the face of it barred by law. The very arguments which have been advanced in appeal show that the suit on the face of it is not barred by law, as the suit has been found to be a suit that has to be dismissed after consideration of the legal arguments. Therefore we are unable to accept this view of the learned Counsel.

The Calcutta High Court in the case of Sreedam Chandra Bhur Vs. Tencori Mukherjee and others reported in A.I.R. 1953 Cal. 222 also held that Order VII rule 11(d) was attracted only when on the admitted facts as appearing from the plaint itself the suit was prima facie barred. The Division Bench in this connection observed as follows:-

"This clause is attracted only when on the admitted facts as appearing from the plaint itself the suit is prima _facie barred. As for instance when from the statements made in the plaint it appears that the cause of action arose beyond period of limitation fixed under the statute and no indication is given that limitation has been saved, the plaint may be rejected. Even in such a case, an opportunity is to be given to the plaintiff to amend the plaint by setting out an acknowledgement in writing signed by the defendant within the period of limitation if it is so prayed, and that without passing an order for rejection of the plaint. `Gunnaji Bhavaji Vs. Makanji Khoosal Chand', 34 Born. 250. As was observed in 'Ratan Chand V. Secy. of State 18 Cal. WN 1340, action is to be taken under Or. VII, r. 11 of the Code of civil Procedure only if there is a clear and specific admission in the plaint from which it follows that the suit is barred. Reference may also be made to the observations of this Court.' Prankrishna Vs, Kripannathl. 21 Cal. WN 209 held:

"Let us now consider whether on the plaint as filed the Court will be justified in rejecting in limine the plaint under cl.(d), r.11, Or. VII, Civil P.C. In the body of the pliant there is no admission .for the Council of the Assembly is the Government under s. 80, Civil P.C. On the other hand, it is seriously contested on behalf of the plaintiff that neither of the two bodies can even be deemed to be the government. The learned Subordinate Judge refers to his order vaguely to the Trend of French Statutes conferring greater and greater powers on the French Settlement in India and creating a 'Council du Government' there and later a cutting out Chandernagore from the Federation and conferring on Chandernagore all those powers with a separate .delegate

of the 'Commissionaire de la re-oblique, it is evident that the Chandernagore administration is a government in the grammatical and ordinary sense of the word though its functions may fall short of the those of the Governments existing in India. We do not think it necessary to refer to other points urged before us by the contending parties. Suffice it to say that the question whether even if the Code of Civil Procedure applies, whether s. 80 would be attracted or not cannot be decided merely on the plaint as it stands. The Court should have registered the plaint, issued notices on the defendants and allowed them to file their written statements. After issues were raised it would have been open to the Court to take up one or more of the issues as preliminary ones and decide the same. Objection that had been raised by the Court `suo-motu' and such other objection as may be raised by the defendants would have to be tried on the merits, and only after all the necessary facts and materials are brought before the Court. "

19. There is no reason to differ from the above principles of law. In the instant case, there is nothing on record to show that on the admitted facts as appearing from the plaint itself the suit is prima facie barred. So the rule 11(d) is not at all attracted here and the plaint cannot be rejected on that score.

20. In the case of Sundar Ali being dead his heirs: Mannan and others Vs. Md. Serajul Islam Sarker and others 56 DLR(AD) 210 held:

"For the ascertainment of the cause of action the Court is required to read the plaint in its entirety.

21. In the case of Abdul Malek Sawdagar Vs. Md. Mahbubey Alam and others 57 DLR(AD) 18 held:

"The question whether the plaint is liable to be rejected being barred by law must be apparent from the statement made in the plaint itself and not from the written statement or any other material other than that has been put in the plaint.

22. In the case of Md. Abul Khair Vs. Pubali Bank Ltd. and another 21 BLD (AD)32=53 DLR (AD) 62 held:

Where in a suit an application under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code is filed for rejecting the plaint on the ground that the averments made in the plaint do no disclose a cause of action for the suit, the Court is not called upon to decide the suit on merit on taking evidence. It is only the averment made in the plaint which are to be considered to come to a finding as to whether those disclose a cause of action. The Court while deciding such application is not permitted in law to travel beyond the averments made in the plaint. "

23. In view of the above, the Court below without considering the materials on record and aforesaid principles of law, by rejecting the plaint of the suit committed an error of law. Therefore, the impugned judgment and decree of the Court below is liable to be interfered by the High Court Division in exercise of power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

<u>24. Moreover the impugned order in its entirety is not well founded in the facts and circumstances of the case. So, the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the appellant prevails and appears to have a good deal of force. We have gone through the decisions as referred by the learned Counsel of the respondents. We are in respectful agreement with the principles enunciated therein but the facts leading to those cases are quite distinguishable to that of the instant case. Therefore we are unable to accept his submissions.</u>

25. In the light of discussions made above and the preponderant judicial views emerging out of the authorities referred to above, we are of the view that the impugned judgment and decree suffers from legal infirmities which calls for interference by this Court. Thus the appeal having merit succeeds.

26. In the result, the appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and decree dated 21-10-2014 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, fifth Court, Dhaka in Money Suit no. 35 of 2012 is hereby set-aside. The suit shall proceed in accordance with law.

27. The office is directed to send down the record of the Court below and communicate the order at once.

End.

parties:
Noor Afroze Banoo and others
Vs.
Md. Rafique Ahmed being dead his heirs 1(A) 
Nasima Begum and others
full_judgment:
A.K.M. Shahidul Huq, J: This rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1(a) to (c) to show cause as to why the impugned order No. 46 dated 06.03.2014 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 438 of 2009 allowing the application for local inspection under Order 39 Rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The short facts leading to the disposal of the rule is that the opposite party Nos. 1-3 as plaintiffs tiled Title Suit No. 438 of 2009 before the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka against the petitioners as defendants for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession. The case of the plaintiff is that the original owner of the suit land was Admond Alekgender William and his name was duly recorded in C.S. khatian No. 73 and he sold that property to one Abdul Latif and he took over the property over the suit land and he died leaving behind two sons and two daughters and the predecessors of the plaintiffs Rezia khatun got Ka schedule of property by amicable settlement and she gifted schedule land to her son plaintiff Mr. Rafique Ahmed, predecessor of the plaintiffs and transferred the possession of the plaintiffs and transferred the possession of the suit land and subsequently the defendants dispossessed the plaintiffs from the floor of the suit land and claimed the suit property, hence filed the suit.

3. Thereafter filed an application under Order 39 Rule 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 18.08.2009 for temporary injunction and the learned Joint District Judge issued show cause notice upon the defendant Nos. 1-3 and after receiving the show cause notice the defendants filed written objection.

4. The case of defendants is that Rezia Khatun, wife of Daliluddin transferred .07 acres of land in favour of Daliluddin on 07.05.1959 vide deed No. 5267 and on the same day Rezia Khatun transferred .04 acres of land in favour of Daliluddin vide deed No. 5266. Daliluddin owning and possessing that .11 acres of land transferred .07 acres of land in favour of Abdul Kader, Abdul Malek and Ekramul on 10.09.1960 vide deed No. 11676 and on the same day Daliluddin transferred .04 acres of land in favour of Abdul Kader, Abdul Malek and Fkramul vide deed o. 11677. Abdul Kader, Abdul Malek and Ekramul transferred 2 katha 13 Chatak land in favour of Kazi Obaidul Islam on 11.01.1961 and on the same day they transferred 2 katha 7 chatak land in favour of Sharifunnesa. Kazi Obaidul Islam and Shari funnesa sold their land to Wahiduddin Wara on 10.04.1965. Wahiduddin Wara mutated his name, paid rent to the Government and municipal holding and this Wahiduddin Wara transferred the land to his wife Rabea Khatun by registered sale deed on 31.11.1969 and Rabea Khatun owning and possessing the same by mutating her name transferred the land to Akter Banu, mother of the opposite party Nos. 1, 2 and 3. Akter Banu mutated his name both in Government Seresta and Dhaka City Corporation and paid electricity, gas bill etc. Akter Banu for construction of multistoried building over the suit land i.e. holding No. 9 of Eskaton Road submitted plan and after investigation that was approved by the RAJUK on 25.09.1979 and construction 3 storied building and possessing the same through Bharatia. In present city survey khatian, the land was correctly recorded in the name of Akter banu in plot No. 5265. Akter Banu had been in peaceful possession and died leaving behind one son and two daughters i.e. defendant Nos. 1-3. On 01.09.2008, the father of the defendant Nos. 1-3 made an agreement with BRAC Bank for letting out the suit premises for 10 years and the name of the building is "SHANAZ TOWER", 9, Eskaton road and the suit land with 3 storied building has been possessed by defendant Nos. 1-3 through Bharatia. The plaintiffs never possess the suit land.

5. The learned Joint District Judge after hearing the injunction application rejected the same on 23.10.2012 against which the plaintiff filed Civil Revision No. 3464 of 2012 before the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, High Court Division and obtained an order of status-quo and finally the plaintiff converted the Civil Revision into a First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 44 of 2014 that is pending for hearing.

6. During the pendency of the First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 44 of 2014 the plaintiffs all on a sudden without serving any notice to the defendants on 02.01.2014 filed an application for local inspection and the learned Joint District Judge allowed the same and appointed Mr. Md. Abdul Halim Faruq, the learned Advocate as Advocate Commissioner.

7. On 24.03.2014 the learned Advocate Commissioner served a notice to the defendants for local inspection.

8. Mr. Md. Nurul Amin, learned Advocate appearing with Sheikh Mohammad Tariqul Islam, appearing for the petitioner while Ms. Saleha Islam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties.

9. Mr. Md. Nurul Amin, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the plaintiffs without serving any notice to the defendants filed an application for local inspection and the learned Judge allowing the same which is highly illegal. The learned Judge instead of rejecting the application for local inspection allowed the same which has caused serious miscarriage of Justice resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

10. He next submits that the plaintiff case is for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession but the plaintiff stated in his application that ‘বাদিনী নালিশী সম্পত্তি ষোল আনা এককভাবে ভোগ দখলে বিদ্যমান রহিয়াছে।’

11. He further submits that the suit is recovery of khas possession but the plaintiff stated in his application for local inspection that ‘কাজেই নালিশী সম্পত্তি কাহার দখলে রহিয়াছে, উহা নির্ণয় করা প্রয়োজন।’ it is a settle principle of law that ascertaining the possession of the suit land is a matter of evidence and as such the application for local inspection is not maintainable. In view of the above fact the learned Joint District Judge has committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in allowing the application for local inspection.

12. He also submits that the subject matter of the inspection is to be decided by taking evidence and without taking evidence that can not be decided by local inspection and as such the learned Joint District Judge committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in allowing the application for local inspection.

13. In support of his contention he has referred the case of Union of India and another Vs. M/s. Kripal Industries reported in AIR 1998 page 224.

14. He has next referred the case of Shall A. Chowdhury and another Vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 6 BUT (AD) 164.

15. As against this Ms. Saleha Islam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties submits that the impugned order has been passed by the learned Joint District Judge does not suffer from any illegality legal infirmity and material irregularity as such the impugned order of the learned Joint District Judge does not deserve any interference under the revisional jurisdiction of this Hon'ble Court as laid down under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and as such the impugned order of the learned Joint District Judge is immune from attack under the revisional jurisdiction and consequently she prayed for discharge of the rule.

16. Heard the learned Advocate of both sides perused the impugned order passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court Dhaka in Title Suit No. 438 of 2009 allowing the application for local inspection under Order 39 Rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

<u>17. In order to arrive at a proper finding in the instant rule it is very much pertinent to discuss the provisions of law as contain in Order 39 Rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure which runs as follows:-</u>

<u>Order 39 Rule 7: "R. & Detention, preservation, inspection, etc, of subject-matter of suit. (1) The Court may, on the application of any party to a suit, and on such terms as it thinks fit,</u>

<u>(d) Make an order for the detention, preservation or inspection of any property which is the subject-matter of such suit, or as to which any question may arise therein;</u>

<u>(e) For all or any of the purposes aforesaid authorize any person to enter upon or into any land or building in the possession of any other party to such suit; and</u>

<u>(f) For all or any of the purposes aforesaid authorize any samples to be taken, or any observation to be made or experiment to be tried, which may seem necessary or expedient for the purpose of obtaining full information or evidence."</u>

<u>18. On perusal of the impugned order of the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court Dhaka find the impugned order has been passed in utter violation of the provisions of law as contain in Order 39 Rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure and also the settled principles of law as decided in the case of Union of India and another Vs. M/S Kripal Industries reported in AIR 1998 Rajasthan page 224 where it is held that:-</u>

<u>"Appointment of Commissioner for making enquiry about fact of possession of property in dispute-Improper as same can be adjudicated upon by framing issues and recording evidence."</u>

19. In another case of Shall A. Chowdhury and another Vs. Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary Ministry of Industries and another reported in 6 BLT (AD) page 164 where our Apex Court held that:-

“In the facts and circumstances of the present case it will not be fit and proper to allow an inspection when the plaintiffs admittedly obtained possession of the suit unit in 1984 and when after having unilaterally enjoyed possession thereof for five years applied for inspection in 1989 when the unit was still in its possession it will be an idle exercise to allow inspection at this stage."

20. The aforesaid citation as referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner in support of his contention is fully applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present Dhaka is not at all sustainable in law and the case same is liable to be set aside.

21. On due and proper consideration of the materials on record and the decisions as referred on this point by the learned Advocate in support of his contention I find that the impugned order of the learned Joint District Judge Court Dhaka passed in Title Suit No. 438 of 2009 has suffered from serious legal perversity material irregularity and thus caused serious miscarriage of Justice which has occasioned in failure of justice. I am in full agreement with the citations as referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner in course of his submissions. I have no other alternative but to interfere with the impugned order of the learned Joint District Judge,1st Court Dhaka dated 06.03.2014 passed in title suit No. 438 of 2009 allowing the application for local inspection under Order 39 Rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure which has suffered from gross illegality and material irregularity as such the impugned order of the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court Dhaka deserves my interference under the revisional jurisdiction of this Hon'ble Court as laid down in section 115(1) of the Code of civil Procedure.

22. In view of the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case the impugned order of the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court Dhaka is not at all sustainable in law and the same is liable to be set aside.

23. Accordingly, the impugned order No. 46 dated 06.03.2014 passed in Title Suit No. 438 of 2009 is hereby set aside. Consequently the application filed under Order 39 Rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure is hereby rejected.

24. In the result, the rule is made absolute without any order as to cost.

25. The order of stay as granted at the time of issuance of the rule is hereby re-called and vacated.

26. The learned Joint District Judge, Court Dhaka is hereby directed to dispose of Title Suit No. 438 of 2009 expeditiously as far as practicable preferably within 4(four) months from the date of receipt of the copy of the judgment positively.

27. The office is hereby directed to transmit a copy of this judgment to the concern Court forthwith for information and necessary action.

End.

full_judgment:
A.K.M. Shahidul Huq, J: This rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-3 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 27.04.2015 (decree signed on 06.06.2015) passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Jhalakati in Civil Appeal No. 17 of 2012 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 22.01.2012 (decree signed on 26.01.2012) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Is Court, Jhalakati in Title Suit No. 02 of 2005 dismissing the suit should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The short facts for disposal of the rule is that the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 as plaintiffs filed Tile Suit No. 2 of 2005 before the learned Joint District Judge, Court, Jhalakati against the petitioner and other opposite parties for specific performance of contract.

3. The contention of the plaint of opposite party Nos. 1 and 2, in short, is that Kartik Chandra Das got 9.59 acres of land which includes the schedule land (5.19 acres of land) in 1360 BS by way of partition. But S.A. record was wrongly prepared in the name of Jitendra Nath, Binoy Bhuson and others whereupon the said Kartik Chandra Das filed Title Suit No. 280 of 1962 before the learned V' Sub-Judge, Barisal and got judgment and decree dated 18.08.1962 (decree signed on 25.08.1962) in his favour. Thereafter Kartik Chandra Das filed Mutation case No. 3880 of 1963 before the Revenue Deputy Collector and got order dated 06.07.1963 in his favour and accordingly the relevant khatian were corrected in his name Kartik Chandra Das had been possessing the schedule land by giving rents to the government. Thereafter Kartik Chandra Das declared to sell the schedule land and the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 agreed to purchase the same upon consideration of Tk. 4,50,000/-. Accordingly on 13th Falgun 1408 Bs i.e. on 25.02.2002 Kartik Chandra Das took Tk. 4,30,000/- from opposite party Nos. 1 and 2, executed an agreement for sale and also hand over physical possession of the schedule land in favour of opposite party Nos. 1 and 2. According to the terms and conditions of the said agreement for sale Kartik Chandra Das would execute Saf-kanala deed in favour of opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 after collecting the necessary papers and receiving the rest Tk. 20,000/-. The opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 several times requested Kartik Chandra Das to take rest Tk. 20,000/- and execute saf-kabala deed in their favour but he failed to do so. Thereafter Kartik Chandra Das died in the month of Bhadra of 1411 BS leaving behind the petitioner and opposite party No. 3. The opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 also requested the petitioner and opposite party No. 3 to execute saf-kabala deed in their favour but on 8th Falgun 1411 i.e. 20.02.2005 the petitioner and opposite party No. 3 denie3d to execute sal-kabala deed in their favour for which the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 2 of 2005.

4. The petitioner contested the suit by submitting written statement. The contention of the written statement, in short, is that Kartik Chandra Das was the owner and possessor of the schedule land Kartik Chandra Das died on 9th Bhadra, 1411 i.e. on 24.08.2004. Kartik Chandra Das did not execute the disputed agreement for sale deed on 25.02.2002 or any other date in favour of the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 or anybody else and there was no reason for executing such agreement for sale. Kartik Chandra Das never proposed to sale the schedule land to the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 or to anyone else. Kartik Chandra Das did not receive Tk. 4,30,000/- from the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 or anyone else on 25.02.2002 or any other date. Kartik Chaqndra Das did not also handover physical possession of the schedule land in favour of the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 or anyone else. The disputed agreement for sale dated 25.02.2002 is fabricated, forged and without consideration. The opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 in collusion with the brother of the petitioner i.e. opposite party No. 3 collected old stamps and created the said agreement for sale dated 25.02.2002 and the same is forged. On 25.01.2004 Kartik Chandra Das executed a power of attorney deed in favour of the petitioner, opposite party No. 3 and Josna Rani Das regarding 6.95 acres of land which includes the schedule land. If the signature of Kartik Chandra Das present in the power of attorney deed dated 25.01.2004 and in the agreement for sale deed dated 25.02.2002 is compared, then it will be easily realized that the signature of Kartik Chandra Das present in the agreement for sale dated 25.02.2002 is forged. The petitioner and opposite party No. 3 Kalipodo Das took loan of Tk. 15,000/- from Bangladesh Krishi bank on 01.03.2004 on the basis of the said power of attorney deed dated 25.01.2004 and also mortgaged the schedule land in favour of Bangladesh Krishi Bank. The agreement for sale dated 25.02.2002 is forged.

5. The opposite party No. 3 in collusion with opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 filed written statement and solenama in Title Suit No. 2 of 2005.

6. The learned trial judge, framed 4(four) issues, examined 3 (three) witnesses on behalf of the plaintiffs and 2 (two) witnesses on behalf of the defendant and dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 22.01.2012 (decree signed on 26.01.2012).

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 22.01.2012 (decree signed on 26.01.2012), the plaintiffs appellants opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 preferred Civil Appeal No. 17 of 2012 before the court of learned District Judge, Jhalakati who transferred the same to the learned Additional District Judge, Jhalakati for disposal. Thereafter the learned Additional District Judge, Jhalakati allowed the appeal by his judgment and decree dated 27.04.2015 (decree signed on 06.05.2015) and reversed the judgment and decree of the trial judge.

8. Mr. Tapan Kumar Chakraborty with Mr. Sarkar Mohammad dedar Mahedy, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the petitioner on the other hand Mr. Md. Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties to oppose the rule.

9. Mr. Tapan Kumar Chakraborty, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the learned lower appellate court misconceived the facts and evidence on record and allowed the appeal without applying his judicial mind and the same is not tenable in law.

10. He next submits that the learned Additional District Judge, Jhalakathi committed error in law resulting in error in decision occasioning failure of justice in not considering the genuineness of the signature of Kartik Chandra Das present in the disputed agreement for sale deed dated 25.04.2002 and as such the impugned judgment and decree dated 27.04.2015 is liable to be set aside.

11. He also submits that the lower appellate court failed to consider all the evidence on record and allowed the appeal only on the basis of the statements of opposite party No. 3. The opposite party No. 3 was examined as P.W 2 and during cross-examination he told that there is suit/case between him and the petitioner Thus it is evident that though the petitioner and opposite party No. 3 are brothers but there is enmity between them. But the learned lower appellate court below failed to consider such evidence on record and illegally allowed the appeal and as such the impugned judgment and decree dated 27.04.2015 is liable to be set aside.

12. Learned Advocate further submits that the petitioner claimed in his written statement as well as in his examination in chief that the signature present in the disputed agreement for sale dated 25.02.2002 is not that of Kartik Chandra Das but the opposite party No. 1 and 2 did not take any steps for expert opinion regarding the said signature. And as such the impugned judgment and decree dated 27.04.2015 is liable to be set aside.

13. He also submits that the during trial of Title Suit No. 02 of 2005 the present petitioner submitted an application for expert opinion and that application was allowed and accordingly the disputed agreement for sale dated 25.02.2002 along with Sub-kabala deed No. 927 dated 22.04.1993 were sent to the expert for his opinion whereupon the expert observed that the 3 (signature) present in the disputed agreement for sale deed has over writing mistakes. But the learned lower appellate court below failed to consider such evidence and illegally allowed the appeal and as such the impugned judgment and decree dated 27.04.2015 is liable to be set aside.

14. He further submits that the learned trial judge himself examined the 3 (three) signatures present in the disputed agreement for sale deed dated 25.02.2002 and observed that those 3 (three) signatures differ from each other and ultimately hold that those signatures are not that of Kartik Chandra Das. But the learned lower appellate court kept silence in this regard and erroneously allowed the appeal and as such the impugned judgment and decree dated 27.04.2015 is liable to be set aside.

15. He next submits that the opposite party No. 1 and 2 as plaintiffs did not stated in their plaint that on whose presence Kartik Chandra Das received Tk. 4,30,000/- from them. But opposite party No. 1 Md. Jahangir Hossain as P.W.1 told in his cross-examination that Kartik Chandra Das received the said money in the deed writer's chamber and Chitto Ranjan Shit, Mobarak Hossain and Kalipodo Das were present during such transaction. But Kalipodo Das (P.W 2) told in his cross-examination that he did not know how much money his father Kartik Chandra Das has received before executing the disputed agreement. He also said that Chitto Babu, Mobarak Mollie, Khorshed and 4/5 other persons were present during such execution. On the other hand, the deed writer Khorshed alam (P.w. 3) did not say anything about transaction of money and he said that Kartik Chandra Das, Kalipodo Das and Chitto Babu were present during such execution. Thus the statements of all P.Ws differ from each other regarding transaction of Tk. 4,30,000/- and the number of witnesses who were present during the execution of the disputed agreement for sale dated 25.02.2002. But the learned lower appellate court did not consider such evidence and illegally allowed the appeal and as such the impugned judgment and decree dated 27.04.2015 is liable to be set aside.

16. As against this the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties submits that since the defendant No. 1 admitted the agreement for sale as such under section 58 of the evidence act. Admitted fact need not be proved and under order 12 rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that the court can pass order on the basis of admission defendant No. 1 was the attesting witness in the agreement for sale. As such the defendant No. 2 as a brother of defendant No. 1 is hereby estopped from denying the transaction between the predecessor of defendant and the plaintiff.

17. The learned Advocate also submits that exhibit K 3-5 LCR proved that the signature in the bainanama has been manipulated by the defendant No. 1 which will be crystal clear from the photocopy of the bainanama that was duly considered by the appellate court and the appellate court rightly found by the solenama was rightly correctly by the predecessor of defendant No. 1 and 2. The learned advocate for the petitioner submits that defendant No. 1 filed a written statement thereafter in collusion with the plaintiff filed a based solenama which is not at all tenable in law.

18. The learned Advocate for the opposite party in support of his contention has referred the case of Md. Wazed Ali Sardar Vs. Md. Afsaruddin Sardar and others reported in 16 BLD (AD) =page 4. He has next referred the case of Mst. Johara Begum Vs. Rafiqul Kader reported in 25 DLR (HC) page 91.

19. He further referred the case of Shajahan Khan Vs. A.D.C. (Rev.) and others reported in 11 BLT (AD) page 60.

20. Learned Advocate further referred the case of Kurshid Ali and others Vs. Noorjahan Bewa and others reported in 15 BLD (AD) page 82. Learned Advocate lastly referred the case of Hazari Bala Sana Vs. Niron and others reported in 17 BLD (AD) page 294 in support of his contention.

21. Heard the learned Advocate perused the impugned judgment and decree of the last court of fact considered the statement made in the revisional application and also considered the submissions as advanced by the learned Advocate for the petitioner as well as the learned Advocate for the opposite party and also considered the citation as referred by the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party in support of his contention in order to arrive at a correct finding. It is very much pertinent to refer the case of Kurshid Ali and others Vs. Noorjahan Bewa and others reported in 15 BLD (AD) page 82, where our Apex Court held that:-

"When the appellate court as the final court of fact decides questions of fact and records its findings on consideration of the evidence on record the High Court Division while exercising revisional jurisdiction cannot interfere with findings of facts unless the High Court Division is satisfied that the said findings are perverse. When the material findings of the appellate court are upheld by the High Court Division and in doing so it commits no error of law, the decision of the High Court Division calls for no interference by the Appellate Division."

22. Thus the High Court Division referred the appellate court's consideration as to the plaintiff Noorjahan Bewa's possession.

"So far as the question of possession is concerned the petitioners adduced simply oral evidence. They appear to have examined 3 witnesses including plaintiff No. 1. P.W.I is plaintiff No. 1 herself. Her evidence shows that during the life time of her husband be had all along paid rent but not a single rent receipt was produced in court to show payment of rent. It appears that the learned Additional District Judge believed her oral evidence. Her evidence of possession was corroborated at the trial Court by P.W. 2 Khadem Ali and P.W. 3 Wahed Ali and the learned Additional District Judge also noticed some misreading of the evidence by the trial court in his judgment. On the other hand, the learned Subordinate Judge appears to have believed the oral evidence of the contesting defendants, mainly for failure of the plaintiffs-respondents to produce any documentary evidence of their possession such as rent receipts showing payment of rent etc. The learned Subordinate Judge appears to have placed much reliance on the rent receipts but the learned Additional District Judge, discarded these rent receipts holding that these could be easily manufactured. Since the learned Additional District Judge came to this finding of fact on proper consideration of evidence, this court, in its revisional jurisdiction, cannot interfere with the said findings of fact un less this court is satisfied that the said finding was absolutely perverse."

23. The material finding of the appellate court, the last court of fact, was rightly' upheld by the High Court Division. The matter does not call for any interference. The appeal is dismissed. There will, however, no order as to cost.

<u>24. Now let us see how the Appellate Division settled the principle of law as decided in the case of Hazari Bala Sana and another Vs. Niron Alias Niranjan Mandal and others reported in 17 BLD (AD) page 294 where our Apex Court held that:-</u>

<u>"It is a settled principle that the findings of fact. Whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate court. Which is the final court of fact, is binding on the High Court Division, as a revisional court except in certain well defined exceptional circumstances, such as non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence affecting the merit of the case?"</u>

<u>25. In the instant case, from the judgment of the appellate court it is found that in arriving at its findings the said court carefully considered all the material facts and circumstances of the case find the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, and this citation of our Apex Court is fully applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case.</u>

26. On the point of service of summons it is very much pertinent to refer the case of Md. Wazed Ali Sardar Vs. Md. Afsaruddin Sardar and others reported in 16 BLD (AD) page 4 where our Apex Court held that:-

"In an application under Order IX, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for setting aside the exparte decree the whole onus is upon the plai9ntiff to prove that summons was duly served upon the defendant. Respondent No. 1 failed to prove by adducing cogent evidence that summons was duly served upon the appellant. Although the learned Judge of the High Court Division noticed that the return of the summons alleged to have been served upon the appellant and the vokalatnama alleged to have been filed by the appellant were missing from the record gave much stress to the order dated 25.03.1976 and without considering the report submitted by the Bench Assistant erroneously found that the trial court was wrong in holding that summons was not served upon the appellant. The learned Judge of the High Court Division also erred in law in holding that the court was wrong in comparing the signature of the appellant appearing in the alleged application dated 25.03.1976 with his admitted signatures. Rather the learned Judge of the High Court Division exceeded his jurisdiction in revision in entering into a question of fact and in comparing the signatures himself to arrive at a contrary finding of fact. The findings of fact as to non-service of summons made by the trial court was not perverse, nor was it such as could legitimately justify an interference by the revisional court on accepted principles. For the reasons stated above the judgment and order of the learned Judge of the High Court Division it liable to be set aside."

27. Last of all 1 would like to refer the case of Mst. Zohara Begum Vs. Rafiqul Kader reported in 25 DLR (1973) page 91 it is held that:-

“From the language of rule 19, it is very clear that where the summons is returned under rule 17, the court shall, lithe return under that rule has not been verified by the declaration of the serving officer, and may, if it has been so verified, examine the serving officer on oath, or cause him to be so examined by another court, touching his proceedings. This rule further enjoins upon the court to ascertain by inquiry in the matter as it thinks fit, as to whether summons has been duly served or not, and either declare that the summons has been duly served or order such service as it thinks fit. Rule 19A provides, that a declaration made and subscribed by a serving officer shall be received as evidence of the facts as to the service or attempted service of the summons. It is true as the language of rule 19A shows that service return duly submitted is to be accepted as evidence of the facts as to the service or attempted service of the summons, but rule I 9A does not give a go-bye to the mandatory provisions of 19. It only provides that such a declaration duly subscribed by the serving office should be received as a piece of evidence in making necessary inquiry by examining the serving officer on oath, or making such further inquiry in the matter as the Court thinks fit. Rule 19A cannot be read to take away the responsibility of the court as provided in rule 19, nor can it be read to justify recording in the order sheet as a matter of routine summons duly served. This point was also considered by me in the case of Joynal Abedin Sardar and another Vs. Abdul Latif Sardar and others in F.M.A 37 of 1961. Judgment was delivered on 8th March, 1972. In the present case I had further opportunity to examine the point to a greater extent."

28. As regards the service of summons in the said case the High Court Division held that:-

“Rule 19 A cannot be read to take away the responsibility of the court as provided in rule 19, nor can it be read to justify recording in the order sheet as a matter or routing 'summons duly served.”

29. Provisions of rule 19 cannot be treated as a dead letter or absolute. Provisions of rule 19 are mandatory and same must be complied with due diligence, and the court after making necessary inquiry in the matter record a clear findings of due service or otherwise. In the absence of declaration made and subscribed by the process-server, as required under the rules, the service return cannot be accepted as evidence of due service, And in the absence of an inquiry made by the court as provided in rule 19 and distinct declaration of due service recorded, there is no presumption of service of summons. Presumption of service arises when record shows that process was rightly and duly served.

30. On due and proper consideration of the submissions as advanced by the learned Advocate for the petitioner as well as for the opposite party, the attending facts and circumstances of the case and the submissions as advanced by the learned Advocates of both the parties in support of their respective cases and the citation as referred by the learned Advocate for the opposite party in support of his contention I am of the view that the learned last Court of fact on due and proper consideration and appreciation of both oral and documentary evidence on record and the materials passed the judgment and decree and as such the judgment and decree of the last Court of fact is immune from attack under the revisional jurisdiction of this Hon'ble Court as laid down in section 1 15(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

31. I do not find any merit in the revisional application filed under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

32. In the result, the rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 27.04.2015 and 06.05.2015 passed by learned Additional District Judge, Jhalakathi in Civil Appeal No. 17 of 2012 allowing the appeal reversing the judgment and decree dated 22.01.2012 passed by learned Joint District Judge, Court, Jhalakathi in Title Suit No. 2 of 2005 dismissing the suit is hereby affirmed.

33. The order of stay as granted at the time of issuance of the rule is hereby re-called and vacated and also the order of status-quo in respect of position and possession of the suit land stands vacated. The operation of stay of the suf kabala deed No. 2209 dated 06.07.2015 is hereby re-called and vacated.

34. Send down the lower courts record along with a copy of this judgment to the concern court forthwith for information and necessary action.

End.

Jeans Care Limited Represented By Its Managing Director
