full_judgment:
J.B.M. Hassan, J: The above mentioned 03(three) writ petitions arise out of three BLL cases filed by three employees of the National Sports Council challenging dismissal orders of their respective service. The said cases as well as the appeals thereof were heard analogously and disposed of by a single judgment by the labour court and the Labour Appellate Tribunal respectively. Thus, the Rules Nisi issued therein involves similar questions of law and facts. Hence, all the writ petitions have been heard together and are being disposed of by this common judgment.

2. In all the writ petitions, the Rules Nisi were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 17.04.2011 analogously passed in Appeals No. 61 of 2010, 60 of 2010 and 59 of 2010 by the Chairman, Labour Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka allowing the appeals setting aside the judgment and order dated 20.06.2010 analogously passed in BLL Cases No. 66 of 2008, 65 of 2008 and 67 of 2008 by the Chairman, 2nd Labour Court, Dhaka allowing the cases and thereby reinstating the petitioners in their respective former posts with all back wages and other legal dues should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

3. Relevant facts involved in writ petition No. 7467 of 2011, are inter alia, that the petitioner, Md. Jahangir Alam was a Despatch Rider of the National Sports Council (the NSC), a statutory body created by the National Sports Council Act, 1974 (the NSC Act). He was also a General Secretary of the trade union, namely, Jatiya Krira Parishad Karmachari Union. A departmental proceeding was initiated by the NSC against the petitioner on the allegations of remaining unauthorized absent from his duties and illegally leasing out the shops of the swimming pools owned by the NSC. Eventually, on observance of required procedure, the petitioner was dismissed from service by the NSC vide letter dated 04.12.2007 under rule 42(7) of the National Sports Council Service Rules, 1995 (shortly, the NSC Service Rules). Against the said dismissal order, the petitioner submitted grievance petition on 18.12.2007 under section 33(1) of "hiwmicn nEj BCe, 2006 (shortly, the Act, 2006) praying for reinstatement with all back wages and others dues. But there being no positive response, the petitioner filed BLL Case No. 36 of 2008 on 30.01.2008 under section 33(3) of the Act, 2006 before the 1st Labour Court, Dhaka.

4. Writ Petition No. 7468 of 2011 has been filed by the petitioner, Md. Munir Hossain who was a Welder of the NSC and he was the Organizing Secretary of the trade union of the NSC, namely, Jatiya Krira Parishad Karmachari Union. He faced a disciplinary action initiated by the NSC relating to the allegations of bringing procession and creating unlawful situation and also for misbehavior with the Secretary of the NSC. Ultimately, on the basis of domestic enquiry report this petitioner was dismissed from service by the order dated 04.12.2007 under rule 42(7) of the NSC Service Rules. He unsuccessfully filed grievance petition and thereafter filed the BLL Case No. 35 of 2008 before the 1st Labour Court, Dhaka under section 33(3) of the Act, 2006 praying for reinstatement with all arrear wages.

5. The petitioner of writ petition No. 7469 of 2011, namely, Md. Ruhul Amin was a Driver of the NSC and Member Secretary of the registered trade union of the NSC. He also faced a disciplinary action undertaken by the NSC relating to the allegations of kicking the door of the Secretary bringing procession and for misbehavior with the Secretary of the NSC. On observance of the required procedure providing in the NSC Service Rules, the petitioner was dismissed from service by order dated 04.12.2007 under rule 42(7) of the NSC Service Rules. Against the said order of dismissal, the petitioner unsuccessfully filed grievance petition under section 33(1) of the Act, 2006 and thereafter he filed the BLL Case No. 34 of 2008 on 30.01.2008 before the 1st Labour Court, Dhaka.

6. After lapse of certain period the petitioners came to know that the local jurisdiction of the NSC was covered by the 2nd Labour Court, Dhaka and so they filed applications in their respective cases on 04.05.2008 for returning the complaints in order to file the same before the appropriate Court. After taking back the respective order to file the same before the appropriate Court. After taking back the respective complaints on the basis of the order dated 04.05.2008 passed by the 1st Labour Court, Dhaka, the petitioners submitted the same before the 2nd Labour Court, Dhaka on the very next day on 05.05.2008 and the cases were renumbered as BLL Cases No. 66 of 2008, 65 of 2008 and 67 of 2008 respectively.

7. The NSC contested the cases by filing written objections in the respective cases contending amongst others that the cases were not maintainable and that after holding a proper domestic enquiry on the basis of show cause notice relating to allegations brought against the respective complainants, they were dismissed from service on observance of the procedure as provided in the NSC Service Rules. The petitioners in their respective cases produced one witness while the NSC produced lour witnesses in the respective cases. The parties concerned also produced documentary evidences in support of their respective cases. After analogous hearing of the above mentioned cases, the 2nd Labour Court, Dhaka by the common judgment and order dated 20.06.2010 allowed the BLL Cases setting aside the dismissal orders and thereby directed the NSC to reinstate the petitioners in their respective former posts with all arrear wages and dues.

8. Challenging the aforesaid judgment and order of the Labour Court the NSC preferred Appeals No. 61 of 2010, 60 of 2010 and 59 of 2010 before the Labour Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka under sections 217/219 of the Act, 2006. After hearing the aforesaid appeals, the Tribunal by the common judgment and order dated 17.04.2011 allowed all the appeals setting aside the judgment of the Labour Court. In this backdrop, the petitioners filed the respective writ petitions before this Court and obtained the Rules Nisi therein.

9. None appears to represent the respondents in the above mentioned Rules.

10. Mr. Saqeb Mahbub, the learned Advocate with Mr. Md. Ariful Haque, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners in all the writ petitions submits that on consideration of material evidences the Labour Court allowed the BLL cases of the petitioners directing to reinstate them in their respective former posts with all arrear wages but the Tribunal without considering those materials allowed the appeals on point of maintainability. He further submits that the Tribunal passed the impugned judgment on misconception of the 'ratio' laid down in the case of Chairman, DIT and another Vs. Chairman, 2nd Labour Court and another reported in 34 DLR (AD) 37. Drawing our attention to the budget of the NSC for the year 2016-2017 (annexed with the supplementary affidavit) Mr. Mahbub also submits that from sale proceeds of stadium tickets, leasing out car parking area, renting spaces of the 20 storied NSC building and by publication of magazine, the NSC generates its income and uses the same for its expenditure and as such, section 1(4)(g) of the Act, 2006 cannot be applied to determine the status of the NSC. Therefore, the Tribunal misconceived the legal position and thereby allowed the appeals holding the cases not maintainable. Referring to the case of Palli Daridra Bimochon Foundation Vs. Palli Daridra Bimochon Foundation Karmachari Union Bangladesh (Proposed) and others reported in 57 DLR (AD) 155, Mr. Mahbub again submits that although this Foundation runs not for profit and thereby prima facie appears to have fallen within the criteria of section 1(4)(g) of the Act, 2006, yet, the apex Court held that in view of its nature, business and activities, it will not fall within the purview of section 1(4)(g) of the Act, 2006. He again submits that although the purpose of the NSC is to provide training for the development of sports but in view of its nature of earning by selling tickets and publishing magazine, its status is almost similar to “পল্লী দারিদ্র বিমোচন ফাউন্ডেশন” and as such holding the view of our apex Court, barred on consideration that the Act, 2006 being a special law providing specific time for tiling the cases, there was no scope to file cases beyond the prescribed time.

11. We have gone through the writ petitions, the supplementary affidavits thereto and the relevant laws as well as the cited cases.

12. It appears that three employees having the posts of Despatch Rider, Welder and Driver respectively were charged with different allegations by their employer, the NSC. On observance of required procedure i.e show cause notice, consideration of reply and holding domestic enquiry as well as serving second show cause notice as provided in the NSC Service Rules, the petitioners were dismissed from service by the NSC. After unsuccessfully filing grievance petitions under section 33(1) of the Act, 2006, the petitioners filed their respective BLL cases before the Labour Court, Dhaka for settings aside the dismissal orders and also praying to reinstate them in their respective former posts with back wages and other dues. The concerned Labour Court heard the labour cases simultaneously and eventually, by the common judgment and order dated 20.06.2010 allowed the labour cases setting aside the dismissal orders of the respective petitioners and directed the NSC to reinstate them in their respective posts with all back wages. Against the said judgment and order, the NSC preferred three appeals being Appeals No. 61 of 2010, 60 of 2010 and 59 of 2010 respectively before the Labour Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka. After contested hearing, the Tribunal by judgment and order dated 17.04.2011 allowed all the appeals and thereby set aside the judgment of the Labour Court.

13. On perusal of the impugned judgment, it appears that the appeals were allowed on two counts, firstly, the BLL cases were time barred having not been filed within the stipulated period provided by the special law and secondly, relying upon the 'ratio' enunciated in the case of Chairman, DIT and another Vs. Chairman, 2nd Labour Court and another reported in 34 DLR (AD) 37 the cases were not maintainable in view of section 1(4)(g) of the Act, 2006.

14. In the aforesaid scenario, let us see whether the Tribunal properly considered the appeals and came to the findings in accordance with law.

15. First of all regarding question of limitation, it appears that against the order of dismissal dated 04.12.2007 the petitioners filed their respective grievance petitions on time and there being no reply they filed the cases on 30.01.2008 before the 1st Labour Court, Dhaka which were very much within the stipulated time as provided in the Act, 2006. Subsequently, on 04.05.2008 the petitioners filed bonafide applications in their respective cases pending before the 1st Labour Court for returning the complaints to file the same before the appropriate Court stating that they came to know that the location of employer, the NSC was within the territorial jurisdiction of the 2nd Labour Court, Dhaka. The 1st Labour Court on the very day i.e by order dated 04.05.2008 assigning the reasons returned the complaints to the respective petitioners. On the very next day i.e on 05.05.2008 the petitioners submitted their respective complaints before the appropriate Court of jurisdiction i.e 2nd Labour Court, Dhaka.

16. Certainly, the cases filed on 05.05.2008, before the 2nd Labour Court were not within the prescribed time but a question arises whether the 2nd Labour Court can condone such delay in filing the BLL cases beyond the limitation period provided by the special law, the Act, 2006, in particular, when the delay occurred due to pendency of the cases before a wrong forum. In this regard let us see the provisions of section 29 (2) of the Limitation Act which run as follows:

"29. Savings-

(1)--------------

(2) Where any special [* * *] law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different form the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule, the provisions of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefor in that schedule, and for the purpose of determining any period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special [* * *] law-

(a) the provisions contained in section 4, sections 9 to 18, and section 22 shall apply only 	insofar as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special [* 	* *] law; and

(b) the remaining provisions of this Act shall not apply."

17. On a plain reading of the aforesaid provision, it appears that as per section 3 of the Limitation Act an application under the special law cannot be filed beyond limitation period prescribed in the said law. However, for the purpose of determining any period of limitation under the special law sections 4, 9-18 and 22 of the Limitation Act shall apply unless they are not expressly excluded by such special law and that the other provisions of the Limitation Act including section 5 shall not apply in determining limitation under the special law.

18. Here, we find that within the limitation period the petitioners filed the BLL cases on 30.01.2008 before the Labour Court, Dhaka which had no territorial jurisdiction to adjudicate the cases. Having come to know about the wrong forum, the petitioners filed the same on 05.05.2008 before the proper forum i.e 2nd Labour Court, Dhaka taking back the same from the earlier Court in accordance with law but it was, of course, beyond the prescribed period. In the aforesaid facts, it is now a question as to whether the time from 30.01.2008 to 04.05.2008 consumed in the wrong forum can be excluded in determining the limitation period for filing these cases under the Act, 2006, a special law. To get answer to this question, let us first examine section 14 of the Limitation Act, relevant portion of which runs as follows:

14. Exclusion of time of proceeding bonafide in court without jurisdiction-

(1)------------

(2) In computing the period of limitation prescribed for any application, the time during which the applicant has been prosecuting with due diligence another civil proceeding, whether in a Court of first instance or in a Court of appeal, against the same party for the same relief shall be excluded, where such proceeding is prosecuted in good faith in a Court which, from defect of jurisdiction, or other cause of a like nature, is unable to entertain it.

Explanation I-In excluding the time during which a former suit or application was pending, the day on which that suit or application was instituted or made, and the day on which the proceedings therein ended, shall both be counted.

Explanation II-For the purpose of this section, a plaintiff or an applicant resisting an appeal shall be deemed to be prosecuting a proceeding.

Explanation For the purposes of this section misjoinder of parties or of causes of section shall be deemed to be a cause of a like nature with defect of jurisdiction."

19. Thus section 14 of the limitation Act provides that to determine limitation in filing an application, the time consumed before the wrong forum shall be excluded.

<u>20. According to section 29(2)(a) of the Limitation Act, under the special law section 14 of the said Act is applicable for determining limitation period unless it is expressly excluded in the said special law. Here, the BLL cases were filed under section 33 of the Act, 2006 and we do not find here that section 33 of the Act, 2006 or any relevant provision of the said Act excludes application of section 14 of the Limitation Act. Therefore, in view of section 29 (2) of the Limitation Act, we are led to hold that section 14 of the Limitation Act is applicable in these particular cases under the Act, 2006 and so, excluding the time consumed before the wrong forum, the cases were filed before the 2nd Labour Court. Dhaka well within the limitation period in view of section 14 read with section 29 of the Limitation Act. We, therefore, hold that the Tribunal misconceived the legal position in holding the cases time barred.</u>

<u>21. In arriving at this finding, the Tribunal relied upon the case of Syed Ahmed Bhuyan and others Vs Karnaphali Fertilizer Company Limited reported in 10 MLR (AD) 153 wherein their Lordships held that the grievance petition was not submitted within the prescribed time provided by the relevant Act and it was being under special law delay could not be condoned. In that particular case, there was no fact of any pending proceeding before the wrong forum and so question of applicability of sections 14 and 29 of the Limitation Act did not arise. The case in hand having distinguishable fact, the aforesaid case cannot be applied in this particular case. Rather, the view of ours finds support from the case of The Manager, Spencer & Co. (Pak) Limited Vs. Spencer Employees Union reported in 25 DLR (HCD) 102 wherein their Lordships held as under:</u>

<u>"Mr. Behtar Ali, the learned Advocate for the Management has firstly contended that the award of the Second Labour Court is illegal and without jurisdiction in view of the fact that the case as filed by the first party Union was barred by limitation. Mr. Behtar Ali has pointed out that section 6 of the said Act provides that a party to whom a certificate is issued under sub-section (4) of section 5 is entitled to file a labour case of this nature within a period of 90 days from the date of the issue of such certificate of failure. In the present case, he contended that the case was actually filed before the Second Labour Court which is the appropriate forum on 14.3.68, though the certificate of failure was issued on 7.8.67. According to the learned Advocate, the case is, therefore, clearly barred by limitation. It is to be noticed that the first party Union filed the case on 10.8.67 i.e. three days after the issue of the certificate of failure before the First Labour Court and the First Labour Court kept the matter pending before them until 14.3.68 and it is only not hat day. i.e 14.03.68 that the First Labour Court returned the plaint to the first party Union. A question therefore arose whether the first party is entitled to the extension of the period from 10.8.67 to 14.3.68 in computing the period of limitation. It is claimed by the first party that this period was bonafide spent in pursuing the legal relief before another forum and as such they are entitled to the benefit of the extension of this period as provided under section 14 of the Limitation Act. Mr. Behtar Ali, however, has contended that section 14 of the Limitation Act cannot be applicable in the labour dispute case under the provisions of the Labour Disputes Act. Sub-section (2) of section 12 of the said Act clearly provides that the Labour Court for the purpose of adjudicating and determining any Labour dispute shall he deemed to be a Civil Court and shall have the same powers as are vested in Courts under Code of Civil Procedure. Section 29 of the Limitation Act provides that where any special or local law prescribes a period of limitation which is different from that of the First Schedule of the Limitation Act, then the provisions of section 3 of the Limitation Act will apply and for the purpose of determining any period of limitation for any suit, appeal or application under any special or local law the provision as contained in section 4, sections 9 to 18 and section 23 shall apply provided the same is not specifically  negative by the special law. It is obvious therefore, that section 14 of the Limitation Act will have application in these matters, in view of the fact that there is no specific prohibition of the application of such law.  In view of the above, we are satisfied that the period from 10.8.67 to 13.3.68 during which the first party were prosecuting their relief bonafide and with due diligence before another court should he excluded and as such the case should be held to have been clearly filed within time. The point raised by the learned Advocate for the appellant on this ground, therefore, appears to have no substance. The case of Ice Factories Workers' Union Vs. Messers Enulji Dinshaw Ice Factory Karahi, 1967 PLC 437 and P.W.R. Union vs. Chairman, Pakistan Western Railway, Labour, 1969 PLC 370 as relied upon by Mr. Behter All have no application to the facts and circumstances of this case." (Underlined)</u>

22. Therefore, we hold that the BLL cases were not barred by limitation and the finding of the Tribunal in this regard was erroneous.

<u>23. Now the second question arises as to maintainability of the case. In this regard, we have gone through two cited cases i.e 34 DLR (AD) 37 and 57 DLR (AD) 155. In the case reported in 34 DLR (AD) 37, the apex Court held that the DIT not being a commercial</u>

<u>establishment its employees can not invoke the provisions of the labour law. On the other hand, in the case reported in 57 DLR (AD) 155 the employer was “পল্লী দারিদ্র বিমোচন ফাউন্ডেশন”. Question of applicability of Labour law in respect of workers of this Foundation having arisen in this case, the apex Court held as under:</u>

<u>"Petitioner Palli Daridra Bimochon Foundation (the Foundation) has been established under the provision of Palli Daridra Bimochon Foundation Act, 1999 (Act XXIII of 1999) (the Act). The activities of the Foundation have been spelled out in section 15 of the Act. In section 15(2) (Ka) and (Kha) of the Act it has been mentioned:</u>

<u>“(ক) এমন কোন চুক্তি সম্পাদন করা যাহাতে ফাউন্ডেশনের বিবেচনায় যথাযথ ফিস বা সুদ পরিশোধের শর্ত কোন সুবিধাভোগীকে ঋন প্রদানের ব্যবস্থা থাকে।</u>

<u>(খ) ফাউন্ডেশন সুদ প্রদানের শর্তসহ উহার বিবেচনায় যথাযথ অন্যান্য শর্তাদিতে কোন সুবিধাভোগীর নিকট হইতে সঞ্চয় বা বিনিয়োগ সেবা প্রদানের জন্য অর্থ গ্রহণের চুক্তিতে আবদ্ধ হওয়া।”</u>

<u>24. In section 16 manner of formation of the Foundation has been given and the clause ‘চ’ of sub-section 1 of section 16 reads as:</u>

<u>‘(চ) ব্যবসায় এবং অন্যান্য কায্যাক্রম হইতে প্রাপ্ত মুনাফা এবং আয়।”</u>

<u>It was the definite case of the respondent No.1 herein that the petitioner herein charges interest @ 16% to 18% from its loanees. This fact has not been disputed. If this fact is considered along with the provisions of section 15(2) (ক) and (vi) and section 16 (1) (চ) then it becomes clear that the Foundation is engaged in business as well as trade and thus is an industry in the light of the definition of industry given in section 2 (XIV) of the IRO. Since the Foundation answers the definition of industry as defined in section 2(XIV) of the IRO the employees of the Foundation. Who answer the definition of worker' as defined in section 2(XXVIII) of the IRO, are very much entitled to form a Trade Union and that having had done, they had a right to get registration of the Trade Union in case of satisfying the requirement of law as in section 8 of the IRO and that the 2nd Labour Court having had found that the members of the respondent No.1 therein satisfied the requirement of law as in section 8 of the IRO and thereupon in making direction to the Registrar of Trade Unions to register the respondent No.1 as the Trade Union as did not commit any illegality, the High Court Division in refusing to interfere with the order of the Labour Court impugned in the Writ Petition was not in error since the Foundation is engaged in economic activities i.e. it charges interest from its loanees at a high rate and, as such, the activities of the Foundation cannot be considered as non-profit making activities and for that matter the Foundation cannot be considered as non-profit making organization or out and out a philanthropic organization and consequently, as the Foundation answers the definition of industry as in section 2(XIV) of the IRO, its employees, who answer the definition of 'worker' as in section 2(XXVIII) of the IRO, are very much competent to form 3 Trade Union and to get the same registered. The learned Counsel for the petitioner in support of his submission that the organizations which are organized and run without motive of profit making, formation of Trade Union has been disapproved by this Court and in support thereof has referred to the cases reported in 52 DLR 151 and 43 DLR 655. Facts of the said 2 cases are quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant case and, as such, the same have no relevancy to and bearing on the question that calls for adjudication in the instant case."</u>

25. Relying upon this case, Mr. Saqeb Mahbub vehemently argues that the nature and activities of the NSC are identical with those of “পল্লী দারিদ্র বিমোচন ফাউন্ডেশন” and so, as per 'ratio' laid down by the apex Court, the labour law is applicable in respect of employees of the NSC. To strengthen this submission, he draws our attention to the National Sports Council Act, 1974 and the budget of the NSC whereupon he tried to point out that the NSC earns profit by' way of selling tickets, publication and marketing of the magazine and expends the same for running the organization, the NSC. Mr. Mahbub has also draws our attention to the relevant provisions of “পল্লী দারিদ্র বিমোচন ফাউন্ডেশন আইন, ২০০৯” (shortly, the Act, 1999).

26. Section 1(4) of the Act, 2006 (labour law) provides that this Act shall not apply to certain establishments and workers thereof as mentioned therein. Relying upon section 1(4) (f) of the Act, 2006, the Tribunal came to the finding as to maintainability and so, let us scans the same which runs as follows:

“১। সংক্ষিপ্ত শিরোনাম, প্রবর্তন এবং প্রয়োগ।–

(১)-(৩)-----------

(৪)উপ-ধারা (৩) এ যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন, এই আইন নিম্নলিখিত প্রতিষ্ঠান সমূহ বা শ্রমিকগণের উপর প্রযোজ্য হইবে না, যথাঃ-

(ক)-(চ)

(ছ) শিক্ষা, প্রশিক্ষন বা গবেষনা প্রতিষ্ঠান;

(জ)-(ত)-----------”

27. In the light of aforesaid provision, let us now see the status of the NSC in order to determine the question of applicability of the labour law as the Tribunal held. Admittedly, the NSC has been created by the National Sports Council Act, 1974. (shortly the Act, 1974). The preamble of the said Act are as follows:

"An Act to provide for the constitution of a Council for the development and regulation of sports and co-ordination of sports activities in Bangladesh.

Whereas it is expedient to provide for the constitution of a Council for the development and regulation of sports and co-ordination of sports activities in Bangladesh and for matters connected therewith;"

28. Further, relevant portions of sections 10 and 15 of the said Act are as follows:

"10. The functions of the Council shall be-

(a)-(c)

(d) the institution and execution of training and coaching schemes for international sports 	events;

(e) - (k)

15. (1) There shall be a fund to be called the [National Sports Council Fund] to which shall be credited all receipts of the Council including:-

(a) grants from the Government;

(b) member ship fees;

(c) donation in cash or kind;

(d) sale proceeds from tickets, or any fee or other payment released, for entry into any 	sports event arranged by the Council.

(2) The [National Sports Council Fund] shall be applied to meet all such expenditure, including payment of salaries of the officers and employees of the Council, as is necessary to carry out the purposes of the Act, and shall be administered in such manner as may be prescribed by rules and, until such rules are made, in such manner as the Executive Committee, with the approval of the Chairman, direct.

"29. On a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions, it appears that the NSC was established for the purpose of developing and regularization of sports and co-ordination of sports in Bangladesh by the functions' amongst others, by the institution and execution of training and coaching schemes for international sports events. Referring to its activities by way of selling tickets of the stadiums and publication of magazine relating to sports events, the learned Advocate submits that although in the functions of the NSC, training and coaching scheme have been provided but the Council itself generates fund by selling tickets and publication of magazine and thereby gains profit and as such the Council does not come within the purview of section 1(4)(g) of the Act, 2006 and referring to section 15 of the NSC Act, the learned Advocate has compared with section 16 of the Foundation Act, 1999 providing Fund of the Foundation.

30. On careful scrutiny of both the Acts, we find that the Council (NSC) has been established to develop sports of the country. Although it has got some activities of generating fund by way of selling tickets and publication of magazine but in course of function, as to training and coaching, the Council itself does not generate any fund or profit as section 1(4)(g) of the Act, 2006 attracts and considering this view the Tribunal rightly held that the Act, 2006 is not applicable in respect of employees of the NSC and so any activity under the labour law including activities of trade union are not permitted in the NSC in view of section 1(4)(g) of the Act, 2006.

31. We have also gone through the case of the Palli Daridra Bimochon Foundation Vs. Palli Daridra Bimochon Foundation Karmachari Union Bangladesh (Proposed) and others reported in 57 DLR (AD) 155 as well as “পল্লী দারিদ্র বিমোচন ফাউন্ডেশন আইন, ১৯৯৯” (shortly, the Act, 1999) by which the said Foundation was created. The preamble of the said Act, 1999 provides as follows:

“যেহেতু দারিদ্র বিমোচনের জন্য গণপ্রজাতন্ত্রী বাংলাদেশ সরকার ও কানাডা সরকারের সাহায্যপৃষ্ট এবং বাংলাদেশ পল্লী উন্নয়ন বোর্ড কর্তৃক পরিচালিত আরডি-১২ প্রকল্প, আর,বি…পি, এবং আর,বি…আই,পি,ক দরিদ্র ও অসুবিধাগ্রস্ত ব্যক্তিদের সেবার নিয়োজিত একটি স্ব-শাসিত সুদৃঢ়, আর্থিক স্বনির্ভর ও অমুনাফাকাঙ্খী সংস্থা হিসাবে গড়িয়া তোলার উদ্দেশ্যে একটি স্ব-শাসিত নন-ব্যাংকিৎ আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানে রুপান্তর করিবার সিদ্ধান্ত গৃহীত হইয়াহে;

এবং যেহেতু দারিদ্র বিমোচন, দরিদ্র ও অসুবিধাগ্রস্ত ব্যক্তিদের অর্থনৈতিক ও সামাজিক অগ্রগতি বৃদ্ধি ও নারী-পুরুষ সমতা বিকাশের উদ্দেশ্যে পল্লী দারিদ্র বিমোচন ফাউন্ডেশন প্রতিষ্ঠা করিবার এবং তৎসম্পর্কিত অন্যান্য বিষয়ের জন্য বিধান করা সমীচীন ও প্রয়োজনীয়।”

32. Moreover, section 16 of the said Act, 1999 provides as follows:

“১৬। (১) ফাউন্ডেশনের একটি তহবিল থাকিবে যাহাতে জমা হইবে,-

(ক) সরকার কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত অনুদান ও ঋন;

(খ) বিদশী এজেন্সী ‘ও সংস্থাসমুহ হইতে প্রাপ্ত অনুদান ও ঋন

(গ) অন্যান্য উৎস হইতে প্রাপ্ত ঋন;

(ঘ) সম্পত্তি, বিনিয়াগ এবং বন্ড ও ডিবেঞ্চার বিক্রয় হইতে প্রাপ্ত আয়;

(ঙ) দাতা সংস্থাসমূহ হইতে প্রাপ্ত অনুদান ও সহায়তা

(চ) ব্যবসায় এবং অন্যান্য কার্যক্রম হইতে প্রাপ্ত মুনাফা এবং আয়;

(ছ) ফাউন্ডশন কর্তৃক প্রাপ্ত অন্যান্য অর্থাদি।

(২)-(৩)

(Underlined)

33. On a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions and activities of the Foundation, it

appears that although it is a philanthropic organization but the Foundation itself is doing the business of microcredit financing in accordance with its preamble “নন-ব্যাংকিং আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান”. We are, therefore, of the view that the character and nature as well as the activities of the Foundation are not similar to those of the NSC. Therefore, the views expressed by the apex Court in the case of Palli Daridra Bimochon Foundation Vs. Palli Daridra Bimochon Foundation Karmachari Union Bangladesh (Proposed) and others reported in 57 DLR (AD) 155 are distinguishable and so we are unable to accept the submission of Mr. Saqeb Mahbub as to maintainability of the case under section 33(1) of the Act, 2006.

34. Regard being had to the above, we do not find any impropriety in the judgment of the Tribunal so far as it relates to the point of maintainability of the Labour Case.

35. In view of the above discussions, we are not inclined to interfere with the judgment and order passed by the Tribunal in all the appeals mentioned above.

36. Accordingly the Rules Nisi issued in the Writ Petitions no. 7467 of 2011, 7468 of 2011 and 7469 of the 2011 are discharged without any order as to costs.

37. Communicate a copy of the judgment and order to the respondents at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Borhanuddin, J: As common question of law and facts are involved in these reference applications and the parties being same they are heard together and are being disposed of by this judgment.

2. It has been stated in the Reference Application No.129 of 2007 that the assessee applicant is a Private Limited Company incorporated under the companies Act engaged in the business of manufacturing and marketing M.S. rod, bar, angles and also in the business of ship breaking. The assessee applicant submitted its income tax return for the assessment year 2004-2005 showing total income at taka 1,79,01,099/- on the basis of audited books of account. But the concern Deputy Commissioner of taxes (hereinafter referred to as the DCT) without accepting the return issued notice under Section 83(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 (hereinafter referred to as the Ordinance, 1984). Pursuant to the notice, authorized representative of the assessee appeared before the DCT with supporting documents maintained by the assessee. After hearing the authorized representative and considering submitted papers/documents, the DCT concern ignoring audited books of account made assessment adding taka 62,04,614/- to the assessee applicant's income for the said assessment year. The assessee applicant being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the assessment order of the DCT filed Income Tax Appeal no.43/Coy-2/T:Z: -1/2005-2006 before the Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal), Taxes Appeal Zone, Chittagong, challenging various disallowances and additions made in the assessment order. The Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal) vide order dated 30.05.2006 modified order of the DCT by granting some relief's to the appellant. Against the order passed by Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal), the assessee applicant preferred Income Tax Appeal no.1853 of 2006-2007 before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Chittagong Bench, Chittagong. After hearing the parties, Taxes Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal in part vide order dated 07.12.2006, which is impugned herein.

3. It has been stated in the Reference Application No.184 of 2008 that the assessee applicant is a Private Limited Company incorporated under the companies Act engaged in the business of manufacturing and marketing M.S. rod, bar, angles and also in the business of ship breaking. The assessee applicant submitted its income tax return for the assessment year 2005-2006 showing net loss at taka 2,71,77,285/- on the basis of audited books of account. But the concern DCT without accepting the return issued notice under Section 83(l) of the Ordinance, 1984. Pursuant to the notice, authorized representative of the assessee appeared before the DCT with supporting documents maintained by the assessee. After hearing the authorized representative and considering submitted papers/documents, the DCT concern ignoring audited books of account assessed income of the assessee applicant at taka 2,28,11,740/- for the said assessment year. The assessee applicant being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the assessment order of the DCT filed Income Tax Appeal No.75/Coy-2/T:Z: -1/2006-2007 before the Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal), Taxes Appeal Zone, Chittagong, challenging various disallowances and additions made in the assessment order. The Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal) vide order dated 07.06.2007 modified order of the DCT by granting some reliefs to the appellant. Against the order passed by Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal), the assessee applicant preferred income Tax Appeal no.1443 of 2007-2008 before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Chittagong Bench, Chittagong. After hearing the parties, Taxes Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal in part vide order dated 30.12.2007, which is impugned herein.

4. Pursuant to the notice, authorized representative of the assessee appeared before the DCT with supporting documents maintained by the assessee. The Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal) vide order dated 24.07.2008 modified order of the DCT by granting some reliefs to the appellant. Against the order passed by Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal), the assessee applicant preferred Income Tax Appeal No.1899 of 2008-2009 before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Chittagong Bench, Chittagong. After hearing the parties, Taxes Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal in part vide order dated 29.01.2009, which is impugned herein.

5. It has been stated in the Reference Application No.I68 of 2008 that the assessee applicant is a Private Limited Company incorporated under the companies Act engaged in the business of manufacturing and marketing M.S. rod, bar and angles. The assessee applicant submitted its income tax return for the assessment year 2005-2006 showing net loss at taka 13,05,820/- on the basis of audited books of account. But the concern DCT without accepting the return issued notice under Section 83(1) of the Ordinance, 1984. Pursuant to the notice, authorized representative of the assessee appeared before the DCT with supporting documents maintained by the assessee. After hearing the authorized representative and considering submitted papers/documents, the DCT concern ignoring audited books of account assessed income of the assessee applicant at taka 58,17,945/- for the said assessment year. The assessee applicant being aggrieved by' and dissatisfied with the assessment order of the DCT filed Income Tax Appeal No.76/Coy-2/T:Z: -1/2006-2007 before the Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal), Taxes Appeal Zone, Chittagong, challenging various disallowances and additions made in the assessment order. The Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal) vide order dated 07.06.2007 modified order of the DCT by granting some solace to the appellant. Against the order passed by Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal), the assessee applicant preferred Income Tax Appeal no.1444 of 2007-2008 before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Chittagong Bench, Chittagong. After hearing the parties, Taxes Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal in part vide order dated 30.12.2007, which is impugned herein.

6. It has been stated in the Reference Application No.100 of 2009 that the assessee applicant is a Private Limited Company incorporated under the companies Act engaged in the business of manufacturing and marketing M.S. rod, bar and angles. The assessee applicant submitted its income tax return for the assessment year 2006-2007 showing net loss at taka 5,85,360/- on the basis of audited books of account. But the concern DCT without accepting the return issued notice under Section 83(1) of the Ordinance, 1984. Pursuant to the notice, authorized representative of the assessee appeared before the DCT with supporting documents maintained by the assessee. After hearing the authorized representative and considering submitted papers/documents, the DCT concern ignoring audited books of account assessed income of the assessee applicant at taka 66,05,842/- for the said assessment year. The assessee applicant being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the assessment order of the DCT filed Income Tax Appeal No.31/Coy-2/T:Z: -1/2007-2008 before the Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal), Taxes Appeal Zone, Chittagong, challenging various disallowances and additions made in the assessment order, The Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal) vide order dated 21.05.2008 modified order of the DCT by granting some solace to the appellant. Against the order passed by Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal), the assessee applicant preferred Income Tax Appeal no.1070 of 2008-2009 before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Chittagong Bench, Chittagong. After hearing the parties, Taxes Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal in part vide order dated 27.11.2008, which is impugned herein.

7. In all these reference applications the following questions have been formulated for answer under Section 160 of the Ordinance, 1984:

"i) Whether the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was justified in maintaining estimation of sales and thereby making addition with total income of the company discarding trading version as audited in accordance with law and without complying the provision of section 83(2) and 30A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984?

ii) Whether the Taxes Appellate Tribunal just was j maintaining disallowance of expenses from profit and loss accounts without complying the provision of section 83(2) and 30A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984?

8. In all reference applications it has been contended that the Appellate Tribunal failed to consider that the accounts of applicant companies were duly audited and prepared complying provisions of Section 35 of the Income Tax Ordinance and disclosed its true income in return pursuant to notice under Section 83(1) of the ordinance, 1984. Applicant-Companies did not deviate from the method of accounting maintained in the earlier years and as such, true profit could easily be deduced but the books of account prepared and certified by a chartered accountant were rejected without pin pointing any defect in the accounts specifying reason in violation of Sections 35(4) and 30A of the ordinance, 1984. It is also contended that the Appellate Tribunal did not consider that mandatory requirement of Section 83(2) of the ordinance, 1984, was not complied with inasmuch as it is provided in law that if the concern Deputy Commissioner of Taxes disagree on any specified point of the audited account then it is incumbent upon the DCT to issue further notice.

9. Mr. Mosharraf Hossain, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the assessee-applicant in all reference applications submitted that the Taxes Appellate Tribunal failed to consider that assessee-applicant prepared books of account complying provisions of section 35(3) of the Ordinance, 1984, and disclosed its true income in return in compliance with the notice served under section 83(1) of the Ordinance but DCT concern rejected the books of account certified by a chartered accountant without' pin pointing any defect in the account specifying reason in violation of Sections 35(4) and 30A of the Ordinance, 1984. He also submitted that Tribunal failed to consider that DCT concern did not comply requirement of the mandatory provision of law inasmuch as section 83(2) of the Ordinance provides that the DCT after hearing the person appearing or considering evidence produced pursuant to notice under Section 83(1) of the Ordinance, if he require any explanation on certain point it is incumbent upon the DCT to issue another written notice to consider other evidence on that point. Ile next submitted that mandatory obligation on the part of the DCT is to issue further notice under section 83(2) of the Ordinance, 1984, if he disagree on any specified point of the audited account submitted by the assessee. He again submitted that Tribunal failed to consider that appellate authority disposed appeal of the assessee-applicant without complying provisions of section 155(5) of the Ordinance, 1984. He submitted that the appellate tribunal being the last court of fact disposed of the appeal without complying provisions of section 159(2) of the Ordinance, 1984. He further submitted that the DCT concern rejected book version relating to disallowance claimed by the assessee-applicant in trading account without specifying reason for such disallowance or deduction in violation of the mandatory provision of section 30A of the Ordinance, 1984. Mr. Mosharraf Hossain relied much on the findings of the case of Mark Builders Limited-Vs- Commissioner of Taxes, reported in 59 DLR 463, to substantiate his submission relative to further notice under Section 83(2) of the Ordinance, 1984. In support of his other submissions, learned Advocate referred to the case of Commissioner of Income -Tax, East Pakistan, Dacca-Vs- Messrs. Rathna Tea Estate, Dacca, 19 DLR(SC) 538, the case of Fazkir Rahman Chowdhry-Vs- Deputy Commissioner, Dacca and others, reported in 19 DLR (SC) 543.

10. On the other hand, Mr. Sarder Rashed Jahangir learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the respondent in all reference applications at the very outset submitted that the case of Mark Builders Limited vs. Commissioner of Taxes, reported in 59 DLR 463, is not applicable in the present case because assessment year of the mark builders limited case was 1998-1999 i.e. income year was 1997-1998 when there was a specific provision in Section 83(2) of the Ordinance, 1984, to serve further notice but said provision was repealed by the Finance Act 1998. He also submitted that service of notice is a disputed question of fact and cannot be determined in reference application and the question of law relating service of notice does not arise from the order of Taxes Appellate Tribunal. He next submitted that no further notice under section 83(2) of the Ordinance, 1984, requires after issuance of notice under sections 79 and 83(1) of the Ordinance, 1984. He again submitted that it is apparent from assessment order that the DCT concern in allowing or deducting trading account or profit and loss account of the assessee pin pointed reasons for such disallowance or deduction complying provisions of section 30A of the Ordinance, 1984. He also submitted that section 155(6) of the Ordinance provides that if the assessee was prevented by sufficient cause from producing any evidence before the DCT then he can produce the same before 1st Appellate Authority assigning reason for not producing the same to the DCT concern. He submitted that it was duty of the assessee-applicant to produce all relevant documents in support of his return which cannot be shifted to the taxing authority. He again submitted that section 181(5) of the Company Act provides that the voucher relevant to any entry in books of account is a part of such books of account and as such DCT concern rightly rejected disallowances claimed by the assessee-applicant for want of relevant vouchers. He further submitted that it is already settled by our apex court that merely because a particular method of accounting was followed and audited by a chartered accountant firm, the same cannot be said to be sacrosanct when the expenditures were not verifiable. In support of his submissions, learned Deputy Attorney General referred to the case of Eskayef Bangladesh Ltd.-Vs- Commissioner of Taxes, reported in 58 DLR 531; the case of Commissioner of Income Tax A-Chittagong-Vs-Harendra Kumar Shil, reported in 34 DLR (AD)298.

11. Heard learned advocate for the assessee-applicant and learned Deputy Attorney General for the respondent. Perused reference applications, affidavits-in-reply, supplementary affidavits, relevant provisions of law and decisions cited by the learned Advocates.

12. On perusal of all reference applications, it appears that questions of law formulated in the applications under 160 of the Ordinance are identical which relates to sections 83(2) and 30A of the Ordinance, 1984. Admittedly, the assessee-applicant submitted its return under section 75 of the Ordinance, 1984. Section 77 of the Ordinance provides for notice for filing return which is not relevant here. When an assessee submits return under section 75 of the Ordinance, 1984, and the DCT concern is not satisfied without requiring presence of the person who filed the return or the production of evidence that the return is correct and complete, lie shall serve on such person a notice under section 83(1) of the Ordinance, 1984, to appear before the DCT concern or to produce before him or at his office any evidence in support of his return. Question is whether it is incumbent upon the DCT concern to serve 2nd notice upon the assessee under Section 83 (2) of the Ordinance, 1984, if the DCT require further explanation/evidence on certain point after completion of the formalities under Section 83(1) of the Ordinance, 1984. Learned Advocate for the assessee-applicant submitted that service of written notice under Section 83(2) of the Ordinance, 1984, is mandatory, if further explanation or evidence requires. He cited the case of Mark Builders Limited vs. Commissioner of Taxes, reported in 59 DLR 463, in support of his submission.

13. Learned Deputy Attorney General pointed out that the case of Mark Builders Limited-Vs- Commissioner of Taxes, relates to assessment year 1998-1999 i.e. income year 1997-1998. The case was decided on the basis of unamended Section 83 of the Ordinance, 1984, which was amended by the Finance Act 1998. Let us peruse the language of unamended Section 83 as it was before commencement of Finance Act, 1998, and amended version of Section 83 of the Ordinance, 1984.

14. Section 83 as it was before 1998 is quoted herein under:

"83. Assessment after hearing and consideration of evidence-

(1) Where a return or revised return has been filed by a person under Chapter VIII and the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is not satisfied with the income shown in the return or with the accounts or the evidences submitted with the return, he  shall give a notice to such person in writing specifying therein the defects or shortcomings in the return or any other reason for his dissatisfaction so as to provide an opportunity to the person to furnish in writing his explanation or clarification for rectifying or removing the defects or shortcomings or the reason for dissatisfaction, as the case may be, and the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes shall, if satisfied with such explanation or clarification, assess, within thirty days of the receipt of the explanation or clarification, recording his finding and the basis of computation of total income in the assessment order, the total income of the assessee and determine the tax payable by him, and communicate the order to the assessee within thirty days next following.

(2) Where the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is not satisfied with the explanation or clarification furnished under sub-section (1) or where no such explanation or clarification is furnished, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes shall serve on the  person concerned a notice requiring him,  on a date therein to be specified, to appear before him, or to produce or cause to be produced before him or at his office, any evidence in support of the return and after hearing the person appearing, or considering the evidence produced before him, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes shall assess, recording the basis of computation in the assessment order, the total income of assessee and determine the tax payable by him, within thirty days after the  completion of the hearing or consideration, as the case may be, and communicate the order to the assessee within thirty days next following."

<u>15. Said section 83 is amended by the Finance Act, 1998. Amended Section 83 of the Ordinance, 1984, runs as follows:</u>

<u>"83. Assessment after hearing:</u>

<u>(1) Where a return or revised return has been filed under Chapter VIII and the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is not satisfied without requiring the presence of the person who filed the return or the production of evidence that the return is correct and complete, he shall serve on  such person a notice requiring him, on a date to be therein specified, to appear before the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, or to produce or cause to be produced before him or at his office, any evidence in support of the return.</u>

<u>(2) The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes shall, after hearing the person appearing,  or considering the evidence produced in  pursuance of the notice under sub-section (1) and also considering such other evidence, if any, as he may require on  specified points, by an order in writing assess, within thirty days after the completion of the hearing or consideration, as the case may be, the total income of the assessee and determine the sum payable by him on the basis of such assessment, and communicate the order to the assessee within thirty days next following."</u>

16. Upon close scrutiny of the language of unamended Section 83 of the Ordinance, 1984, it appears that there was a provision in unamended Section 83(2) of the Ordinance to serve further notice upon the assessee to appear or to produce any evidence in support of his return and afford him an opportunity of hearing in addition to notice and formalities under Section 83(1) of the unamended Section 83 of the Ordinance, 1984. But on plain reading of amended Section 83 of the Ordinance, 1984, it is evident that there is no provision to serve further notice under Section 83(2) after completion of formalities under Section 83(1) of the Ordinance, 1984.

17. It is apparent from the language of amended Section 83 that the DCT concern shall hear the person who appear pursuant to notice under Section 83(1) of the Ordinance, 1984, and consider his evidence, if any. On plain reading, I do not find that the DCT concern is bound to serve another notice under section 83(2) of the Ordinance, 1984. Rather it appears from the language of amended Section 83(1) and (2) of the Ordinance, 1984, that after hearing the assessee or his authorized agent and considering his evidence pursuant to notice under section 83(1) and considering such other evidence, if any, as may require on specified points, the DCT concern under Section 83(2) shall assess total income of the assessee and determine the sum payable by him within thirty days after hearing or consideration under Section 83(1) of the Ordinance. There is no scope for further hearing or consideration of evidence under Section 83(2) of the Ordinance, 1984.

18. Apart from that, question of further notice under section 83(2) of the Ordinance, 1984, was not before the Tribunal. In the case of commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay vs. Scindia Steam Navigation Company Ltd. reported in AIR 1961(sc) 1633, their lordships held:

"a question of law is neither raised before the tribunal nor considered by it, it will not be a question arising out of its order notwithstanding that it may arise on the finding given by it."

19. Learned Advocate argued that the assessee-applicant prepared books of account complying provisions of Section 35(3) of the Ordinance, 1984, but the DCT concern rejected the books of account certified by the chartered accountant without pin pointing any defect in the method of accounting or arrived at an opinion that income of the assessee cannot be properly deduced therefrom.

20. This issue is settled by this court earlier. In the case of Eskayef Bangladesh Limited-Vs- Commissioner of Taxes, reported in 58 DLR 531, a Division Bench of this court held:

"Merely because a particular method of accounting was followed and audited by a chartered accountant firm the same cannot be said to be sacrosanct when the expenditures were not verifiable".

<u>21. In the case of Commissioner of Income Taxes-Vs- Harendra Kumar Shil, reported in 34 DLR (AD) 298, our apex court held:</u>

<u>"The assessing officer has been given the power to reject the accounts of the assessee and take recourse to the proviso to section 13".</u>

22. In that case, it also decided that determination of rate of gross profit for the particular year in respect of particular business or trade is purely a question of fact, and that being so it could not be made a ground for making a reference application.

23. Now remains the question of law relating to section 30A of the Ordinance, 1984. Section 30A is quoted herein below:

"30A. Provision for disallowance:-

Notwithstanding anything contained in sections 28, 29 and 30 the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes shall not make any disallowance or deduction for any year from any claim made by an assessee in the trading account or profit or loss account without specifying reason for such disallowance or deduction".

24. From the assessment order appended with reference applications, it appears that in disallowing or deducting disallowances claimed by the assessee-applicant, the DCT concern assigned reason for disallowances or deductions. Authorized representative of the assessee-applicant claimed before the 1st appellate authority that the assessee applicant produced necessary bill, vouchers in support of their expenses but the DCT concern without considering the same disallowed and deducted claimed amount appellate authority categorically observed in its order:

“বিজ্ঞ প্রতিনিধি শুনানীতে তাহার আপত্তির সমর্থন গ্রহণযোগ্য প্রাসংগিক সমুদয় প্রমানাদি উপস্থাপন করিতে পারেন নাই।”

25. Still 1st appellate authority modified order of the DCT reducing in certain heads as well as estimated sale of M. S. rod and scrap. Taxes Appellate Tribunal further reduced estimated sales price of M. S. rod and scrap and also reduced disallowance in certain heads.

26. Learned Advocate for the assessee applicant submitted that the 15 appellate authority disposed appeals without complying provisions of section 155(5) of the Income Tax Ordinance. Section 155(5) of the Ordinance is reproduced below:

"155. (5) Procedure in appeal before the Appellate Joint Commissioner or the Commissioner (Appeals):

The Appellate Joint Commissioner or the Commissioner of (Appeals) may, before disposing of an appeal, make such inquiry as he thinks fit or call for such particulars as he may require respecting the matters arising in appeals or cause further inquiry to be made by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes."

27. Learned Advocate also referred section 159(2) of the I.T. Ordinance to substantiate his argument that the appellate tribunal also failed to dispose of appeals in accordance with law.

28. As it is stated above questions of law formulated in all these reference applications under Section 160 of the I.T. Ordinance relates to Sections 83(2) and 30A of the I.T. Ordinance. No question of law formulated by the assessee-applicant relating to Sections 155/159 or any other Section of the Ordinance, 1984.

29. Section 161(2) of the Ordinance runs as follows:

(1) -----------------------------------------

(2) The High Court Division shall, upon hearing any case referred to it under Section 160, decide the question of law raised thereby and shall deliver its judgment thereon stating the grounds on which such decision is founded and shall send a copy of such judgment under the seal of the Court and signature of the Registrar to the Appellate Tribunal which shall pass such orders as are necessary to dispose of the case in conformity with the judgment.

30. According to above provision of law, High Court Division is under obligation to decide only the question of law raised by assessee applicant under Section 160 of the Ordinance, 1984.

31. From argument of the learned advocate for assessee-applicant, it assumes that whole burden is on the taxes authority to provide opportunity to the assessee if he fails to explain on any point or adduce any evidence. It cannot be a proposition of law. When an assessee file his/her return under Section 75 or revised return under Section 78 of the Ordinance, 1984, it is his/her duty to provide all evidence with the return or revised return.

32. From the discussions made above, we find no illegality with the order passed by the Taxes Appellate Tribunal so as to answer the questions formulated in the reference applications in the negative and in favour of the assessee-applicant. Accordingly, the questions in all the reference applications are answered in the affirmative and in favour of the department.

33. No order as to cost.

End.

parties:
Zamiruddin Ahmed, advocate, Supreme Court of Bangladesh, 40, Dhanmondi Residential Area, Road No 4A, Dacca-9 ----- Petitioner.
