full_judgment:
Amirul Islam Chowdhury, J.—In this matter the hearing was concluded on 2nd April, 1981 and the judgment was reserved. After the Proclamation of Emergency on 30th May, 1981 the matter has been placed today for further hearing. By an affirmed application the petitioner has stated that in view of the Proclamation of Emergency suspending enforcement of fundamental rights granted under the Constitution he will not press the application on the basis of the fundamental rights. It is, however, prayed by the petitioner that the application may be heard and disposed of on other grounds available to him. Since the petitioner is not pressing the application for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights we propose to dispose of the matter after further hearing.

2. In this application under Article 102 of the Constitution the petitioner, Zamiruddin Ahmed, constituted attorney and sister's husband of Air Vice Marshal M.G. Towab (Retired) hereinafter referred to as Towab) has called in question the impugned act of refusing Towab to re-enter Bangladesh or his expulsion therefrom on 1.7.80.

3. The petitioner's case in short is that he is the constituted attorney and sister's husband of Towab, a citizen of Bangladesh by birth. Towab was the Chief of the Air Staff and the Deputy Chief Martial Law Administrator of Bangladesh till 13.4.76 when he resigned from the active service and left Bangladesh on the same day i.e.13.4.76 and went to Federal Republic of Germany and started residing there. During his stay in West Germany his father died. After the death of his father with a view to settling urgent question of inheritance and distribution of the properties of his deceased father and other private matters. Towab arrived at Tejgaon Airport, Dacca on 1.7.80 at about 12.15.P.M. by the Thai International Air Lines flight No. TG-303 from Bangkok holding Bangladesh Passport No. C-183020, valid till 10.4.84 (Annexure 'A') and issued in Bonn on 11.4.79 by the Embassy of Bangladesh. The immigration department checked his passport and other documents and cleared him by stamping his passport. The health authority also gave him clearance. The customs authority also checked his personal effects an allowed him to go. At this stage, one Muzaffar Islam, S.P. Special Branch and officers of respondent with the help of a good number of metropolitan police and armed police forcibly took Towab to the VIP room and detained him there for about 7 hours without assigning any reason. The aforesaid officer asked Towab to go back as he would not be allowed to re-enter Bangladesh and the said officer also informed Towab that this was the decision of the Government of Bangladesh. Towab protested and requested the said officer either to allow him to re-enter Bangladesh or to show him any such decision of the Govt. of Bangladesh in writing, but without any success. He also requested the said officer to allow him to see some lawyers so that he could take action according to law against such decision of the Govt. but this was also denied to him. On the same day i.e. on 1.7.80 at about 6 P.M. one Journalist and one photographer came inside the VIP room and introduced themselves to Towab. But the photographer and the journalist were physically, removed from the VIP room by the police officers present there. At about 7 P.M. on the same day one person in civil dress came in and without introducing himself informed Towab that the Govt. has decided that he should leave for Bangkok by the Thai International Airlines flight No. TG-304. The same evening at about 8 P.M. Towab repeated his requests but without any success. He was forced to board the plane and was supplied with a ticket for the route Dacca-Bangkok Penang of Thai International Airlines by the officer of the respondent. The passport of Towab was returned to him only when he took his seat in the aircraft and it was then found that the stamp of the immigration put in his passport was crossed out. Towab thus failed to re-enter Bangladesh and went back to West (Germany where he is still residing.

4. Respondent contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. Respondent's case has been stated in paragraph 8 of the affidavit-in-opposition which reads as follows:-

"That the allegations as made in paragraphs Nos. 7 to 1, of the petition are incorrect and as such denied it is stated that these are questions of fact and as such petitioner is required to prove the same. The allegation that he was detained in the VIP room is not correct as the Airport Security Officials per-formed their mere routine duties, Mr. M.G. Towab was issued a gratis Bangladesh Passport N.B. 134505 on 11.11.75 while he was acting as the Chief of Air Staff and Deputy Chief Martial Law Administrator. He was holding a diplomatic passport also in that capacity. Since he was relieved on resignation of the offices held under the Government of Bangladesh he was not entitled to hold the diplomatic passport. He did not also change the profession shown in the gratis passport in order to reflect his correct status. Before expiry of the validity of the gratis passport (No. B 134505) he obtained a fresh passport No. 183020 on 13.4.79 from Bangladesh Mission at Bonn, suppressing the fact of his already holding two passports. The requirement of law in such cases is that the applicant must surrender the passport already with him before obtaining a fresh one. The passport issuing authority on receipt of application will cancel the existing passports before issuance of a new one prayed for. Mr. Towab did neither declare nor surrender the passports issued to him earlier and thus came under the mischief of rule 9 of the Bangladesh Passport Rules 1974. This he did presumably with some ulterior motive. He was, therefore, not allowed entry into Bangladesh with the passport obtained in a clandestine manner.'"

5. An affidavit-in-reply has been filed reiterating the statement made in the petition in reply to paragraph 8 of the affidavit-in-opposition. The deponent has stated in paragraph 9 of the affidavit-in reply:

"9. That the statements made in paragraph 8 of the said affidavit are incorrect, misconceived, misleading, evasive and motivated and are denied. This deponent states that the deponent of the said affidavit has affirmed the same without at all consulting the records and/or files of Air Vice Marshal ( Rtd.) M.G. Towab. It is stated that the passport No. B134505 was an official passport issued to him on 11.11.75 under the authority of the present Govt. and he was described thereon as 'Air Vice Marshal'. Thereafter, another passport was issued to him being Diplomatic Passport bearing No. D-00587 while he was performing his duties as the Deputy Chief Martial Law Administrator of Bangladesh. This is the passport which he was holding when he was forced to leave Bangladesh on 30.4.76. On his being forced out of Bangladesh he arrived in West Germany and had to obtain a residence visa as Bangladeshi citizen on the basis of his Bangladesh Passport No. B134505. In keeping with his education and sense of propriety he did not use the Diplomatic Passport he was carrying at that time. The pages of the said Passport having been exhausted he applied for and duly obtained another passport bearing No. B-037483 issued by the Bangladesh Embassy in Born. The pages of the said passport having been exhausted again a new Bangladesh Passport bearing No. 212020 was duly issued to him and thereafter for the same reason another passport bearing No. C-183020 was issued to him duly by the Bangladesh Embassy in Bonn and on the basis of this passport he travelled to Bangladesh on 1.7.1980. He has been described thereon as a "Business Executive" The allegations made by the respondent that Bangladesh passports were renewed by suppressing the fact of old Bangladesh passport and did not give his correct status are not only baseless and Frivolous, but these are also irrelevant for deciding the issue before this Hon’ble Court. It is stated that the respondent did not assign any such reason on 1.7.80. The fact of suppression of holding passports by Mr. Towab, even if true which is denied, does not and deed cannot empower the respondent to prevent a citizen of Bangladesh from interring Bangladesh or to expel him there from. Such an action by the respondent is tantamount to violation of the fundamental right of a citizen of Bangladesh to re-enter Bangladesh as guaranteed under Article 36 of the Constitution. The photocopies of relevant pages for the Bangladesh passports bearing Nos. B-037483, B-212020 and C-183020 issued in favour of Mr. Towab are lumped together and annexed hereto as Annexure 'X'.

<u>6. In the course of the hearing, an application was filed for amendment of the cause title as to the description of the application. In the cause title of the application the petitioner has been described as Mr. Zamiruddin Ahmed, Advocate Supreme Court of Bangladesh, 40, Dhanmondi R. A., Road No. 4 (A), Dacca-9. The amendment sought reads as follows:</u>

<u>"Mr. Jamiruddin Ahmed, advocate, the constituted attorney of Air Vice Marshal Mohammad Golam Towab (Rd), 40, Dhanmondi R. A. Road No. 4(A), Dacca-9".</u>

<u>The application for amendment of the cause title as to the description of the petitioner has been opposed. Mr. M. Sohrab Ali, the learned Deputy Attorney General, submits that the amendment if allowed would change the nature and character of the case and as such the application for amendment should be rejected.</u>

7. In paragraph 1 of the Writ Petition it has been stated this Jamiruddin Ahmed is a close relation and the constituted attorney of (Air Vice Marshal) Towab (Rd). In paragraph 1 of the affidavit to the writ petition Jamiruddin Ahmed has described himself as the constituted attorney of (Air Vice Martial M. G. Towab). In view of the fact that in paragraph 1 of the writ petition and in paragraph 1 of the affidavit to the said petition Jamiruddin Ahmed has disclosed that he is the constituted attorney of Towab we are of the opinion that the amendment prayed for is to be allowed. Moreover, we are of the opinion that the amendment would not in any way change the nature and character of the case. Accordingly, the prayer for amendment of the cause title of the writ petition as to the description of the petitioner is allowed.

<u>8. In the course of hearing a supplementary affidavit has been filed by the petitioner for bringing on record the power of attorney (Annexure 'E') granted by Towab in favour of Jamiruddin Ahmed. The learned Deputy Attorney General submits that the supplementary affidavit should not be accepted. We do not see any reason to refuse the prayer for accepting the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner. The learned Deputy Attorney General submits that each page of the power of attorney has not been signed by the executant (i.e. Towab ) or by the Notary Public who authenticated the power of attorney, as such it will not be safe to accept the power of attorney as a genuine instrument. The original power of attorney has been produced for our examination by Mr. Mainul Hosain, the learned Advocate for the petitioner. It appears that the power of attorney bears a security thread which has been stamped properly by the Notary Public concerned. The stamp of the Notary Public and the security thread appear to be intact. In this view of the matter we do not find any reason to doubt the genuineness of the power of attorney.</u>

9. The learned Deputy Attorney General submits that the power of attorney is invalid and inoperative, in view of the fact that in paragraph 1 of the power of attorney Towab authorised his attorney to file a writ petition to file a legal suit against the President of Bangladesh. In this connection he referred to Article 52 of the Constitution which reads as follows:

"52(1) without prejudice to the pro-visions of article 53, a President or a Vice President shall not be answerable in any court for anything done or omitted by him in the exercise or purported exercise of the functions of his office, but this clause shall not prejudice the right of any person to take proceedings against the Govt." "(2) During his terms of office no criminal proceedings whatsoever shall be instituted or continued against a President or a Vice-President in, and no process for his arrest or imprisonment shall issue from, any court."

10. Mr. Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the expressions in Articles 52(1) and 52(2) are quite different. Article 52(2) provides that no criminal proceedings should be instituted or continued against the President during his term of office. It further provides that in respect of criminal proceedings no process of any court could be issued against the President during his term of office. Article 52(1) does not prohibit the institution or continuance of a proceeding other than criminal proceedings against the President during his terms of office. It merely provides that in respect of proceedings other than criminal proceedings the President shall not the answerable for his official acts. In the instant case, Mr. Mainul Hosein submits, that by the writ petition in question proceeding has been instituted against the Government of Bangladesh and not against the President of Bangladesh. He further pointed out that in paragraph 1 Towab has also authorised his attorney to take appropriate legal action against the Govt. of Bangladesh. In the instant case the writ petition has been filed against the Govt. of Bangladesh. Rule has only been issued against the Government of Bangladesh. Towab has authorised his attorney to take legal action against the Govt. of Bangladesh. Proceeding has been initiated by this application against the Govt. of Bangladesh. In the facts of the instant case, we do not find any substance in the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney General that the power of attorney is invalid and inoperative as it is hit by Article 52 of the Constitution.

11. Section 2 of the Power of Attorney Act, 1882 reads as follows:

"The donee of a power of Attorney may, if he thinks fit, execute or do any assurance, instrument or thing in and with his own name and signature, and his own seal, where sealing is required by the authority of the donor of the power and every assurance, instrument and thing so executed and done, shall be as effectual in law as if it had been executed or done by the donee of the power in the name, and with the signature and seal of the donor thereof."

"This section applies to powers of attorney created by instruments executed either before or after this Act comes into force."

In the case of Standard Vacuum Oil Company Vs. The Trustees for the Port of Chittagong reported in PLD 1961 Dacca 278(289) it was observed as follows:—

"An application for the writ of the nature mentioned in the petition under Article 170 of the Constitution can only be made at the instance of a person who is himself an aggrieved party and if someone, who is not himself aggrieved by an action makes such an application, it must be shown that he is competent under the law to make an application."

In the facts of the instant case we are of the opinion that this application at the instance of the petitioner as attorney of Towab against the Govt. of Bangladesh is maintainable.

12. Mr. Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that in the instant case petitioner Zamiruddin Ahmed has filed the writ petition as constituted attorney and sister's husband of Towab. Apart from being the constituted attorney petitioner Zamiruddin Ahmed is also sister's husband of Towab. The application by the petitioner is maintainable as the petitioner is a close relation of Towab, inasmuch as he is interested in the welfare of Towab. It has been stated that Towab's father is dead. It was necessary for Towab to come to Bangladesh for setting the inheritance as to properties left by his deceased father. It is not disputed that Zamiruddin's wife is a sister of Towab. As such Zamiruddin's wife is entitled , to inherit the properties of Towab's deceased father in accordance with Muslim law Zamiruddin is as such also interested in the inheritances which accrued in favour of Zamiruddin's wife in respect of the estate of Towab's father. In this view, of the matter it cannot be said that Zamiruddin Ahmed, sister's husband of Towab, is not adversely affected by the refusal to allow Towab to re-enter into Bangladesh on 1.7.80. As such it cannot be said that Zamiruddin Ahmed is not an aggrieved person within the meaning of Article 102(1)(a) of the Constitution. With regard to the meaning of aggrieved person reference can be made to the case of the Tariq Transport Co., Lahore Vs. The Sargodha Bhera Bus Service, Sargoda and another reported in (1959) 11 DLR (SC) 140-1958 PLD SC 437; Mia Fazaluddin Vs. Lahore Improvement Trust reported in (1969) DLR (Sr) 225—PLD 1969 SC 223; Dr. A. M. Mahmood Vs. The Syndicate of Dacca University reported in (1966) 18 DLR 33-1970 PLD Dacca 85; Province of East Pakistan Vs. Mitalal Agarwala reported in (1970) 22 DLR (SC) 399-970  PLD SC 399 and Attorney General of the Gambia Vs. N'jie reported in (1961) 2 All England Law Reports 504 (511).

13. In the case of the Tariq Transport Co., Lahore reported in (1959) 11 DLR (SC) 140 it was observed as follows:—

"In a petition for a writ the first question that the court has to consider is whether the petitioner has the locus standi to invoke the extraordinary jurisdiction of the Court and I consider it to be a basic principle that a person seeking judicial review of administrative or quasi judicial action must show that he has a direct personal interest in the act which he challenges before his prayer for review is entertained.

"A petitioner", says. Mr. Justice Frankfurt in his concurrent opinion in Giant Anti-Fascist Refugee Committee V. Mograth, (I) "does not have standing to sue unless he is interested in and affected adversely by the decision of which he seeks review. His interest must be of a personal and not of an official nature. An application for an order of certiorari can only be made by an aggrieved party and not merely by one of the public R.V. Nicholson (2), and in the case of any application for an order of mandamus it is an established rule that the applicant must show that there resides in himself a legal right to the performance of a legal duty by the party against whom the mandamus is sought R.V. Lewisham Union (3)".

14. In the case of Mian Fazal-Din Vs. Lahore Improvement Trust, Lahore reported in 1969 PLD SC 223 (231) it was observed as follows:-

"It is clear from the above that the right considered sufficient for maintaining a proceeding of this nature is not necessarily a right in the strict juristic sense but it is enough if the applicant discloses that he had a personal interest in the performance of the legal duty which if not performed or performed in a manner not permitted loss, law would result in the loss of some personal benefit or advantage or the curtailment of a privilege or liberty or franchise.

15. In the case of East Pakistan Vs. Hiralal Agarwalla reported in (1970) 22 DLR (SC) 399-1970 PLD SC 399 it was observed as follows:-

"With his father incarcerated in prison under a wholly illegal order, it is difficult to appreciate that his son who was naturally afflicted by this tragedy, with an inherent legal right and interest to avert it, was not an aggrieved person within the meaning of Article 98.

In the said decision, their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan refused to ascribe a narow meaning to the term aggrieved person

16. In the case of Dr. A.M.M. Mahmood Vs. The Syndicate of the University of Dacca reported in (1966) 18 DLR 353—P.L.D. 1970 Dacca 85 it was observed as follows:

"An application like the one before us, under Article 98 of the Constitution, can be maintained only when a "legal right" or "franchise" appertaining to the petitioner is encroached or other-wise threatened. This restricted application of Article 98 in the shape of the limitation sought to be imposed upon the meaning of the expression, "any aggrieved party" is clearly untenable and would not bear the test of scrutiny. "It thus appears that the right to make an application has been given to an aggrieved party and not merely to such person who has been injured by a violation of "right" or "franchise" or by a threat thereupon. Article 98 does not say that an application, under it, can be made only by such party who can say that the "right" has been invaded upon and that he has therefore been "injured" in such a sense. The expression "right" is a well-known concept in jurisprudence and the converse of it is "injury".

Mr. Ahmed Sobhan drew our attention to the number of cases where the decisions were based on the requirement of law for issuance of a writ of mandamus. It would be noticed in the first place that Article 98 of the Constitution is available to a much wider class of persons than those who could ask for the issuance of a writ of mandamus.

"It is clear that the words "party aggrieved" have to be understood in the context in which they have been used. If an act is without lawful authority, then any person who has been adversely hit by it can come before a Court and ask for a declaration that such an act is without lawful authority. It does not mean that he must establish that he has been "injured" by violation of pecuniary or proprietary right vested in him or by contravention of any franchise that he claims. We may again note the word "injured" as used in section 45 of the Specific Relief Act is distinct from the expression "aggrieved" in Article 98 of the Constitution."

17. In the case of Attorney General of the Gambia Vs. N'jie reported in (1961)2 All England Law Report 504 (511) it was observed as follows:—

"Lord Esher, M.R. pointed out that in re-Reed, Rowen & Co. Ex. P Official Receiver (14) The words "person aggrieved" are of wide import and should not be subjected to a restrictive interpretation. They do not include of course, a mere busybody who is interfering in things which do not concern him; but they do include a person who has a genuine grievance because an order has been made which prejudicially affects his interests.

<u>18. We have considered the decisions referred to above. We are of the opinion that no hard and fast meaning could be ascribed to the term "aggrieved person." The meaning of the term "aggrieved person" is to be determined with reference to the facts and circumstances of each case. Since we have already held that the applications by petitioner Zamiruddin Ahmed as Attorney of Towab is maintainable, we do not like to express our opinion as to whether Zamiruddin Ahmed as sister's husband of Towab could be regarded as an "aggrieved person" within the meaning of Article 102 (1)(a) of the Constitution in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. We should not be taken to have decided this question.</u>

<u>19. The learned Deputy Attorney General submits that the application suffers from non-joinder of necessary party whose presence is essential for the disposal of the rule. In this connection he relied on the case of Joinal Abedin Vs. The Collector of Central Excise and Land Customs (West Zone), Chittagong reported in 1959 PLD, Dacca 342. In the said case the petition was directed against the Collector of Central Excise and Land Customs (W. Zone) Chittagong who had merely carried out the orders of the Central Board of Revenue. The Board was not made a party in the Writ petition. The Writ was issued against the Collector alone. It was held that the writ issued will not be effective because the Collector will not be in a position to carry out the mandate of the court. Mandamus will not go when it appears that it would be futile in its result. In the instant case writ has been issued against the Govt. of Bangladesh who has not denied that on 1.7.80 Towab was not allowed to re-enter Bangladesh by some of its officers. In the facts of the instant case the writ asked for and issued would not be futile in the absence of the officers of the Govt. of Bangladesh who refused Towab's re-entry into Bangladesh.</u>

<u>In the facts of the instant case the case reported in 1959 PLD Dacca 342 appears to be inapplicable.</u>

<u>20. The learned Deputy Attorney General submits that no demand of justice notice has been served on the respondent as such the application is not maintainable. In this connection he relied on the cases of Dacca National Medical Institute Vs. Province of East Pakistan reported in (1958)10 DLR 343=1963 PLD Dacca 741 (744) and District Magistrate, Lahore Vs. Syed Raja Kazin reported in (1961) 13 DLR (SC) 66= 1961 PLD SC 178 186. In the case reported in (1961) 13 DLR (SC) 66 it was observed as follows:-</u>

<u>The accepted conditions for the grant of a writ of this nature are that it must be preceded by a demand of justice and the refusal thereof and that there should be no other equally expeditious, inexpensive and officious remedy available to the person seeking this extraordinary remedy.</u>

<u>In the case of Dacca National Medical Institute reported in (1958) 10 DLR 343 it was observed as follows:-</u>

<u>"It is now well settled that before issuing a discretionary writ of mandamus, Court insist that the petitioner should make a demand for a justice and that the same should be refused. This is the general and normal practice of the Court and it is only in exceptional cases, that a departure from this practice is allowed. An exception is made only when the Court is of opinion that such a demand for justice and its refusal would be futile."</u>

<u>"If there had been special circumstances in this case which might have led us to hold that it would have been futile to make a demand of the aforesaid description we might not have insisted on the fulfillment of this obligation on the part of the petitioner."</u>

<u>In the case of Sardis Ray Vs. Municipal Commissioner of Sari and others reported in AIR 1956 Cal. 456 it was observed as follows:</u>

<u>"Taken as a writ of mandamus there is a significant absence of any demand for justice" "If it is taken as a writ of certiorari then of course no previous demand is necessary,"</u>

<u>21. In the instant case Towab is living abroad and from the facts and circumstances of the case it can be said that there are special circumstances in this case which would justify a departure from a well-established practice. A demand for justice and its refusal would be futile. For this reason we do not think that the application should be rejected for not serving the demand of justice notice on the respondent.</u>

22. The learned Deputy Attorney General submits that the affidavit of the writ petition not being in conformity with order 19 rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and rule 28 of the High Court Rules, Volume I, the application is liable to be rejected. In this connection he relied on the cases of Vice-Chairman EP Enemy Property, Management Board Vs. Shaha Golam Nabi and others reported in 27 DLR (Appellate Division) 156 and Mritun Joy Paul Vs. Province of East Pakistan reported in (1962) 14 DLR 568= PLD 1963 Dacca 754.

23. In the case reported in 27 DLR (A.D.) 156 it was observed as follows:—

"The reason for conforming with the provisions of verification rule is very weighty, because the purpose of verification of affidavit, is to enable the court to find out which of the facts can he said to be proved by affidavit evidence of rival parties" ...... The essence of verification is to enable the court to find out whether it will be safe to act on such affidavit evidence."

A similar view was also expressed in the case reported in 14 DLR 568.

24. The learned Deputy Attorney General contends that Zamiruddin Ahmed has no personal knowledge of the facts stated in the petition. He has not disclosed the source of his knowledge. In the instant case in paragraph 3 of the supplementary affidavit it has been stated that Zamiruddin Ahmed and his wife were at the relevant time at Tejgaon Airport, Dacca and Zamiruddin Ahmed himself saw the occurrence as such we do not find any substance in the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney General that the petition is liable  to be rejected in as much as the affidavit is not in conformity with Order 19, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and rule 23 of the High Court Rules, Vol. I. It may be mentioned here that the respondent has not denied in the affidavit-in-opposition that Towab holding Bangladesh Passport No. C-183028 arrived at Tejgaon Airport, Dacca on 1.7.80 and that Towab was refused re-entry into Bangladesh, rather in the affidavit-in-opposition the respondent has admitted the fact of refusing Towab to re-enter into Bangladesh.

25. The learned Deputy Attorney General contends that he who seeks remedy under article 102 of the Constitution must come with a clean hand. In the instant case he contends that false statements have been made in the petition suppressing, material facts. In this connection he relied on the cases of Mozaharul Quyyum Hazi reported in PLD 1957 Karachi 773 ; Sind Industrial Estate Ltd. Vs. First Assistant Judge, Hyderabad, W.P reported in PLD 1960 Karachi 826 and Sabir Ahmed Chowdhury. Vs. The Province of East Pakistan reported in 1960 PLD., Dacca 1025. In these decisions the courts were of the view that a petitioner who wants a relief in exercise of the extra ordinary jurisdiction of a writ under the Constitution disentitles himself to obtain relief if he makes misrepresentations or suppresses material facts. In the instant case the allegations against the respondent are that Towab holding Bangladesh Passport No. Cl 83020 arrived at Tejgaon Airport, Dacca on 1.7.80 and was refused re-entry into Bangladesh. These allegations have not been denied in the affidavit in oppositions in the facts and circumstances of the instant case we do not find any substance in the contention of the learned Deputy Attorney General.

26. The learned Deputy Attorney General next submitted that a mandamus has never been issued merely for declaring that an act of a person is unlawful or for declaring the title of a person to an office In this connection he relied on the case of M A. Khaleq Vs. Pakistan reported in (1957) 9 DLR 340 = PLD 1957 Dacea 437 (447). In the said case, it was observed as follows:-

"It is however, contended that since our powers under Article 170 are not restricted merely to issuing writs but also extend to issuing directions or orders, therefore, we could even make a declaration that the petitioners were still employees or that the order terminating their service was null and void. The Rule however in the present case is for a mandamus and for an order in the nature of a mandamus and a mandamus has never issued merely of declaring that an act of a person is unlawful or for declaring the title of a person to an office. The respondents are here to answer the Rule issued against them and not any other case. In this view of the matter, it is not necessary for us to enter into the question as to whether the directions or orders mentioned in Article 170 of the Constitution extend to the making of mere declaratory orders or decrees and we should not be taken to have decided this question."

In the instant case the respondent has not denied the allegations that Towab holding Bangladesh Passport No. C-18 0020 arrived at Tejgaon Airport Dacca on 1.7.80 and was refused re-entry into Bangladesh. The respondent has answered to the rule issued against him and we are required to dispose of the Rule. Moreover, in the facts of the instant case the case reported in DLR 340 is inapplicable.

Mr. Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that on 1.7.80 Towab arrived at Tejgaon Airport with a valid Bangladesh Passport but was refused entry into Bangladesh arbitrarily and without lawful authority.

27. On behalf of the respondent it is contended that the time of obtaining pass-port No. 183020 Towab "did neither declare nor surrender the passports issued to him earlier and thus came within the mischief of Rule 9 of Bangladesh Passport Rules, 1974" (framed under P.O. 9 of 1973) and hence he "was not allowed entry into Bangladesh with the passport obtained in a clandestine manner."

Rule 9 of Passport Rules, 1974 reads as follows:

"Issue of additional passport or travel document-(1) Subject to sub-rule (2) a person holding a passport or travel document shall not be entitled to another passport or travel document unless he surrenders the passport or travel document held by him.

(2) Separate passports or travel documents may be issued to a person if it is necessary to do so for facilitating his visit to different countries."

28. On the basis of rule 9 (2) Mr. Mainul Hosein, the learned advocate for the petitioner, submits that the said rule authorises that additional passport or travel document may be issued to a person if it is necessary to do so for facilitating his visit to different countries. In other words, under rule 9(2) a person may hold more than one passport or travel document if the circumstances so require. There is no absolute prohibition for holding more than one passport or travel document at the same time by a person. Mr. Mainul Hosein further submits if a person obtained a passport on suppression of material facts P.O. 9 of 1973 in article 7 has provided for dealing with such cases.

29. Under article 7 (2) (b) if a passport or travel document has been obtained on suppression or material facts the passport authority may impound or cause to be impounded or revoke the passport or travel document. Article 7 does not authorise anybody to refuse entry into Bangladesh a person holding a Bangladesh passport obtained on suppression of material facts. As such Mr. Mainul Hosein submits that even if the allegation of obtaining the passport in question on suppression of material facts is accepted nobody has been authorised by law to refuse entry into Bangladesh to the holder thereof. in this connection Mr. Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate, also referred to Article 11 of P.O. 9 of 1973 which reads as follows:-

"(1) Whoever—

(a) contravenes the provisions of Article 3 or

(b) knowingly furnishes any false information or suppresses any material fact with a view to obtaining a passport or travel document under this order or without lawful authority alters or attempts to alter or causes to alter the entries made in a passport or travel document; or

c) fails to produce for inspection his document (whether issued under this order or not) when called upon to do so by the prescribed authority; or

d) knowingly uses a passport or travel document issued to another person; or

e) knowingly allows another person to use a passport or travel document issued to him shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to Tk. 2000/- or with both.

2) Whoever abets any offence punishable under clause (1) shall be liable to punishment provided in that clause for that offence.

3) Whoever contravenes any condition of a passport or travel document or any provision of this order or any rule made thereunder for which no punishment is provided elsewhere in this order shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to Tk. 500/- or with both".

30. Under Article 11 (I) for the offence enumerated in clauses (a) to (e) the offender may be punished with imprisonment for a term not exceeding 6 months or with fine not exceeding Tk. 2000/- or with both. For the offences enumerated under Article 11 (3) the offender may be punished with imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3 months or with fine not exceeding Tk. 500/- or with both.

31. Mr. Mainul Husein submits that under Article 11 no one is empowered to reuse entry to a Bangladesh citizen into Bangladesh holding prima facie a valid passport. If non-compliance of rule 9(1) of the Passport Rules 1974 be regarded as an offence, then the offender could be punished with imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3 months or with fine not exceeding Tk. 500/- or with both for such an offence. The holder of the passport could not be refused entry into Bangladesh under the law. Mr. Hosein submits that if there has been any contravention of Passport Act or Rules then Towab could be prosecuted in accordance with law and/or his passport could be impounded. He further submits that no case has yet been filed against Towab for contravention of any law.

32. The learned Dy. Attorney General submits that Passport Act, 1920 and the Rules framed thereunder in 1955 have not been repealed. The Passport Act, 1920 and the Rules framed thereunder are still in force. In this connection the learned Dy. Attorney General referred to section 5 of the Passport Act, 1920 and rule 6 of the Passport Rules, 1955. Section 5 of the Passport Act, 1920 reads as follows:

"Power of removal:—The Bangladesh Government ( may by general or special order, direct the removal of any person from Bangladesh) who in contravention of any rule under section 3 prohibiting entry into Bangladesh without passport has entered therein, and thereupon any officer of the Govt. shall have all reasonable powers necessary to enforce such direction."

Rule 6 of Passport Rules, 1955 reads as follows:

"Duty of person in charge of aircrafts, etc. (1) no person in charge of any aircraft or ship shall bring into Bangladesh from a place outside Bangladesh any person who has pot in his possession a valid passport specifically endorsed by a competent authority, whether by way of visa or otherwise as valid for entry into Bangladesh under these rules.

(2) If any person is brought into Bangladesh in contravention of sub-rule (i) any authority empowered by the Bangladesh Govt. generally or specially in this behalf may direct the owner or person in charge of the aircraft or ship, as the case may be, to take the person back on board and remove him from Bangladesh or otherwise to arrange for the immediate removal from Bangladesh of the said person, and the owner or, as the case may be, the person in charge of the aircraft or ship shall comply with such direction"

33. The learned deputy Attorney General submits that the passport in question being obtained on suppression of material facts cannot be regarded as valid passport. As such the authority was empowered to refuse Towab entry into Bangladesh. It appears from section 5 of the Passport Act, 1920 that the Govt. has power to direct the removal of any person from Bangladesh who in contravention of any rule made under section 3 prohibiting entry into Bangladesh without passport has entered therein and thereupon any officer of the Govt. shall have reasonable power necessary to enforce such direction. In section 5 the words "without passport" have been used. In the instant case Towab arrived at the Tejgaon Airport holding Bangladesh Passport in question. In cannot be said that he was without any passport.

Rule 3 of Passport Rules, 1955 reads:

"Condition for entry into Bangladesh: Subject to the provision herein after contained, no person proceeding from any place outside Bangladesh by sea or by air or by land unless he is in possession of a passport".

34. In the instant case Towab was holding Bangladesh Passport. It is not alleged by the respondent that the passport in question is forged or faked.

Section 4 of the Passport Act, 1920 reads: -

"4 Power of arrest. (1) Any officer of police, not below the rank of a sub-inspector, and any officer of the Customs Department empowered by a general or special order of the Government in this behalf may arrest without warrant any person who has contravened or against whom a reasonable suspicion exists that he has contravened any rule or order made under section 3.

(2) Every officer making an arrest under this section shall, without necessary delay, take or send the person arrested before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case or the officer in charge of the nearest police station and the provision of section 61 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 1898 (V of 1898), shall so far as may be, apply in the case of any such arrest."

35. Section 4 provides for arrest without warrant of any person who has contravened or against whom a reasonable suspicion exists that he has contravened any rule or order made under section 3. It also provides for producing the arrested person before a magistrate.

Rule 4 of Passport Rules 1955 reads: "Requirements of a valid passport: Every such passport:

(a) shall have been issued or renewed by or on behalf of the country of which the person to whom it relates is a subject and shall be within the period of its validity.

(b) shall, except in the case of passports issued to a pardanashin woman, have affixed to it a photograph of the person to whom it relates, duly authenticated by the issuing authority

(c) when issued by on behalf of her Majesty's Government in any part of the Commonwealth, shall have been made valid for entry into Bangladesh unless it is already endorsed as being valid for Commonwealth Countries.

(d) when issued by or on behalf of the Government of a foreign country shall have been endorsed by way of visa for Bangladesh by a Bangladesh diplomatic consular or passport authority or where there is no such authority by an authority authorized in this behalf by the Bangladesh Government. Such visa shall be of one of the following kinds, namely:

(i) a single journey visa valid for six months or for such shorter period as may be specified therein for one journey only to Bangladesh for any legitimate purpose specifying therein the period of stay in Bangladesh not exceeding three months.

(ii) a transit visa valid for six months or for such shorter period as may be specified therein (provided that in no case shall it be valid for country of ultimate destination is valid). For one or more direct journeys through Bangladesh undertaking for the sole purpose of reaching the territory of a foreign state or of a Commonwealth country and occupying in such case not more than fifteen days in Bangladesh, unless an extension of the time for such journey be allowed by a competent authority; or

(iii) a multiple journey visa valid for six months or for such shorter period as may be specified therein for any number of journeys to Bangladesh within a specified period not exceeding one year for any legitimate purpose. The period of stay in Bangladesh specified under such visa shall not exceed three months at a time."

36. Reference in this connection may be made in the Passport (Offences) Act (LVI of 1952). Section 3 of the said Act reads: "Penalties for certain offences relating to passport—

(1) Any person who,—

(a) makes, attests or verifies any statement which he does not know or believe to be true in any document which he knows or has reason to think will be used for obtaining a passport or;

(b) makes use of any statement which he knows or has reason to think to be untrue in any document for obtaining a passport for another person; or

(c) willfully conceals any fact which under the circumstances he ought to disclose for the purpose of obtaining a passport for another person; or

(d) forges, alters or tampers with any passport or with any document which he knows or has reason to believe will be used for obtaining a passport.

(e) uses a passport which he knows or has reason to believe to be forged altered, or tampered with; or

(f) is in wrongful possession for any purpose prejudicial to the interests of the state of a passport not lawfully issued to him ; or

(g) traffics in passport ; shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to two years or with fine or with both. Explanation:—A person who bonafide works for an applicant through it may be for gain does not traffic in passports within meaning of this section.

(2) No court shall take cognizance of any offence under this section, except with the previous sanction in writing of the Bangladesh Government."

<u>37. The respondent has not brought on record any material on which it could be said that the passport which Towab was holding at the time of his arrival at Tejgaon Airport is not a valid passport. It is not alleged by the respondent that the passport in question in forged or faked. The only contention of the respondent is that Towab obtained the passport in question on suppression of material facts in "a clandestine manner," without declaring or surrendering the passports issued earlier to him. On the test applied under rule 4 of the Passport Rules 1955 it cannot be said that the passport which Towab was holding at the time of his arrival at Tejgaon Airport was not a valid passport. On the allegation that Towab obtained the passport in question on suppression of material faction a clandestine manner he may be appropriately dealt with in accordance with law but he could not be refused entry into Bangladesh on such allegation.</u>

<u>For the reasons stated above we hold that the impugned act of refusing Towab to re-enter Bangladesh or his expulsion therefrom on 1.7.80 was done without lawful authority.</u>

The Rule is accordingly made absolute without any order as to costs.

M. H. Rahman, J.—I agree.

End.
