Benoy Bhusan Bardhan being dead, his heirs, Pronoy Bhusan Bardhan and others  ------- Appellant.
Vs.
The Sub-Divisional Officer, Brahmanbaria and another ------- Respondents.
case_source: From the Judgment and Order dated 1-2-1969 passed by the Dacca High Court in Writ Petition No. 440 of 1967.
full_judgment:
Debesh Chandra Bhattacharya J. - This appeal by special leave is against a judgment of a Bench of the High Court of East Pakistan modifying, under Article 98 of the late Constitution of Pakistan two orders of the Sub-Divisional Officer Brahmanbaria, relating to lease of certain lands said to be enemy properties.

2. The Sub,-Divisional Officer, Bhahmanbaria. Respondent No.1, served a notice upon the appellant on 11-11-76, stating therein that the appellant was in unauthorised occupation of the properties belonging to Indian nationals without any valid document and directing him to show cause why the said properties should not be declared as enemy properties. In compliance with the direction contained in the laid notice, the appellant submitted a petition stating, inter alia, that he had been in possession of certain properties, which stood in the name of one Paresh Chandra Bardhan, on the basis of valid documents, that certain other lands standing in the name of Chittotosh Bardhan were debutter properties dedicated for the worship of the ancestral family deity of the appellant, who, being the eldest member of the family, had been managing the said debutter properties for the Sheba Puja of the deity and that the remaining properties were the ejmali properties of the appellant and his co-sharers, one of whom had left the country after relinquishing his interest in favour of the appellant and other co-sharers. On 30-5-67 the appellant was served with another notice to show cause why he should not be liable for compensation to the Government for unauthorised occupation of 55.22 acres of land. In compliance with the said notice the appellant submitted a petition stating, inter alia, that out of the said 55.22 acres of land he was in possession of only 28.98 acres of land of which 17.67 acres were debuttor properties, 3.80 acres of land which stood in the name of Paresh Chandra Nandi were really benami property belonging to the appellant, and 7.51 acres of land were the joint properties of the appellant and his co-sharers in possession, the absent co-sharer having relinquished his interest in favour of the appellant and other co-sharers, and that the possession of the appellant therein was not unlawful. Respondent No.2, Additional Sub-divisional Officer, Brahmanbaria, rejected the contention of the appellant by his order dated 29-7-67 and declared the disputed properties as enemy properties and recommended lease of the said lands to the other persons.

3. The appellant moved the High Court of East Pakistan under Article 98 of the 1962 Constitution of the then Pakistan challenging the validity of the notice dated 30-5-67 and the order dated 29-7-67 referred to above, on the grounds, inter alia, the respondents being neither the Deputy Custodian nor the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property had no jurisdiction to deal with the disputed properties in any manner, that there having been no partition of the properties which were joint between the appellant and his co-sharers and the appellant being in possession thereof, the Custodian of Enemy Property could not take possession of the said properties except on partition through Court in accordance with law, that some of the properties being debuttor properties for the worship of the family deity, of which the appellant was in management for performing the Sheba Puja of the deity, and the other properties standing in the name of Paresh Chandra Nandi being really the benami properties belonging to the appellant, they could not be regarded as enemy properties.

The High Court having issued a Rule upon the respondents they opposed the said Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition and contending, inter alia, that the disputed properties excepting certain items were enemy properties and the respondents were authorised to manage the same.

4. The learned Judges of the High Court disposed of the Rule by their judgment dated 1-12-69 on holding that the respondents were authorised to exercise necessary powers for taking possession of the disputed lands which were enemy properties but directed the Custodian of the Enemy Property to look into the records properly and leave out the legitimate share of the appellant in the properties in question before taking possession of the shares of the Indian nationals.

5. Special leave was granted by the Supreme Court of Pakistan to consider the questions whether the Sub-Divisional Officer was competent to exercise the powers of the Assistant Custodian of the Enemy Property and that whether the Custodian could take possession of any ejmali land of which the appellant was in possession as a co-sharer without partition of the said lands in accordance with law.

6. After the emergence of Bangladesh the Government of Bangladesh seems to have been interested in the properties which vested in the Custodian, Deputy Custodian or Assistant Custodian of Enemy Properly, as appointed by the Government of Pakistan or that of East Pakistan, in view of the provisions of Bangladesh (Vesting of Property and Assets) Order (President's Order No.29 of 1972), Government of Bangladesh has therefore been added as a respondent in this appeal.

7. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, learned Counsel appearing for the appellant, has submitted that the impugned notice issued on 30-5-67 whereby the appellant was asked to show cause why he should not be held liable to pay compensation for use and occupation of enemy properties as well as the order made on 29-7-67, which recommended leasing out the properties in possession of the appellant as enemy properties were by the Sub-Divisional Officer of Brahmanbaria, who had no authority to issue the said notice and to make the said order. According to the learned Counsel, it is the Custodian of Enemy Property which term includes Deputy Custodian and Assistant Custodian, who alone was authorised to take any action with regard to an enemy property and the Sub-Divisional Officer not being any of the said categories of officer the said notice and order were without any legal authority.

8. Learned Counsel has further contended that the Custodian of Enemy Property did not acquire under the Defence of Pakistan Rules any right better and larger than that enjoyed by the enemy owner and that the appellant being in possession of the disputed lands in exercise of his own right the respondents were not entitled to take possession of the same without establishing their right in respect thereof in a properly framed suit. Learned Counsel has also submitted that the appellant being in possession of the said lands also as a co-sharer, the Custodian of Enemy Property representing a co-sharer, who is out of possession, was not entitled to go into possession without demarcating the enemy owner's share of land through civil court in a suit for partition.

9 Mr. Anwarul Haq Chowdhury, learned Counsel appearing for Respondent No.2, has submitted that the Sub-divisional Officer Brahmanbaria having been duly authorised by the Deputy Commissioner of the district and also the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property to take necessary steps for recovery of possession of enemy property in unlawful possession of the appellant and to realise compensation in respect thereof, the impugned notice and order were with lawful authority. Learned Counsel has submitted that the appellant having failed to produce any evidence to show that the appellant had some right to manage the disputed properties as debuttor properties or personal properties, the respondents were right in seeking to enforce surrender of the disputed properties and to recover compensation in respect thereof under the provision of the East Pakistan Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966. Learned Counsel has further submitted that the respondents having sought to take possession of only the share of the lands belonging to the enemy owner without disturbing the right of the appellant and others in respect of the remaining land, no offence was committed by the said respondents.

Mr. B. B. Roy Chowdhury, Assistant Attorney-General having appeared on behalf of the Govt. of Bangladesh, added respondent, has generally supported the contentions of Mr. Anwarul Huq Chowdhury.

10. Before we go into the discussion of the merits of the respective contentions of learned Counsel appearing for the parties, it seems necessary to refer to the relevant provisions of the law relating to enemy property and the powers of Custodian, Deputy Custodian and Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property, as the answers to the questions raised in this appeal are to be sought in the light of the said provisions.

11. On the commencement of hostilities between Pakistan and India on the 6th of September, 1965 a proclamation of Emergency was issued by the President of Pakistan under clause (1) of Article 30 of the then Constitution of Pakistan and on that very day Defence of Pakistan Ordinance (Ordinance No. XXIII of 1965) was promulgated in exercise of the powers under clause (4) of article 30 read with clause (2) of Article 131 of the said Constitution to meet the emergency and to provide for special measures to ensure the security, the public safety and interest and the defence of Pakistan and for the trial of certain offences. Section 3(1) of the Ordinance conferred generally upon the Central Government the power to make such rules appeared to it to be necessary or expedient for ensuring the security, the public safety and interest and the defence of Pakistan or for securing the maintenance of public order or the efficient prosecution of war or for maintaining, supplies and services essential to the life of the community. Subsection (2) enu-merated certain specific subjects of rule making power of which reference may be made to clause (iv)(d) and clause (xxiv) of Section 2, watch are as follows:

"3. (2) Without prejudice to the generality of the powers conferred by subsection (1), the rules may provide for or may empower any authority to make orders providing for all or any of the following matters, namely:-

* * *

(iv) preventing anything likely to assist the enemy or to prejudice the successful conduct of war, including—

(d) advance of money to, or contracts or commercial dealing with the enemy, enemy subjects or persons residing, carrying on business, or being in enemy territory;

* * *

(xxiv) the requisitioning of any property, movable or immovable, including the taking possession thereof, and the issue of any orders in respect thereof;

In exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of the Ordinance, the Central Government of Pakistan made on the same day i.e. the 6th September, 1965. The Defence of Pakistan Rules of which Part XVI is relevant for our present purpose.

12. Rule 182 is contained in Part XVI of the Rules, which deals with, as the heading of the said Part implies, control of enemy firms. An enemy firms means, according to Rule 169 (2), an enemy subject, or a company or firm, of which a member or officer is an enemy subject, or a person or body carrying on business in Pakistan, under the control or for the benefit of an enemy subject. So the main object of the provisions of this Part seems to be the control of the business which is carried on by an enemy subject or in which an enemy subject is interested. All the substantive rules of this Part except rule 182 deal mainly with the matters relating to the trading or the carrying on business with enemy firms. It is rule 182 which deals with enemy properties, but it deals also with matters relating to an enemy firm, viz, payment of money to an enemy firm. The relevant provision of rule 182, as it stood on the promulgation on the 6th of September, 1965, was to the following effect:

“182. Collection of debt of enemy firm and custody of property.— (1) With a view to preventing the payment of money to an enemy firm, and preserving enemy property in con temptation of arrangement to be made at the conclusion of peace, the Central Government may appoint a Custodian of Enemy Property for Pakistan and one or more Deputy Custodian or Assistant Custodians or Assistant Custodians or of Enemy Property for such local areas as may be prescribed and may by order—

(a) * * *

(b) vest or provide for vesting in the prescribed Custodian such enemy property as may be prescribed;

* * *

13. This rule provides for the appointment of the Custodian, Deputy Custodians and Assistant Custodians of Enemy Property and the vesting of enemy properties in any such custodian.

<u>14. The main purpose of such vesting, as appears from its provisions, was to prevent the payment of any money to an enemy firm and collect the same and to preserve the enemy properties during the War. This purpose was further made clear and elucidated in the Enemy Property (Custody and Registration) Order, 1965 which was made by the Central Government of Pakistan on the 9th September, 1965 in exercise of the powers conferred by sub rule (1) of rule 182 referred to above. Paragraph 4 and 5 of this Order, which are quoted below, are significant:</u>

<u>"4. (1) Whenever by order made under Sub-rule (1) of rule 182, the property of an enemy is vested in the Custodian, the Custodian may take, or authorize the taking of such measures as he considers necessary or expedient for preserving the property, and, where the property belongs to an individual enemy subject, may incur such expenditure out of the property as he considers necessary or expedient for the maintenance of that individual or of his family in Pakistan.</u>

<u>(2) Without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing provision, the Custodian or such person as may be specially authorized by him in this behalf, may, for the said purpose,—</u>

<u>(i) carry on the business of the enemy;</u>

<u>(ii) take action for recovering any money due to the enemy;</u>

<u>(iii) make any contracts, and execute any documents in the name and on behalf of the enemy;</u>

<u>(iv) institute, defend or continue any suit or other legal proceeding, refer any dispute to arbitration and compromise any debts, claims or liabilities;</u>

<u>(v) raise on the security of the property such loans may be necessary;</u>

<u>(4) incur any expenditure, including the payment of any taxes, duties, cesses and rates to Government or to any local authority, and of any wages, salaries, pensions or provident fund contributions to or in respect of any employee of the enemy, and the repayment of any debts due by the enemy to persons other than enemies and</u>

<u>(vii) transfer by way of sale, mortgage or lease, or otherwise dispose of, any property or any easement, interest, profit or right, present or future, arising therefrom or incidental thereto.</u>

<u>(3) In respect of the property of a person who is a citizen of Pakistan or the ruler or a subject of an Acceding State, and who is an enemy within the meaning of clause (b) of rule 161, the Custodian shall have, in addition to the powers mentioned in sub-paragraph (2), the following powers, namely:-</u>

<u>i) the power to make payments to such person and to his dependents;</u>

<u>(ii) the power to make payments on behalf of such person or persons, other than those who are ere Dies under rule 161, of dues outstanding on the date on which such person become an enemy; and</u>

<u>(iii) generally to make such other payments out of the funds of such person may be directed by the Central Government.</u>

<u>5. All enemy property vesting In the Custodian shall be exempt from attachment, seizure or sale in execution of a civil court decree or orders of any other authority."</u>

<u>15. The nature of the right which accrued to the Custodian by virtue of the vesting in consequence of an order made under sub-rule (1)(b) of Rule 182 has been clearly spelt out in the provision of paragraph 4 of the order quoted above. This right was essentially of possession and management of the property with the object of preserving the same and was subject to the ultimate right of the enemy owner. The Defence of Pakistan Ordinance or the Rules framed thereunder did not contemplate the forfeiture or extinction of the private property of a national of an enemy state or of any national including a Pakistani residing in the territory of the enemy state. The Custodian had, no doubt, the right of sale, mortgage or lease, or of disposal by any other means, under clause (vii) of Paragraph 4(2) in respect of the property vested in him, but such right was subject to the general provision contained in paragraph 4(f) which provided that the Custodian in whom an enemy property vested had the authority to take only such steps as he considered necessary or expedient for preserving the property. That is to say, the Custodian had the authority to sell, mortgage, lease or otherwise dispose of the property or part thereof if such sale, mortgage, lease or other method of disposal was necessary for the purpose of the substantial preservation of the property in question. The whole idea underlying the said rule seems to have been that the properties which were enemy properties should be projected and preserved until the War is over.</u>

<u>16. There was an amendment of Rule 182 on 2.11.65 in consequence whereof the word "management" was substituted in place of the word "custody" in the sub-heading of the rule and the expression "preserving enemy property in contemplation of arrangement to be made at the conclusion of peace" was replaced by a new expression viz. "to provide for the administration and disposal by way of transfer or otherwise of enemy property or matter concerned therewith or incidental thereto". The main object of the said Rule does not appear to have been affected in any way by such amendment as the relevant provisions of the Enemy Property (Custody and Administration) Order, 1965 which declared and specified the rights of the Custodian in whom the properties of an enemy had vested did not undergo any alteration whatsoever.</u>

17. The Government of East Pakistan issued an omnibus notification being No.1199 Gen. dated 3-12-65 which was published in the Dacca Gazette Extraordinary on 4-12-65 and was to the following effect:

"Whereas the Central Government have directed the Provincial Government to exercise the powers and duties under Rule 182 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules; Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred by clause (b) of sub-rule (1) of Rule 182 of the said Rules, the Governor is pleased to order.

(a) that all lands and buildings which are enemy property within the meaning of sub-rule (4) of Rule 169 of the said Rules and which are not connected with any ‘enemy firm’, as defined in sub-rule (2) of that Rules, shall vest in the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Land and Buildings) with effect from the date of this order;

18. On the 8th January, 1966 the Governor of East Pakistan promulgated East Pakistan Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order 1966 which contained the provisions relating to the powers and duties of a Custodian in whom any enemy property had vested. The word, ''Custodian" as used in this Enemy Property appointed by the Provincial Government. The relevant previsions of paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 of the Order, which require examination for the proper appraisal of the nature and extent of the powers of a custodian within the meaning of the Order, are to the following effect:

“3. Powers and duties of Custodian.- When any enemy property is vested in the Custodian under clause (b) of sub-rule (1) of Rule 182-

(i) the Custodian shall have all the rights, powers, duties and liabilities of the owner of such property;

(ii) all sums due from any person in respect of such property shall be payable to the Custodian or to such other persons as may be authorised by him in this behalf and any payment made in contravention of this provision shall not be treated as a valid discharge;

(iii) The Custodian shall take such measures as may be necessary for the management and protection of the property, for the assertion of the title thereto and for obtaining or maintaining possession thereof, and may, for such purposes do all acts and incur all expenses, which are necessary or incidental;

(iv) the Custodian, where the enemy property belongs to an individual enemy subject or any individual resident in enemy territory may incur such expenditure out of the income of the property as he considers necessary or expedient for the maintenance of that individual or of his family in Pakistan.

(v) the Custodian shall maintain a separate account of the property of each enemy or such group of enemies whose property, vested in him, had been jointly managed in the past, and shall cause to be made therein entries of all receipts and payments; and (vi) the accounts maintained clause (v) shall be subject to inspection and audit at such intervals and by such persons as may be decided by the Provincial Government. 4. Disposal of property (1) Except as provided in sub-paragraph (2) the Custodian shall not transfer or otherwise dispose of any enemy property vested in him without the previous approval of the Provincial Government.

(2) The Custodian may grant lease of, or let out, any such enemy property for a period not exceeding one year at a time.

(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any agreement, a person to whom any enemy property is leased or let out under sub paragraph (2) shall not acquire any right of occupancy in such property and shall not be entitled to hold over after the expiry of the period of lease.

(4) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any agreement, the lessee or tenant in respect of any enemy property leased or let out under sub-paragraph (2), shall be liable to be evicted without notice from such property at the expiry of the term of the lease.

5. Surrender of enemy property by trespassers.

(1)(a) If any enemy property is found in unlawful possession of any person, the Custodian may require the Deputv Commissioner of the district in which such property is situated to recover possession of such property and place it in the possession of the Custodian.

(b) The Deputy Commissioner, on receipt of the requisition from the Custodian will issue notice on the person in unlawful possession of the enemy property, to show cause within a period not exceeding 7 days as to why he will not be ejected therefrom and after hearing him, may enforce surrender of such property by such person to the Custodian and the Deputy Commissioner or any officer empowered by the Deputy Commissioner in this behalf may use or cause to be used such force as may be necessary for taking possession of the property.

(c) If enemy property after being vested in the Custodian comes under the lawful possession of any person, the Deputy Commissioner of the district in which such property is situated or any other officer who may be empowered in this behalf by such Deputy Commissioner may, on the application of the Custodian, enforce surrender of such properly by such person to the Custodian and the Deputy Commissioner or the officer so empowered by the Deputy Commissioner may use or cause to be used such force as may be necessary for taking possession of the property.

(3) The person in unlawful possession of the property shall be liable to pay to the Custodian such compensation as the Custodian may fix for unlawful occupation of the property and such compensation shall be recoverable from him as a public demand".

<u>19. The provisions of clause (i) of paragraph 3 of the Order clearly shows that the Deputy Custodian in whom an enemy property had vested under the notification dated 3.12.1965 stepped into the shoes of the enemy owner and had all the rights, powers, duties and liabilities of such owner. Clause (iii) of the paragraph required the Deputy Custodian to take all measures necessary for the management and protection of the property and incur all expenses in respect thereof and under clause (v) of the paragraph he was required to maintain necessary accounts of the property. Clause (iv) of the paragraph authorised the Deputy Custodian in whom the property had vested to incur expenses out of the income of the property belonging to an enemy subject or resident in enemy territory, or his own maintenance or that of his family. Paragraph 4 imposed a restriction upon the power of disposal of the property which the Deputy Custodian or Assistant Custodian naturally possessed under clause (i) of paragraph 3 and there could not be any permanent transfer of any interest in an enemy property without previous approval of the Government.</u>

<u>Paragraph 5 conferred certain summary powers upon the Deputy Commissioner of the district and authorised him to use force when necessary for recovery of possession of an enemy property when such property was in unlawful possession of any person. Paragraph 8 makes such property immune from attachment or sale in execution of a civil court decree or a certificate under the Public Demand Recovery Act.</u>

<u>20. From all these provisions it is manifest that it was never the intention of the law-making authority to divest an individual enemy owner of his title in respect of his property lying in the territory of the hostile belligerent state. Its primary concern appears to have been that such property might not be used in a way which would be prejudicial to the prosecution of the war affecting the defence of Pakistan or which might render some benefit to the enemy state in any manner. Such concern was however accompanied by an anxiety that the ultimate interest of the individual owner might not be affected in any way. Elaborate provisions were therefore made in the Enemy Property (Custody and Registration) Order 1955 as issued by the Central Government of Pakistan and in the East Pakistan (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order 1966 as made by the Governor of East Pakistan for the protection and management of such property. The whole idea behind those provisions seems to be that during the Emergency which was declared on the commencement of the War, the individual enemy owner was not considered suitable or safe for the management of his property, or it might be that because of restrictions on his movement or detention in prison an enemy subject was incapable of managing his property properly and as such it was necessary to make adequate provisions for the protection and management of such properties. To carry out this purpose, the property was caused to be vested in an officer of the Government of Pakistan or the Government of East Pakistan, who was charged with the responsibility of protecting and managing the properties, realising the money or compensation which was due to the enemy owner and keep proper accounts of the same, so that the interest of the enemy owner might not be substantially affected. The right, title and interest of the enemy owner was not sought to be extinguished in any way, but were purported to be placed in a state of temporary hibernation, so to say, during the continuance of the Emergency. These were essentially temporary measures for "the management and protection of the property", as stated in clause (iii) of paragraph 3 of the Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order and the right which accrued to the Deputy Custodian or Assistant Custodian by virtue of the vesting in consequence of the order made under Rule 182 (1)(b) of The Defence of Pakistan Rules was no larger right than that of protection and management of the property, the benefit of which would ultimately redound to the credit of the enemy owner. It was a binding obligation of the managing custodian to maintain a separate account of all receipts and payments respecting each enemy property vested in him, in accordance with the provision of clause (v) of paragraph 3 which was to be subject to periodical inspection and audit. The subsisting interest of the enemy owner is highlighted by the provision of clause (iv) of paragraph 3 which authorised the custodian concerned to incur expenditure for the maintenance of the individual enemy owner or his family.</u>

<u>21. The predominant idea behind taking over and management of the enemy property under these Emergency Legislations seems to have been the prevention of certain acts which might be prejudicial to the war efforts of the Government of Pakistan and the protection of the said properties during the continuance of the War. It seems to have been never in the contemplation of the Government of the country to acquire for itself any beneficial interest in the properties of an individual enemy owner under the said provisions, but to protect and manage the properties, so that the rightful owners could get back their properties on the conclusion of peace.</u>

22. The first point for which the special leave was granted relates to the question of the competency of the Sub-divisional Officer, Brahmanbaria to issue the notice dated 30-5-67 asking the appellant to show cause why he "should not be held liable to pay compensation to Government for use and occupation of such property" and to make the order dated 29-7-69 approving of "the proposals of the lease to the landless refugees". This notice and the order were purported to have been issued and made under the provisions of paragraph 5 and 4 of the Administration and Disposal Order, 1966 respectively.

23. From paragraph 5 quoted above it appears that in case where the enemy property which vested in the Custodian of Enemy Property and was in unlawful possession of any person, the Custodian might apply to the Deputy Commissioner of the District in which such property was situated for taking necessary steps for the recovery of the said property and to put the Custodian in possession of the same. The Deputy Commissioner in his turn might authorise some other officer subordinate to him to take specific measures for the recovery of such property. If the property was really an enemy property and it was in illegal possession of certain person the measures which might be adopted to enforce surrender of such property were merely administrative in nature and could certainly be adopted by the Sub-divisional Officer within whose area of administration the said property was situated, when he had been authorised by the Deputy Commissioner in this behalf. Similarly, the Custodian in whom the enemy property vested was entitled to realise such compensation as he might fix for the illegal occupation of the said property from the unlawful occupant under sub paragraph (3) of paragraph 5 of the Order. According to clause (ii) of paragraph 5 of the Order, such compensation was payable only to the Custodian as the case might be or some other person, as might be authorised by such Deputy or Assistant Custodian and to nobody else.

24. In paragraph II of the Writ Petition the contention as to the absence of necessary authority of the Sub-divisional Officer on the ground that he was neither the Deputy Cus-todian nor the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property was raised. The respondents controverted the said contention of the appellant by filing an affidavit-in-opposition in paragraph 13 of which it was stated that the Sub divisional Officer was authorised in this behalf to manage the enemy property on behalf of the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property.

<u>25. The notice dated 30-5-67 appears to have been issued under sub-paragraph (3) of paragraph 5 read with clause (ii) of paragraph 3 of the Order to enforce payment of the compensation which was due under the said clause of paragraph 5 from an unlawful occupant of the enemy property, and the Sub-divisional Officer might exercise the powers under the said provision if he was authorised by the Deputy or Assistant Custodian in this behalf. It appears, however, that the Sub-divisional Officer concerned acted under a misapprehension as to the person to whom such compensation was due, as he stated in his notice that it was due to the Government. This was misconceived. It was payable to the Deputy or Assistant Custodian concerned, who was to maintain a proper account of the same.</u>

26. The order dated 29-7-67 purported to be made by the Sub-divisional Officer under paragraph 4 of the Order presupposed that the appellant, as an unlawful occupant of the enemy property had already been evicted under clause (b) of sub-paragraph (1) of paragraph 5 of the Order. For the enforcement of the surrender of possession the Deputy Commissioner might authorise some other officer to take necessary steps for the recovery of possession of the enemy property and the Sub-divisional Officer if so authorised could lawfully take such steps to evict the illegal occupant. After the recovery of possession of the property from an unlawful occupant, the Custodian was to take such measures under clause (iii) of paragraph 3 of the Order as were necessary for the management and protection of the property and the Custodian might very well under the said provision delegate his authority to manage the property to the Sub-divisional Officer within whose jurisdiction, the property might be situated, for the sake of efficient management and proper protection, subject to the limitation on the disposal of the said property as provided in paragraph 4 of the Order. Having regard to the provisions referred to above, it cannot be said that the Sub divisional Officer was acting without lawful authority in proposing to lease out the land after obtaining possession of the property, if he was authorised in this behalf by the Custodian and the proposed lease was subject to the limitation contemplated in paragraph 4 of the Order.

27. In this order also there seems to have been one lacuna which may not have made the order completely without jurisdiction, but indicates the Sub-divisional Officers lack of adequate appreciation of the nature of his responsibility in managing an enemy property under paragraph 3 of the Order. The Sub-divisional Officer seems to have been swayed more with a kind of humanitarian sentiment in approving of the proposal of lease to landless refugees than with the objective of preservation and good management of the said property, as required under paragraph 3 of the Order referred to above. Here also, the Sub-divisional Officer appears to have been acting under the erroneous view that he was charged with managing a Government property and that the management of such a property should yield in the first place some kind of public good.

<u>28. This appears to have been an absolutely wrong approach. The sole concern of the Sub divisional Office in exercising the powers under paragraph No.3 of the Order was the preservation and good management of the enemy property and not to render benefit to a class of the citizens of the country. It does not, however, appear from the papers which have been brought to the notice of the Court that by approving of the proposal to lease out the land to the landless refugees on the view that it was Government and there was really a transgression of the managing, officers duty of preserving the property, notwithstanding such a wrong approach and misconception and therefore it is difficult to say that the impugned notice and the order referred to above were without lawful authority because of the said misconception as to the nature of the authority in which the property vested and such authorities’ power of management of an enemy property. The Sub-divisional Officer of Brahmanbaria having purported to perform an official act with regard to the properties situated within his administrative jurisdiction may be presumed, in the absence of any contrary evidence, to have the necessary authorisation from the Deputy Commissioner of the District or the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property, who was generally Additional Deputy Commissioner of the district, as contemplated within paragraph 3 or 5 of the Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order.</u>

29. The second point for which the special leave was granted raises an important question as to the extent of the powers of the Custodian of Enemy Property to recover possession of a property which is an enemy property within the meaning of Rule 182 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules and is in the possession of a person who claims a right in the said property.

<u>30. Of the disputed properties, the appellant claims 17.67 acres of land as Debuttor properties dedicated for the worship of his ancestral family deity, of which he was in charge for performing the Sheba Puja of the deity and 3-80 acres of land as personal property standing the benami of one Paresh Chandra Nandi. It is not clear whether the areas of the debuttor and benami properties mentioned above were the entire areas of said properties or they merely represented the share of the absentee co-sharer, which was enemy property. The averments made in the petition and supplementary affidavit in this regard, made by the appellant are extremely vague. The appellant does not appear to have claimed to be in possession of these properties as a co-sharer but asserted his right as the Shebait and the owner in respect of the said properties in his affidavit and the respondents have denied the claim of the appellant in their affidavit-in-opposition. These are disputed questions of fact as to the debuttor and benami character of the said properties. These questions can be effectively decided only on production of necessary evidence and the High Court Division exercising its constitutional jurisdiction is hardly a proper forum for such determination, Such questions can only be conveniently and appropriately adjudicated in a properly framed Civil Suit.</u>

<u>31. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, learned Counsel has, however, contended that the summary powers which had been conferred upon the Deputy Commissioner for taking possession of an enemy property in the possession of a certain person by using force, if necessary should have been used cautiously and only when the officer concerned was satisfied that the person in possession was definitely and clearly an unlawful occupier. Learned Counsel has submitted that when it appears that the person in possession might have had a bonafide claim as to possession, he cannot be thrown out of such possession in exercise of the said summary powers and that for recovery of possession in such a case resort must be taken to a properly framed suit in a Court of ordinary civil jurisdiction.</u>

<u>32. It has been laid down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in construing the provisions of The East Bengal Govt. Lands and Buildings (Recovery of Possession) Act (Act X of 1953) in the cases of Province of East Pakistan Vs. Syed Hatem Ali and others (1968) 20 DLR (SC) 129 and Sufia Khatun Vs. Secretary, Revenue Department, Government of East Pakistan and others (1968) 20 DLR (SC) 18 that the summary procedure provided in the said Act for recovery of possession of the Government land or building in unauthorised occupation of a person cannot be invoked in a case where there is a bona fide dispute as to the title to such land or building. The ratio of the said cases is that the legislative provision being that the summary power can be exercised by the Government to oust a person in unauthorised occupation of Government land or building, such power cannot be exercised in a case where doubt arises as to the clear title of the Government to the said land or building because of certain bona fide dispute with regard thereto, inasmuch as it was not the legislative intent that the decision of the Government as to the title to such land or building should be final.</u>

33. It may of course be rightly contended, relying upon the principle laid down in the said Pakistan Supreme Court decisions, that the summary power as had been conferred under paragraph 5 of the Order could be exercised only when there was no bona fide dispute as to the title to the said land and the land in question was undoubtedly enemy property and the possession of the occupant of the said property was clearly unlawful.

34. In the instant case, however, learned Counsel for the appellant could not place before us any substantial material or circumstance in support of his claim as to the Debuttor or benami character of the said property, from which it could be said that the dispute as to the character of the said property was bona fide and that the provisions of paragraph 5 of the Order are inapplicable to such a case. The appellant may of course establish his right, if any, as claimed by him to the properties, in question in an appropriate Court of civil jurisdiction, if he is so advised in this behalf.

35. The appellant claims to have been in possession of the remaining properties measuring 7.5I acres and appertaining to Khatians No.20, 53, 760 936, 1006, 1023, 1024, 107, 1441 land 1555 of Mousa Birampur as a co-sharer. The records of rights with regard to these Khatians have been filed with the supplementary affidavit of the appellant as Annexure ‘F’ series. Of these Khatians, Khatian No.1006 appellant and therefore it cannot be regarded as enemy property in any way. The lands of Khatians No.1441 and 1555 have been recorded in the names of persons other than the appellant, who does not appear to have prima facie any interest in the said lands. The lands of the remaining Khatians, however, as appear from the records of right referred to above, have been recorded in the name of the appellant in possession of the said lands, as a co-sharer.

<u>36. The provision of para 3 of the Order, is clear enough to show that the custodian could not claim in the instant case a better right than what the co-sharer of the appellant, whose interest had vested in the custodian, was entitled to claim. The Dacca High Court considered this question in a number of decisions which have been cited at the bar, viz. Mumtazuddin Ahmed Chowdhury Vs. Deputy Commissioner and Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property (1968) 20 DLR 375, which dealt with the position of person in possession of an enemy property on the basis of an agreement for purchase of the said property Messrs M. M. Ispahani Vs. Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property, (1968) 20 DLR 493 which was a case of a person in possession of an enemy property by holding over on the expiry of a lease agreement and also on the basis of an agreement for purchase, Ananda Mohan Kusndu and others Vs. Province of East Pakistan, (1968) 20 DLR 976 which was the case of two persons in possession of an enemy property on the basis of an agreement for purchase Shah Ghulam Nabi and others Vs. Vice-Chairman, East Pakistan Enemy Property Management Board (1970) 22 DLR 48, the case of three persons in possession of the premises where a rice and oil mill were situated on the basis of an agreement for partnership and Anil Kumar Dutta Chowdhury Vs. Province of East Pakistan (1971) 23 DLR 108, the case of a co-sharer in possession of a property including the share of an enemy owner. It has been consistently and in our opinion, rightly held in these cases that vesting of property in the Custodian of Enemy Property did not transgress upon the title of, the real owner and that nobody in possession of such property in exercise of right, however imperfect or limited it may be cannot be said to be in unlawful possession within the meaning of paragraph 5 of The Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966. It was correctly observed by Cheif Justice Siddiky, (Addul Hakim. J. agree-ing), who was incidentally a party to the judgment under appeal, on construing the provision of rule 182 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules, in the case of Ananda Mohan Kundu and others Vs. Province of East Pakistan (1968) 20 DLR 976 980:</u>

<u>"What the legislature intended is that all enemy property should vest in the Custodian for the purpose mentioned in rule 182 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules with a view to protecting the enemy properties being utilised in any manner for the benefit of the enemy or in the interest of the enemy State and to the prejudice of Pakistan. Therefore, it amounts to only a control over the enemy property by the Custodian. If after vesting of the enemy property in the Custodian it is found on enquiry that a person who is holding some sort of document of title, though imperfect, from the real owner of the property who happened to be the enemy, then if the occupier is a citizen of Pakistan he cannot be ousted from the property because of mere vesting order of the Government."</u>

<u>37. Relying upon three earlier decisions of the Dacca High Court reported in 20 DLR as have been referred to above, a Division Bench of the said Court laid down in the case of Shah Ghulam Nabi 22 DLR 48 that the petitioners having proved their prima facie title by showing that they were in possession of the disputed Rice and Oil Mills as Managing partners on the basis of a registered deed of partnership entered into by the said petitioners and one Chairaonjiblal Sharaf who acquired the said Rice and Oil Mills on the basis of a decree for specific performance of contract and the illegality of the petitioners' possession being in dispute, the respondents could oust them only by obtaining an order of eviction in a properly constituted suit. Another proposition which was laid down in the said case was that a citizen of a country could not be adjudged an enemy without definite evidence that the said citizen had been, as a matter of fact, residing in India.</u>

<u>38. On an appeal against this judgment in case of Shah Ghulam Nabi, the Supreme Court of Pakistan did not grant to the respondents of the said case any leave to appeal as regards the first proposition referred to above and granted leave only on the question whether the view of the Dacca High Court as to the enemy character of Chairanjib Lal Sharaf was correct. The Appellate Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court by its judgment reported in 27 DLR (AD) 136 has disposed of the said appeal by affirming the decision of the Dacca High Court on the point for which the leave was granted.</u>

<u>39. The Dacca High Court examined the position of a co-sharer in possession of a joint property, of which another co-sharer was an enemy, in the case of Anil Kumar Datta Chowdhury Vs. Province of East Pakistan (1971) 23 DLR 108 and expressed the view that a co-sharer how was presumed to have right title and was in exclusive possession of a joint property could not be said to be in unlawful possession within the meaning of the Enemy Property laws and was not therefore liable to be ousted from the said property without bringing a suit for partition in a civil court according to law.</u>

<u>40. The said view of the Dacca High Court is in consonance with the well-established principle that if a co-sharer was in occupation of a common land without objection from his sharer and with their express or implied consent and if the co-sharers out of possession are dissatisfied with the manner in which the said common land was being used by the said co sharer in possession, their remedy for separate possession of their share of the common land is to bring a suit for partition. If, however, such sole occupation of the common land refine in denial of the rights of the co-sharers out of possession constitute ouster, the ousted co-sharers may also bring a suit for joint possession and compensation. In one of the early decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, Sir Earnest Peacock, in delivering the judgment of the Judicial Committee, laid down the law in this regard, in well-known case of Watson and Company Vs. Ramchand Dutta and others LR 17 IA 110: I.L.R. 18 Cal. 10, in the following words:</u>

<u>"It seems to their Lordships that if there be two or more tenants in common, and one (A) be in actual occupation of a part of the estate and is engaged in cultivating that part in a proper course of cultivation, as if it were his separate property, and another tenant in common (B) attempts to come upon the said part for the purpose of carrying on operation there inconsistent with the course of cultivation in which A is engaged and the profitable use by him of the said part for the purpose of and A resists and prevents such entry, not in denial of B's title, but simply with the object of protecting himself in the profitable enjoyment of the land, such conduct on the part of A would not entitle B to a decree for joint possession."</u>

<u>41. A co-owner of an undivided share of the joint land has his right, title and interest in every grain of the soil constituting the joint land and cannot therefore be said to be in unlawful possession of such land, even if he is in exclusive possession thereof. Only when there has been separation of a co-sharer's share of land as a result of the partition of the joint land by metes and bounds, either through Court or amicably, the possession of the co-owner, after such separation, beyond his separated share of the land without the consent of the owner of such land may be said to be not lawful. Until such separation has been effected, the exclusive possession of a co-owner is not presumed to be hostile or adverse to other co-sharers who are deemed to be in constructive possession of the said land through the co-sharer in possession. In the instant case, 7.51 acres of land said to be belonging to one Nirmal Kanti Bardhan, who had left Pakistan in 1951, were declared to be enemy property and were proposed to be leased out to certain "landless refugees." The appellants contention in regard to the said land is that the said lands were ejmali lands, belonging to the appellant in 8 annas share and to Nirmal Kanti, Amal Kanti and Shyamal Kanti in the remaining 8 annas share and that the appellant and his co-sharers all of whom, excepting Nirmal Kanti, were Pakistani nationals, having been in possession of the said lands including the undivided share of the said Nirmal Kanti Bardhan, who relinquished his interest in favour of his Pakistani co sharers, the said lands cannot be treated as enemy properties. The appellant’s contention as to the relinquishment of the interest of Nirmal Kanti Bardhan in favour of the appellant and his co-sharers in Pakistan cannot, of course, be accepted in the absence of the necessary registered instrument evidencing such relinquishment and the share of the said co-sharer residing in India could very well be enemy property within the meaning of rule 165 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965 and may be deemed to have vested in the Deputy Custodian or Assistant Custodian by virtue of the Notification dated 3-12-1965, but having regard to the principle of a co-sharer's possession stated above, the possession of the absentee co-sharer's undivided share of the land by the appellant and his co-sharers cannot be said to be unlawful and consequently the provisions of The Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966 are not attracted to the facts of the instant case. The Custodian of Enemy Property representing the share of the enemy owner cannot go into possession of the joint land by dispossessing the co-sharers in possession of the said land without partitioning the same according to law nor can be arbitrarily specify certain area representing the share of the enemy owner and lease out the same to others. It is therefore abundantly clear that the notice dated 30-5-67 asking the appellant to show cause as to why he should not be made liable to pay compensation for use and occupation of the enemy property as well as the order dated 29-7-67 approving of the lease of the said property to landless refugee, so far as the lands measuring 7.51 acres, in which the appellant was in possession as a co-sharer, were concerned, were without lawful authority.</u>

<u>In the result the appeal is allowed in part without any order as to costs.</u>

End.
