case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 19-1-76 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Order No. 69 of 1976)
full_judgment:
Debesh Chandra Bhattacharya J. - This appeal by special leave is against an order of a Bench of the High Court Division, allowing an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure made by the respondent, without issuing a Rule upon the appellant, who was the sole opposite party in the said application, and setting aside an order of dismissal of an appeal preferred by the respondent for his failure to put in a sum of Tk. 500/- within the time directed by the appellate Court.

2. The appellant brought a suit in the first Court of Munsif, Sadar, Chittagong, for declaration of title to, and in confirmation of possession in, the land in suit and also for permanent injunction against the predecessor of Respondents No.1 to 11, in the suit. Appellant thereafter delivered certain interrogatories, with the leave of the Court for answers to the said interrogatories by defendant No.1 and the learned Munsif directed the said defendant to answer the interrogatories by 74. 12. 73. As the said defendant did neither file replies to the interrogatories by date fixed for the same nor did take any step in the matter, the learned Munsif directed the said defendant to show cause why the written statement filed by him should not be struck off and fixed 31.12.73 for passing the necessary order. It appears that on 31.12 73 an application was filed on behalf of Defendant No.1 praying for time to file answers to the interrogatories and to show cause for his default in answering the interrogatories but as nobody appeared before the Court to move the said application, the learned Munsif, by an order, rejected the said application and also the written statement filed by Defendant No.1 and fixed 3.1.74 for ex-parte disposal of the suit. The suit was taken up for ex parte disposal on 3.1.74 and after examination of a witness on behalf of the appellant and admitting certain documentary evidence the suit was decreed ex parte.

3. Defendant No.1 filed an appeal being Other Appeal No.53 of 1974 in the Court of the District Judge against the said ex parte decree. Defendant No.1 having died pending the said appeal, Respondents No.1 to 11 filed an application in the said appeal claiming themselves to be the heirs left by Defendant No.1 for their substitution in place of the deceased appellant and the said respondents were substituted in place of the said appellant. It may be mentioned that in the said application Respondent No.1, Abu Zafar, was shown as major and the said application for substitution was verified by him as such. In the Memorandum of Appeal also he was substituted as major and the said appeal was prosecuted by him as major. The appeal was heard by the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong on 30.8.75 and the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the appeal and made the following order:

"That the appeal be allowed on contest without costs. The judgment and decree of the learned lower Court be set aside and the suit be seat back on remand for fresh trial in the light of the observation made above on condition of payment of Tk. 500 (Taka five hundred only) by the defendant-appellant to the plaintiff respondent within 61 days from this date. In default, the appeal will stand dismissed with costs."

4. As Respondents No.1 to 11 did not pay the amount within 60 days from the date of the judgment as directed, the appeal stood dismissed with costs on the expiry of 60 days. On 24-11-75 respondents No.1 to 11 filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong stating therein that on 17-11-75 they came to learn from the Diary that the judgment was pronounced on 30-8-75 and the said respondents having obtained a certified copy of the judgment on 20-11-75 tendered Tk. 500/- for acceptance as costs as directed by the said Court. The appellant filed an objection to the said application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure that the said application was not maintainable as the Court became functus officio after dismissal of the appeal in consequence of the order of appellate Court made on 30-8-75, and that the respondents were aware of the result of the appeal preferred by them, which was duly noted in the Daily Cause List of the appellate Court dated 30 8-75. The learned Subordinate Judge, by this order dated 6-1-76, rejected the application made under section 151 of the Code, holding that the words used in the judgment were words of finality and took effect automatically and that other remedies being available an application under section 151 of the Code was not maintainable.

5. On 19-1-76 Abu Zafar, describing himself as minor, represented by his mother, Shamsunnahar Begum, moved an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the High Court Division against the said order of dismissal of the application under section 151 of the Code and the learned Judges of the High Court Division passed an order ex parte without issuing any Rule upon the appellant, allowing the said revisional application with the following observation:

"Since the deposit has been made and no prejudice has been caused to the plaintiff opposite party we set aside this order and direct that the written statement as filed by the defendant No.1 (a) petitioner be accepted and the suit proceeded with accordingly. Instead of issuing Rule we are passing the final order, inasmuch as the orders suffer from material irregularity."

6. Special leave was granted by the Appellate Division to consider the question (a) whether the application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure made by Abu Zafar, Respondent No.1 as minor, represented by his mother as natural guardian, was maintainable in view of the fact that the appeal in which the impugned order was made the said Abu Zafar was substituted as major; (b) whether the learned Judges of the High Court Division were right in allowing the application under section 115 of the Code ex parte without giving opportunity to the appellant of being heard, and (c) whether having regard to specific direction given in the appellate order allowing Other Appeal No.53/74 on condition of payment of Tk. 500/- within 60 days from the date of the order in default whereof the appeal would stand dismissed with costs, the learned Subordinate Judge was correct in rejecting the application of Respondents No.1 to 11 under section 151 of the Code and the learned Judges of the High Court Division were right in setting aside the said order of the learned Subordinate Judge as well as the order of dismissal of the appeal in exercise of their revisional jurisdiction.

<u>7. It is clear from the application for substitution filed on 88-74 in Other Appeal No.53 of 1974 that Abu Zafar, son of late Abul Khair Chowdhury, defendant No.1 was described in the said application as major. Abu Zafar was the petitioner No.1 in the said application, which was also verified by him and he was impleaded in the appeal on substitution as major. The application for Revision under section 115 of the Code was moved on behalf of one Abu Zafar minor (represented, by his mother Saamsunnahar Begum). The application for revision was not, therefore, moved on behalf of a person who was a party to the appeal in which the order sought to be revised was passed and Abu Zafar, the minor, does not certainly appear to have the locus standi to move the said application. It may, however, be noticed that Saamsunnahar who acted as the guardian of the said minor Abu Zafar was herself a party to the appeal and could make the application on her own behalf if not on behalf of her son, who was already a minor. But the question is whether the order of the High Court Division made on the basis of such a defective application may be held to be without jurisdiction or can be held to be without lawful authority if the order was otherwise unexceptionable. It may be noticed that the provision of section 115 of the Code does not specify the person on whose behalf an application under the said section can be filed. The power under section 115 of the Code is an extraordinary power which the High Court may exercise after calling for the records of any case which has been decided by any Court subordinate to High Court in which no appeal lies to the High Court, if the High Court is satisfied that such subordinate Court acted without jurisdiction or failed to exercise jurisdiction which it had or acted illegally or with material irregularity in the exercise of its jurisdiction in making the order in the said case. In accordance with the general practice it is, of course, at the instance of aggrieved person, who is a party to the litigation in which the order sought to be revised has been made, that a revisional application is made but the provision of section 115 of the Code does not appear to debar the exercise of the power conferred by it if the High Court becomes aware of the illegality contemplated in the said section upon its own knowledge derived from some other records or upon an information received from a person who is not a party to the litigation in which the illegal order has been made. It is of course, in the discretion of the High Court whether in a particular case the High Court will exercise its power only on an application made by an aggrieved party to the said case or may also exercise the said power sou motu or at the instance of a stranger to the litigation in which the order sought to be revised has been made. The High Court has of course in exercise of such discretion laid down procedural rules which permit only an aggrieved party to the litigation to make such an application and the said Court shall not ignore such rules except in an extremely exceptional case. But when the jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code has been exercised in fact and an effective order has been made interfering with an order of subordinate Court, it is difficult to hold the said order of the High Court to be without jurisdiction and in our opinion, to set it aside only on the ground that the Court, in violation of its own procedural rules, acted on an application which was not at the instance of a proper party, if the said order was otherwise a good order under section 115 of the Code.</u>

<u>8. The next point to be considered is whether the High Court Division was within its powers to set aside an ex parte decree in the absence of the decree-holder without giving him an opportunity of being heard in support of the said decree. We had an occasion to consider a similar point in the case of Fazlur Rahman Vs. Rajab Ali and others, Civil Petition No. 173 of 1977 decided on 18-7-77 and we have held therein that although section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not contain any provision as to service of notice upon the opposite party against whom the order is sought to be made but it is incumbent upon the High Court to act judicially and to observe the rule of natural justice and that any order made without giving the affected person an opportunity of being heard in violation of the said principle is without jurisdiction.</u>

<u>9. As regards the third question for the consideration of which special leave has been granted, it is now well settled that where in granting time by a Court for doing any act prescribed or allowed by the Code words of finality have been used, which are capable of operating automatically, bringing the entire proceeding to termination, the Court becomes functus officio and loses jurisdiction to extend the time or make any order thereunder. In the instant case the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong in Other Appeal No. 53/74 made an order on 30-8-75, allowing the appeal and remanding the suit to the trial Court on condition of payment of Tk. 500/- by the defendant-appellant to the plaintiff respondent within 60 days from the said date and added a further direction that in default, the appeal will stand dismissed with costs."</u>

<u>10. It has been noted in many cases that there is a great difference between the expressions "will be dismissed" and "will stand dismissed" as used by the Court in making certain conditional orders. It is clear that the latter expression bears words of finality which do not require any further order from the Court to bring the litigation to a termination. The clear import of such words is that if the amount of money directed to be paid in the said order is paid within the time prescribed, the decree allowing the appeal will stand but if the amount so directed be not paid within the time so fixed the appeal will stand automatically dismissed. On the expiry of the period fixed in the said order, the appeal is brought to a close and completely disposed of and the Court which made the order loses all jurisdiction therein except its power under section 152 of the Code or of review. The Dacca High Court considered similar question in the cases of Manindra Chandra Dey and others Vs. Govinda Prasad (1951) 3 DLR 313 and Sheikh Ayezuddin Vs. Priya Shankar Chowdhury (1954) 6 DLR 505 and the Supreme Court of Pakistan considered this question in Shah Wali Vs. Ghulam Din @ Gamon and Muhammad Din (1967) 19 DLR (SC) 143. The Pakistan Supreme Court case arose out of a suit for pre-emption where a decree was made directing the deposit of a certain sum of money on account of preemption by a certain date with a direction that in default of such deposit the suit would stand dismissed with cost and on appeal the pre-emption money was enhanced with a direction that the amount so enhanced would be deposited within one month of the appellate decree "otherwise the suit will be treated as dismissed with costs". It has been held in the said case that for the Respondent's default in making payment of the correct amount within the time fixed by the appellate decree the suit would stand dismissed and there was no question of extension of time involved either by the original Court or by the appellate Court thereafter, the appeal or revision from the appellate decree having already been dismissed. Hamoodur Rahman J. as he then was, in a separate judgment, agreeing with the main conclusion reached by the other learned Judges in the case, considered the applicability of section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure for the extension of time granted by a Court for doing a certain act and expressed the view in the following words:</u>

<u>"That there is a difference between the words "will be dismissed" and "will stand dismissed" or "will be treated as dismissed has been generally accepted and the Courts have been inclined to invoke their power under section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure where the words used are "will be dismissed" or words or similar import... but where the words used are words of finality and are to take effect automatically this section can have no manner of application and the time cannot be enlarged......</u>

<u>In this view of the matter since the decree passed by the District Judge on appeal contained the words that the "suit shall be treated as dismissed with cost" indicating that the default clause was to operate automatically without any further order from the Court, and this was the decree that was upheld by the High Court, the executing Court could have had no jurisdiction to enlarge the time fixed thereunder. That decree could only pave, been modified on an appeal from the decree itself to a competent Court under Order 41, rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure and not under section 148 of the said Code."</u>

<u>11. The view expressed in the Pakistan Supreme Court decision referred to above was followed in three Single Bench decisions of the High Court Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court in the cases of Rajendra Shirali and others Vs. Mahadev Shirali (1975) 27 DLR 232; Majam Ali Bepari Vs. Abdul Samad and others (1975) 27 DLR 31 and Darogali Sheikh and ors. Vs. Milatannessa Bibi and others (1976) 28 DLR 9, where the applicability of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for the extension of time for similar cases was also considered and it was held that the said provision also could not be invoked in such cases except in the exceptional circumstance of a mistake of the court on Court's officer.</u>

<u>12. After a decree has been made such a decree cannot be altered or added to except under section 152 or on review, as has been provided in Order 20, rule 3 of the Code, and an application under section 151 of the Code to effect an alteration in the terms of the decree after the default clause has become operative is clearly in conflict with the said provision.</u>

13. As it is well established that an inherent power cannot be invoked to evade or circumvent a positive prohibition laid down by a Statute an application under section 151 of the Code for setting aside a Decree comes directly under such prohibition. In that view of the matter, the time which was fixed by the final order in the appeal haying expired the consequence as directed in the order toot effect and the appeal stood dismissed and according to the well-settled principle as to the exercise of inherent power, as has been noticed above, such power cannot be invoked to interfere with the said appellate decree in contravention of the provision of Order 20, rule 3 of the Code. An exception however to the said proposition has been recognised in a case where the default of a party has been caused due to a mistake of the Court or Court's officer, as was held in a Division Bench decision of the Bangladesh High Court in the case of S. M. Yousuf and another Vs. Khandker Hafizur Rahman and others (1974) 26 DLR 124, which was followed in the cases of the High Court Division referred to above. The law was, in our opinion, correctly stated in this regard in the said case. The failure of the respondent to deposit the amount has not been pleaded in the instant case to have been due to the mistake of the Court or Court's officer. The refusal of the learned Subordinate Judge to entertain the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to accept the deposit in spite of the expiry of the period fixed by the order of the learned Subordinate Judge cannot therefore be said to have been not in accordance with law. So the said order of the learned Subordinate Judge did not suffer from any defects as contemplated in section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Having regard to the said view of the matter the learned Judges of the High Court Division did not rightly exercise their jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code.

In the result the appeal is allowed and the order of the High Court Division is set aside and that of the Subordinate Judge restored but as there is no appearance on behalf of the Respondent there will be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer: Serajul Huq and Amir Hossain, Advocates, instructed by S. M. Huq, Advocate-on-Record ----- for the appellants
parties:
Chairman, Power Development Board & Others
Vs.
Chairman, Labour Court, Khulna Division & Another
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.:- These seven appeals by special leave are directed against an order of the High Court Division dated 11-4-77 summarily dismissing corresponding seven Writ Petitions in which a common Judgment and order of a Labour Court was challenged by the appellants. Earlier, the respondents-workers obtained a favorable order in separate applications under section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969.

2. Chairman and some other Officers of the Power Development Board are the appellants, and the respondents are class III and Class IV employees under the appellants. Respondents are all workers under the relevant Labour Law and their designations are "Line helpers." Their pay scale and allowances were governed by the Modified Pay-scales Power 1964 were of the then East Pakistan Water and Development Authority till November 24, Under the Modified Pay-scale there three classes of employees having their same designation of "Line-helpers" and their pay scales varied according to educational qualification, experience and skill. The experienced 'Line helpers' were given the pay-scale of Tk. 50-70 P.M. whereas the Inexperienced Line-helpers were given the Pay Scale of Tk. 40-50 or 35-50 or Tk. 40-55 P.M. But from 24-11-64 the Modified Pay-scale was replaced by the Revised Pay-scale under which the posts of "Line helpers" were abolished altogether and the incumbents were either redesigned as "Lineman "or" Helper. Those who were In the Pay Scale of Tk. 50-70 under the Modified Pay Scale were designated as Linemen and were given the Revised Scale of Tk. 100-160 P.M. ( From 1969 this revised scale was further raised to Tk. 100-250 ). But those who were in the pay scale of Tk. 40-50 or Tk. 35-50 or Tk. 40-55 under the Modified Pay-scale were designated as "Helpers" and were given the revised pay scale of Tk. 70-105 P.M. The pay-scale of Linemen was entered against serial No. 123 of the WAPDA Pay Manual for Class III and Class IV employees (First Edition) 1967, and that of the "Helpers" against serial No.106 of the same Manual. In the Second Edition the Pay Manual, published in 1969, these two posts were shown in serial No.145 and 123 respectively.

3. Some of the respondents were appointed as "Line helpers" before November, 1964, but even after the introduction of the Revised Pay-scale the Employer continued their designation as Line-helpers. Similarly, those who were appointed after November, 1964 as Helpers were also designated as Line-helpers and these facts were entered in their Service-books although there was no pest like Line-helper sine 1964. This designation' was referred to and retained by the Employer simply for the purpose of identification of the Line or section to which the employees were attached, such as Construction-Line.

4. The respondents, however, claimed the designation as well as the pay-scale of 'Linemen' under the Revised Pay-scale contending that the authorities not only issued an Office Order dated 5-7-72 recognizing their claim but also allowed this scale of Tk.100-250 to one Line helper, Khalilur Rahman. When their claim was rejected they individually filed applications before the Labour Court under Section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 for enforcement of their right to the designation and Pay-scale of Linemen. The Labour Court allowed all these applications by a common judgment and order observing that there should be no discrimination between the Linemen. The High Court Division did not interfere with the Labour Court's order observing that the Pay Manual of East Pakistan WAPDA 1968 clearly laid down the grades of Linemen without any distinction."

5. Leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division correctly interpreted the Revised pay-scale for Class III and Class IV employees of the Water and Power Development Board in respect of the Line helpers, Mr. Serajul Huq, learned Advocate for the petitioners, has referred to the Modified Pay-scale, Revised Pay-scale as shown in the Pay Manual and the actual pay scales to which the respondents were appointed. It appears that there was difference between Line-helpers in respect of their pay before these posts were abolished on November 24, 1964. Prior to this date there were two broad categories of Line helpers, one in the pay-scale of Tk. 50-70 P.M., and the other in the pay-scale of Tk. 40-50 P.M. or near about it. But under the Revised pay-scale the posts of Line helpers were abolished altogether and in their place the posts of Linemen and Helpers were created, the former bearing a higher pay scale of Tk. 100-160 and the latter bearing a pay scale of Tk. 70-105. It also appears that only those Helpers who were in the pay scale of Tk. 50-70 P.M. on November 24, 1964 fell into the category Linemen and those who were in the lower scale automatically fell into the category of Helpers. Of the seven respondents, three were appointed before this target date in the lower-scale of Tk. 40-50 or 35-50, and as such they, under the revised pay scale, fall into the category of Helpers in the pay scale of Tk. 70-105. Similarly, the other four respondents who were appointed after this date were found appointed in the pay-scale of Tk. 70-105 and not in the pay scale of Tk. 100-106 and consequently they can "Linemen" It is true respondents November, claim neither the designation of nor the pay scale of Tk. 100-160. It is true that they along with three other who were appointed before 1964, were allowed the designation of "Line-helper," but there was no post like Line-Helpers in the Revised pay-scale effective from November, 1964, and as such mere entry into the service-books or even in their letters of appointment, of this designation will not entitle them to the pay-scale of Linemen.

6. The employer has of course given an explanation for retaining this designation of Line Helpers although there was no such post, but this action, however, in (sic) innocuous it may be, has created a serious confusion not only among the respondents but also for others who have to deal with the subject. Another confusion was created when the employer first admitted the respondent's claim to the designation and pay of the Linemen by an order dated 5-7-72, though they immediately cancelled it within ten days by another order explaining that the officer concerned miss-appreciated the Revised pay-scale of 1964. Still another confusion was created when one Khalilur Rahman, designated as Line-Helper was allowed the designation and pay scale of Line-men. Mr. Serajul Huq has, however, explained that this was allowed by mistake and when detected, the mistake was corrected and the order was cancelled and further payment was stopped.

<u>7. In view of the discussion made above, it is clearly found that both the High Court Division and the Labour Court miss-appreciated the Revised pay-scale of 1964. That the respondents themselves are not sure of their right to the designation and Pay-scale of Linemen appears from their respective applications under section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance in which they prayed for "establishment" of their right to the designation and pay-scale of Linemen and for enforcement of their right thereafter meant for establishment provides for enforcement guaranteed or secured by Section 34 is not of any right, but it of any existing right, law, award or settlement. The respondents have got no such right secured or guaranteed.</u>

In the result, all the appeals arc allowed, the impugned orders of the High Court and the Labour Court are set aside and the applications under section 34 are dismissed. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Md Sajjad Ali Chowdhury, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Syed Humayun Kabir Khadem, Advocate ----- For the Opposite parties.
parties:
Rafiqul Alarn (Md) ----- Petitioner
VS
Md Abdul Awal & others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
On an application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, this Rule was issued calling upon the Opposite party Nos. 1-9 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 24-2-1997 passed by the Sub-ordinate (now Joint District Judge), First Court, Rangpur in Other Appeal No. 140 of 1995 should not be set aside.

2. The necessary facts found for disposal of this Rule are simple. The present petitioner as plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No. 23 of 1993 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Kaunia, Rangpur for declaration that the letter dated 30-10-1993 signed by the defendant No. 1 dismissing him from service i.e. the post of Office Assistant of Mudamudan High School (shortly, the School) was illegal with a further declaration that he was still in service on the averments, inter cilia, that he was appointed as Office Assistant in the School on 16-6-1979 and since then he had been serving in the School for 14 years. On 8-7-1933, a meeting of the Managing Committee of the School was held and thereafter, it served a notice upon the plaintiff asking him to show cause as to why he should not be dismissed from service. On 24-7-1993, the plaintiff submitted his reply. On 5-8-1993, the said Managing Committee suspended the plaintiff informing him that an enquiry would be held on 18-9-1993. Thereafter, on 10-10-1993, the said Managing Committee issued a letter to the plaintiff asking him to show cause as to why he should not be dismissed from service and file a written objection on or before 17-10-1993. The plaintiff submitted his reply stating that the enquiry was not held properly and prayed for holding the enquiry headed by a Magistrate. But the Managing Committee, without considering the prayer of the plaintiff, informed him by letter dated 31-10-1993 that he was dismissed from service on 21-10-1993 as per Rule 11 of the Non-Government Teachers' Service Rules, 1979 (shortly, the Rules). The plaintiff did not commit any offence under the Rules. Hence, the suit for declaration as mentioned above.

3. Defendant Nos. 1 and 3-10 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. They denied the material allegations made in the plaint. Their positive case is that the plaintiff was not competent for the post of Office Assistant and some charge of misconduct and insubordination was brought against him. A proceeding was held and the enquiry committee submitted a report stating that the charge brought against him was proved. On the basis of enquiry report, the plaintiff was dismissed from service.

4. The learned Assistant Judge framed issues on the pleadings and both the parties adduced evidence thereon. The learned Assistant Judge, on perusal of the evidence on record, found that the charge brought against the plaintiff was not proved and the enquiry committee, without taking any evidence, wrongly submitted its report stating that the charge was proved. Upon these findings, the leaned Assistant Judge decreed the suit. The defendant preferred Other Appeal No. 140 of 1995 against that decree in the Court of District Judge, Rangpur which was heard and disposed of by the Joint District Judge, First Court, Rangpur. The appellate Court found that there was no illegality in dismissing the plaintiff as per enquiry report and the enquiry was held without any procedural defect. On such findings, the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and dismissed the suit by the judgment and decree dated 24-2-1997.

5. Being aggrieved by this judgment and decree dated 24-2-1997, the plaintiff preferred this revision and obtained the Rule in the manner stated above.

6. Mr Md Sajjad Ali Chowdhury, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submitted that the lower appellate Court reversed the finding of the trial Court without discussing the evidence on record and thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He further submitted that the learned Assistant Judge, on proper consideration of evidence on record, found that the enquiry committee without taking any evidence most arbitrarily held that the charge brought against the plaintiff by the managing committee was proved, but the learned Joint District Judge without discussing the evidence reversed this finding of fact arrived at by the learned Assistant Judge and allowed the appeal and thereby committed an error of law. Thus, he submitted that the finding of the lower appellate Court was based on misreading and non-consideration of the materials evidence on record calling for interference by this Court. Thus, Mr Chowdhury submitted that the Rule was liable to be made absolute.

7. On the other hand, Mr Syed Md Humayun Kabir Khadem, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 2, 4 and 8 submitted that the plaintiff was not a teacher, but employee of the School and as such, the Rules were not applicable to him. He further submitted that since the plaintiff was an employee of the private school, the master and servant rule was applicable to him. He further submitted that .under master and servant rule, the servant serves under the master at his pleasure and the master has every authority to dismiss and terminate the servant at any time without showing any cause. Mr Khadem has next submitted that the suit is not maintainable under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act without a prayer for mandatory injunction as the plaintiff is admittedly out of service. In support of his submission he has relied on some decision which I shall advert to later on.

8. On this point of maintainability of the suit under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, in reply, Mr Chowdhury submitted that there was no need of seeking consequential relief, and the declaration as prayed for was enough to maintain the suit. In support of his contention, he has relied on some decisions which I shall consider later on. Mr Chowdhury, however, frankly admitted that the Rules were applicable only to the teachers, and not to the employees of the School. He has also conceded that the master and servant rule was applicable to the plaintiff.

9. Admittedly, the plaintiff has filed the suit for declaration that his dismissal order is illegal with a further declaration that he is still in service.

10. Mr Khadem has referred to the decisions held in the cases of Manager Personal Division vs Sazalian Mirth reported in 35 DLR 224 TCB & ANR vs Syed Sajeduzzaman reported in 40 DLR 406 and BJMC Ltd vs Abdul Halim Chowdhury reported in 47 DLR 173. In the cited cases, the principle of law laid down is that a suit for declaration that plaintiff's dismissal is illegal and not binding upon him without asking for consequential relief for enforcing the declaratory decree is not maintainable and enforceable in law being hit by the proviso to Section 42, of the Specific Relief Act.

11. The cases referred to by Mr Chowdhury are Jiban Bima Corporation vs Mustafa Hussain reported in 50 DLR 411 in which a Single Bench of this Court after considering a good number of cases, including the case reported in 35 DLR 224, has held in the following:

"The declaratory decree passed in a case without any prayer for consequential relief is an "annuity". Such decree is a gain and its implementation is dependent on as to whom the decree is passed against. In the instant case the defendant being a statutory Corporation, there is no reason to believe that such Corporation will not implement the decision of the Court."

12. Mr Chowdhury has referred to another decision held in the case of Fazlul Karim is Agrani Bank, 45 DLR 375 wherein their Lord-ships of a Division Bench of this Court considered various cases, including the case of 35 DLR 224, and held that suit for declaration that the order of removal of the plaintiff, a bank officer, from service was void and inoperative and he remained in service was maintainable without any further relief.

13. The next case cited by Mr Chowdhury is of Tamser Ali vs Md Nazrul Islam, 55 DLR 151 wherein his Lordship of a Single Bench of this Court considered . a good number of cases, including the case of 35 DLR 224 and held that a suit for declaration simplicities in service matter without any prayer for consequential relief is maintainable. The similar view has been taken in the case of Nazir Ahmed vs Province of East Pakistan, 31 DLR 399 as referred to by Mr Chowdhury.

<u>14. I have heard the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides and perused the revision petition and the LCR. There is no dispute that the plaintiff is out of service since his dismissal from service. On perusal of the decisions referred to above, it appears that the views are conflicting on the subject. It is to be noted that the case decisions cited at the Bar relate to service matter out of which only in the case of 47 DLR 173 the relationship between the employer and employee was that of a master and servant. It may be mentioned that the decision reported in 35 DLR 224 was approved by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 299 of 1983. The decision of their Lordships of the Appellate Division is that a suit for declaration that the dismissal order is illegal and that the plaintiff is in service is not maintainable and is hit by the proviso to Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.</u>

<u>15. Mr Chowdhury has failed to show that the cited decision of the Appellate Division passed in the CPLA No. 299 of 1983 has been overruled. This being the position, the same is binding upon this Court. The decision of 35 DLR 224 as approved by the Appellate Division should be followed and the same is fully applicable to the instant case. The decisions referred to by Mr Chowdhury cannot be applied to the instant case as the decision of the Appellate Division in CPLA No. 299 of 1983 is prevailing.</u>

16. Apart from the above discussion, there is a broad legal aspect of the case. It is admitted by both Mr Chowdhury and Mr Khadem that the relationship between the employer-School and the employee-plaintiff was that of a master and servant. Here the decision held in the case of Rupali Bank Ltd vs Md Arab Ali reported in 7 BLC (AD) 1 should get consideration. In that case the relationship between the employer and employee was found that of a master and servant and their Lordships of the Appellate Division, in paragraphs 8 and 10 of the report, held in the following:

"Speaking generally, it is the right of the employer to discharge his employee, and that of the employee to quit his employer's service, subject to the right to pay damages for breach of contract. Courts cannot compel a person, against his will, to employ or serve another, notwithstanding the contract of service. A mandatory injunction cannot. be granted for such purposes.

In view of the legal position as discussed above we need not decide the issue as to whether the dismissal from service in question was illegal, but we must hold that the suit is not maintainable on the ground that a declaratory decree will not be enough and that a decree for mandatory injection necessary as a consequential relief is barred under the law. We, therefore, find that neither the trial Court not the appellate Court nor the High Court Division considered this vital issue which cuts at the root resulting the suit not maintainable as framed. The suit ought to have been dismissed on this issue."

17. From what I have stated above considering the facts, evidence and cited case laws, I am of the view that the decision given by the lower appellate Court is sustainable in law in view of the decision of 7 BLC (AD) 1 referred to above though it did not notice the legal aspect of the case discussed above. Accordingly, I do not find any merit in the Rule, which is liable to be discharged.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree dated 24-2-1997 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Rangpur in Order Appeal No. 140 of 1995 in hereby affirmed.

Send down the LCR accordingly.

End.
